// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["msk"] = {"scleroderma":[[31126,"Systemic sclerosis subtype characteristics","

Systemic sclerosis subtype characteristics

Limited cutaneous

  • Scleroderma on head & distal upper extremities
  • Prominent vascular manifestations
    • Raynaud phenomenon
    • Cutaneous telangiectasia
    • Pulmonary arterial hypertension
  • CREST syndrome
  • Anticentromere antibodies
  • Better prognosis

Diffuse cutaneous

  • Scleroderma on trunk & upper extremities
  • Prominent internal organ involvement
    • Scleroderma renal crisis
    • Myocardial ischemia & fibrosis
    • Interstitial lung disease
  • Anti–Scl-70 (topoisomerase type I) antibodies
  • Anti–RNA polymerase III antibodies
  • Worse prognosis

CREST = Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly & Telangiectasia.

"], [93915,"Scleroderma renal crisis","

Scleroderma renal crisis

Risk factors

  • Diffuse, aggressive skin involvement, tendon friction rubs
  • High-dose glucocorticoid therapy
  • Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies (lower risk with anticentromere antibodies)

Clinical
presentation

  • Acute kidney injury
  • Moderate or severe hypertension/malignant hypertension
  • Proteinuria, normal urine sediment
  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

Management

  • Lower blood pressure to previous baseline in ≤72 hr
  • ACE inhibitors (preferred), dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
    (avoid beta blockers)
"]],"_more":[[31233,"Clinical features","

Distinguishing features of fibromyalgia, polymyositis & polymyalgia rheumatica

Clinical features

Diagnosis

Fibromyalgia

  • Young to middle-aged women
  • Chronic widespread pain
  • Fatigue, impaired concentration
  • Tenderness at trigger points (eg, midtrapezius, costochondral junction)
  • ≥3 months of symptoms with widespread pain index or symptom severity score
  • Normal laboratory studies

Polymyositis

  • Proximal muscle weakness (eg, increasing difficulty climbing stairs)
  • Pain mild/absent
  • Elevated muscle enzymes (eg, creatine kinase, aldolase, AST)
  • Autoantibodies (anti–Jo-1, ANA)
  • Biopsy: endomysial infiltrate, patchy necrosis

Polymyalgia rheumatica

  • Age >50
  • Systemic signs & symptoms
  • Stiffness > pain in shoulders, hip girdle, neck
  • Association with giant cell (temporal) arteritis
  • Elevated ESR, C-reactive protein
  • Rapid improvement with glucocorticoid therapy

ANA = antinuclear antibody; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

"], [31638,"Chronic lymphedema","

Chronic lymphedema

Etiology

  • Physical disruption of lymphatic drainage
    • Lymphadenectomy, radiation
    • Malignant obstruction
    • Chronic inflammation (eg, recurrent cellulitis)
    • Parasitic infection (eg, filariasis)
    • Congenital (eg, Turner syndrome)

Clinical presentation

  • Swelling, heaviness, discomfort
  • Early: soft skin, pitting edema
  • Late: firm, dry & thickened skin; nonpitting edema

Treatment

  • Weight loss, limb elevation
  • Compression bandages & physiotherapy
  • Diuretics contraindicated

"], [34701,"Transient synovitis","

Transient synovitis

Epidemiology

  • Age 3-8
  • Often preceded by viral illness

Clinical features

  • Well-appearing, afebrile or low-grade fever
  • Limp (able to bear weight on affected leg)
  • Hip pain (mildly restricted ROM)

Diagnosis

  • Normal (or minimally elevated) WBC count, ESR, CRP
  • Small effusions on ultrasonography

Management

  • Conservative
  • Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

Prognosis

  • Full recovery within 1-2 weeks
  • Recurrence uncommon

CRP = C-reactive protein; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; ROM = range of motion; WBC = white blood cell.

"], [35760,"Supracondylar fracture","

Supracondylar fracture

Clinical features

  • Fall onto outstretched arm
  • Pain, swelling, limited range of motion

Diagnostic findings

  • X-ray with posterior fat pad (occult), fracture line, or displacement of humerus

Treatment

  • Nondisplaced: long arm splint & sling
  • Displaced: surgical reduction & pinning

Complications

  • Neurovascular injury
  • Compartment syndrome
"], [37187,"Clinical features of stress fracture","

Clinical features of stress fracture

Risk
factors

  • Repetitive activities (eg, running, military marching)
  • Abrupt increase in physical activity volume & intensity
  • Low BMD from inadequate nutrition, malabsorption, estrogen deficiency in women (eg, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea)

Clinical
presentation

  • Insidious, gradual worsening onset of localized pain
  • Point tenderness at fracture site
  • Usually negative x-ray in the first 2-3 weeks

Management

  • Analgesia & reduced weight bearing
  • Referral to orthopedic surgeon for high-risk fracture (eg, anterior tibial cortex, 5th metatarsal)

BMD = bone mineral density.

"], [37429,"Telogen effluvium","

Telogen effluvium

Clinical findings

  • Acute, diffuse, noninflammatory hair loss
  • Scalp & hair fibers appear normal
  • Hair shafts easily pulled out (hair pull test)

Triggers

  • Severe illness, fever, surgery
  • Pregnancy, childbirth
  • Emotional distress
  • Endocrine & nutritional disorders

Management

  • Address underlying cause
  • Reassurance (self-limited disorder)
"], [37778,"Female & male pattern hair loss","

Female & male pattern hair loss

Pathogenesis

  • Follicular miniaturization (shortening of hair growth phase)
  • Men: effect of dihydrotestosterone on genetically susceptible follicles
  • Women: isolated/idiopathic (most cases) or hyperandrogenic states (eg, PCOS)

Clinical features

  • Chronic, progressive hair thinning & shortening
  • Men: vertex, frontal hairline, temporal areas
  • Women: vertex, frontal scalp (spares hairline)

Management

  • Men: finasteride, minoxidil
  • Women: minoxidil

PCOS = polycystic ovarian syndrome.

"], [37888,"Acute septic and nonseptic bursitis","

Acute septic and nonseptic bursitis

Septic bursitis

Nonseptic bursitis

Etiology

  • Inoculation from break in skin or local infection
  • Acute trauma/hemorrhage

Clinical features

  • Superficial bursae (eg, olecranon, prepatellar)
  • Fever
  • Erythema, warmth & tenderness
  • Skin lesions or injury
  • No fever
  • Less prominent erythema, warmth & tenderness
  • Intact skin

Bursal fluid analysis

  • Cloudy/purulent or bloody fluid
  • Fluid/serum glucose ratio <0.5
  • High WBC count (>3,000/mm3) with >50% neutrophils
  • Positive Gram stain
  • Clear or bloody
  • Fluid/serum glucose ratio 0.5-1
  • Variable WBC count (usually <1,500/mm3)

WBC = white blood cell.

"], [40315,"Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy","

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy

Clinical features

  • Pruritic, erythematous plaques in striae
  • Spares periumbilical region
  • Spares face, palms & soles
  • Develops in third trimester

Diagnosis

  • Clinical

Treatment

  • Topical corticosteroids
  • Antihistamines

Prognosis

  • No adverse pregnancy outcomes
  • Resolves immediately postpartum
"], [45197,"Pyoderma gangrenosum","

Pyoderma gangrenosum

Clinical features

  • Begins with small papule or pustule
  • Rapidly progressive, painful ulcer with purulent base & violaceous border
  • Precipitation of ulceration at site of injury (pathergy)

Epidemiology

  • Peak onset age 40-60
  • Women > men
  • Association with inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory (eg, rheumatoid) arthritis, malignancy

Diagnosis

  • Exclusion of other causes of ulceration (eg, infection)
  • Skin biopsy: mixed inflammation (neutrophil predominant)

Treatment

  • Local or systemic glucocorticoids
"], [48756,"Complex regional pain syndrome","

Complex regional pain syndrome

Triggers

  • Trauma: fracture, sprain
  • Surgery

Clinical features

  • Pain: severe, regional (not dermatomal), burning/stinging
  • Edema, abnormal sweating
  • Vasomotor changes, altered skin temperature
  • Trophic skin, hair & nail changes

Diagnosis

  • Primarily based on clinical features
  • X-ray: patchy demineralization
  • Bone scintigraphy: ↑ uptake in affected limb

Management

  • Physical & occupational therapy, exercise
  • Medications: NSAIDs, antineuropathic medications (eg, pregabalin, TCAs)

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; TCAs = tricyclic antidepressants.

"], [50730,"Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (trochanteric bursitis)","

Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (trochanteric bursitis)

Risk factors

  • Age ≥50
  • Women > men
  • Obesity
  • Low back & lower extremity disorders (eg, scoliosis, osteoarthritis, plantar fasciitis)

Symptoms

  • Chronic lateral hip pain
  • Pain worse with hip flexion or lying on affected side

Diagnosis

  • Focal tenderness over trochanter
  • X-ray to rule out hip joint pathology
  • Ultrasound: degeneration of tendons, tendinosis

Treatment

  • Exercise, physical therapy, activity modification
  • Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  • Corticosteroid injection
"], [52576,"Alopecia areata","

Alopecia areata

Pathogenesis

  • Autoimmune attack on hair bulb cells
  • Associated with other autoimmune disorders (eg, hypo/hyperthyroidism, vitiligo)

Clinical presentation

  • Diagnosis made by visual inspection (eg, with dermatoscope)
  • Painless, patchy, nonscarring hair loss affecting scalp, face, or body
  • Exclamation point hairs (small hairs with proximal tapering) may be seen

Management

  • Mild/moderate hair loss: intralesional or topical corticosteroid therapy
  • Extensive hair loss: oral Janus kinase inhibitor (eg, baricitinib) or topical immunotherapy (eg, diphenylcyclopropenone)
  • Screen for autoimmune thyroid disease (serum TSH)

Prognosis

  • Regrowth is common in mild cases
  • Recurrence is common
"], [53598,"Infectious tenosynovitis","

Infectious tenosynovitis

Etiology

  • Direct inoculation: bite/puncture wounds, intravenous drug use
  • Hematogenous spread (eg, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, mycobacteria)

Clinical features

  • Kanavel signs:
    • Fusiform swelling (sausage digit)
    • Slight resting flexion of digit
    • Tenderness along tendon sheath
    • Pain with passive extension

Management

  • Aspiration of tendon sheath for culture
  • Parenteral antibiotics
  • Surgical drainage is often needed
"], [55555,"Management of low back pain","

Management of low back pain

Acute pain (<4 weeks)

  • Maintain moderate activity
  • NSAIDs or acetaminophen
  • Consider: muscle relaxants, spinal manipulation

Subacute pain (4-12 weeks)

Chronic pain (>12 weeks)

  • Intermittent use of NSAIDs or acetaminophen
  • Exercise therapy (stretching/strengthening, aerobic)
  • Consider: tricyclic antidepressants, duloxetine

Secondary prevention

  • Exercise therapy
  • Education

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

"], [61738,"Achilles tendinopathy","

Achilles tendinopathy

Risk factors

  • Athletic activity, increase in activity
  • Systemic disorders: psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis
  • Medications: glucocorticoids, fluoroquinolones

Clinical
features

  • Swelling, warmth, pain at posterior heel
  • Tendon rupture: popping sensation & acute pain following rapid acceleration/direction change

Examination
findings

  • Swelling, tenderness 2-6 cm proximal to tendon insertion
  • Rupture: positive Thompson test*

Diagnosis

  • Clinical findings
  • Ultrasonography: swelling, neovascularization
  • MRI

Management

  • Acute: activity modification, ice, NSAIDs
  • Chronic: eccentric resistance exercises

*With the patient prone and feet off the end of the table, squeeze the calf muscles; the absence of plantar flexion indicates tendon rupture.

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

"], [62028,"Femoral neck fracture","

Femoral neck fracture

Clinical presentation

  • Severe hip pain & inability to bear weight after a fall
  • Risk factors: age >65, frailty, osteoporosis

Examination findings

  • Shortened, externally rotated leg
  • Painful range of motion
  • Ecchymosis

X-ray findings

  • Disruption of cortical contour
  • External rotation of distal fragment (prominence of lesser trochanter profile)
  • Shortening of neck
  • Lucency or hazy sclerosis at fracture plane

Management

  • Open reduction/internal fixation or arthroplasty
"], [62043,"Acute glenohumeral dislocation","

Acute glenohumeral dislocation

Mechanism
of injury

  • Blow to abducted/raised arm
  • Fall on outstretched hand
  • Violent muscle contraction (eg, seizure)

Clinical
features

  • Anterior dislocation: arm held in abduction/external rotation, anterior prominence of humeral head
  • Posterior dislocation: arm held in adduction/internal rotation, loss of anterior contour, prominence of coracoid & acromion

Management

  • Closed reduction (uncomplicated), surgical repair
  • Immobilization & progressive rehabilitation

Complications

  • Fracture (glenoid, proximal humerus, clavicle)
  • Rotator cuff injury
  • Recurrent dislocation
"], [62044,"Posterior shoulder dislocation","

Posterior shoulder dislocation

Mechanism

  • Forceful adduction/internal rotation
  • Fall on an outstretched hand
  • Extreme muscle contraction (eg, seizure, electrocution)

Clinical
findings

  • Arm held in adduction, internal rotation
  • Loss of normal anterior shoulder contour
  • Prominence of coracoid & acromion

Complications

  • Humerus fracture
  • Glenoid rim fracture
  • Rotator cuff tear

Management

  • Uncomplicated: closed reduction
  • Complicated: consider surgical repair
"], [62741,"Septic bursitis","

Septic bursitis

Risk factors

  • Local cellulitis, abrasions, or penetrating trauma
  • Bursal instrumentation/injection, prior bursal inflammation
  • Immunocompromised state

Presentation

  • Painful, localized bursal swelling with erythema & warmth
  • ± Fever, chills, myalgias

Diagnosis

  • Consider diagnostic aspiration of bursal fluid
  • Consider x-ray (for suspected fracture, foreign body, or osteomyelitis)

Treatment

  • Systemic antibiotics
  • Drainage in select cases
"], [64412,"Isotretinoin","

Isotretinoin

Indications

  • Severe inflammatory acne (eg, nodular)
  • Moderate inflammatory acne that forms scars or is treatment resistant

Mechanism of action

  • Normalizes follicular epithelial proliferation & desquamation
  • Decreases sebum production
  • Inhibits Cutibacterium acnes proliferation & inflammation

Adverse effects

  • Teratogenic
  • Pseudotumor cerebri
  • Hypertriglyceridemia
  • Transaminase elevation
  • Dry skin or mucous membranes
  • Acne fulminans (initial worsening of acne)

Laboratory monitoring

  • Pregnancy test
  • Liver function test
  • Lipid panel
"], [66161,"Hidradenitis suppurativa","

Hidradenitis suppurativa

Pathogenesis

  • Disordered folliculopilosebaceous units:
    • Ductal keratinocyte proliferation → follicular occlusion → follicular rupture → inflammation
  • Risk factors: smoking, metabolic syndrome (eg, obesity, diabetes mellitus)

Clinical
presentation

  • Chronic & recurrent lesions in intertriginous areas
  • Mild: painful nodules, draining abscesses
  • Moderate: sinus tracts & scarring
  • Severe: extensive sinus tracts, widespread disease

Treatment

  • Mild: topical clindamycin
  • Moderate: oral tetracycline
  • Severe: tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitors (eg, adalimumab), surgical excision

Complications

  • Depression & suicide
  • Squamous cell carcinoma of skin

"], [71768,"Benign neonatal rashes","

Benign neonatal rashes

Diagnosis

Onset

Clinical features

Management/resolution

Erythema toxicum neonatorum

  • Birth to age 3 days
  • Erythematous macules/papules that progress to pustules on trunk & proximal extremities
  • Observation
  • Resolves within a week

Milia

  • Birth
  • Firm, white papules on face
  • Observation
  • Resolves within a month

Miliaria rubra

  • Any age, but not present at birth
  • Erythematous, papular rash on occluded & intertriginous areas
  • Avoid overheating (eg, cool environment, thin/cotton clothing)
  • If severe, topical corticosteroid

Neonatal pustular melanosis

  • Birth
  • Nonerythematous pustules → evolve into hyperpigmented macules with collarette of scale
  • Diffuse, may involve palms & soles
  • Observation
  • Pustules resolve within days
  • Hyperpigmentation may last months

Neonatal cephalic pustulosis

  • Around age 3 weeks
  • Erythematous papules & pustules on face & scalp only
  • Observation
  • Resolves in weeks to months
  • If severe, topical corticosteroid or ketoconazole
"], [72304,"Hydrofluoric acid burns","

Hydrofluoric acid burns

Characteristics
of HF

  • Highly corrosive, lipophilic
  • Widely used (eg, glass etching, cleaning solutions)

Clinical features

  • Local injury: deep tissue damage
  • Possible systemic effects
    • Hypomagnesemia & hypocalcemia
    • Cardiac arrhythmias

Management

  • Copious irrigation & topical calcium gluconate gel
  • Possible intradermal, intraarterial &/or IV calcium gluconate
  • Cardiac & electrolyte monitoring

HF = hydrofluoric acid; IV = intravenous.

Pathophysiology

  • Autoimmune recognition of hidden epitopes (type II collagen, proteoglycans)

"]],"vascular-tumors-of-skin--infantile-hemangioma":[[31290,"Infantile hemangioma","

Infantile hemangioma

Natural history

  • Appears days to weeks after birth
  • Proliferation (age 0-12 months): growth of bright red, soft, raised plaque
  • Involution (age >12 months): deep red/violet lesion that regresses in size

Evaluation

  • Clinical diagnosis
  • Special considerations:
    • ≥5 cutaneous lesions → liver ultrasonography
    • Facial/segmental → echocardiography & MRI of the head (ie, PHACE)
    • Cervicofacial (beard distribution) → laryngoscopy
    • Lumbosacral → spinal ultrasonography

Management

  • Observation for most lesions
  • Beta blocker therapy (eg, propranolol) for high-risk features:
    • Large, facial, segmental, &/or rapidly growing (ulceration/scarring)
    • Periorbital (visual impairment)
    • Hepatic (high-output heart failure)
    • Subglottic (airway obstruction)

PHACE = Posterior fossa anomalies, Hemangioma, Arterial anomalies, Cardiac anomalies, Eye anomalies.

"], [61260,"Hypermetabolic response in burn injury","

Hypermetabolic response in burn injury

Etiology

  • Moderate to severe burn injury (eg, inhalational, high-voltage electrical, TBSA >20%)
  • ↑ Inflammatory mediators, which result in ↑ catecholamines, glucocorticoids & glucagon

Clinical features

  • Hyperdynamic circulatory response: tachycardia, hypertension
  • ↑ Gluconeogenesis & insulin resistance: hyperglycemia
  • ↑ Basal metabolic rate: ↑ basal body temperature
  • ↑ Protein & lipid catabolism: ↑ lean muscle wasting

Treatment

  • Early burn excision & grafting
  • Beta blockade (eg, propranolol)
  • Glycemic control (eg, insulin)
  • Nutritional support & anabolic steroid therapy (eg, oxandrolone)

TBSA = total body surface area.

(eg, alendronate,
risedronate)

  • First-line treatment for most patients
  • Taken with water on an empty stomach an hour before food & other medications
  • Not recommended for patients with renal impairment

  • Risk of infection & skin reactions

  • Modest reduction in fracture risk
  • Reduces pain from fracture

receptor modulators
(eg, raloxifene)

  • Less effective than bisphosphonates
  • May lower risk of breast cancer
  • Increased risk of DVT

Systemic symptoms

  • Jaw claudication: most specific symptom of GCA
  • PMR

  • Aortic wall thickening or aneurysms
  • CNS: TIAs/stroke, vertigo, hearing loss

Visual symptoms

  • Amaurosis fugax: transient vision field defect progressing to monocular blindness
  • AION: most common ocular manifestation

Laboratory results

  • Elevated ESR & CRP

  • GCA: high-dose oral glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone 40-60 mg daily)

Common causes of subacute/chronic heel pain in adults

Condition

History

Physical Examination

Plantar fasciitis

  • Sharp, localized medial plantar heel pain
  • Worse with first steps in morning or after inactivity
  • Typically improves with movement
  • Tenderness at medial calcaneal tubercle
  • Pain with passive toe dorsiflexion

Achilles tendinopathy

  • Posterior heel pain and stiffness, typically 2-6 cm above insertion
  • Worsens with activity, improves with rest.
  • Tenderness, thickening, and possible crepitus along tendon

Retrocalcaneal bursitis

  • Posterior heel pain anterior to Achilles
  • Worsens with dorsiflexion or tight shoes
  • Swelling and tenderness over retrocalcaneal bursa
  • May have palpable bony prominence (Haglund deformity).

Calcaneal stress fracture

  • Gradual onset of deep heel pain
  • Worsens with weight-bearing & impact activity
  • Diffuse calcaneal tenderness
  • Pain with heel squeeze or hopping

Tarsal tunnel syndrome

  • Burning, tingling, or radiating heel/plantar foot pain or numbness
  • Typically worse at night & with prolonged standing
  • Tinel sign over tarsal tunnel
  • Sensory loss or paresthesia in tibial nerve distribution

Heel fat pad syndrome

  • Heel pain worsened by walking barefoot or on hard surfaces
  • Often in older adults
  • Tenderness on plantar heel
  • Diminished fat pad on palpation
"]],"primary-bone-tumors--osteoid-osteoma":[[41342,"Osteoid osteoma","

Osteoid osteoma

  • Benign nidus of unmineralized osteoid that produces prostaglandins

  • No systemic symptoms

Management
& prognosis

"]],"primary-bone-tumors-continued--osteosarcoma-osteogenic-sarcoma":[[41405,"Osteosarcoma vs Ewing sarcoma","

Osteosarcoma

Ewing sarcoma

Epidemiology

features

"], [108335,"Osteosarcoma","

"]],"vasculitides--buerger-disease-thromboangiitis-obliterans":[[43301,"Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)","

"], [87544,"Acute compartment syndrome of the extremity","

Acute compartment syndrome of the extremity

Pathophysiology

  • ↑ Pressure within enclosed fascial space
  • ↓ Blood flow & tissue perfusion

Common causes

  • Crush injury, long bone fracture, rhabdomyolysis
  • Reperfusion after prolonged ischemia
  • Massive fluid resuscitation

Clinical features

  • Early:
    • Progressive, severe pain
    • Rapidly ↑ & tense swelling
    • ↑ Pain with passive stretching
    • Paresthesia
  • Late:
    • ↓ Sensation
    • Weakness (within hours), paralysis (late)
    • Loss of pulses (uncommon)

Management

  • Compartment pressure measurement* can confirm diagnosis
  • Emergency fasciotomy

*Delta pressure (diastolic pressure − compartment pressure) ≤30 mm Hg is consistent with compartment syndrome.

"], [60192,"Growing pains (idiopathic nocturnal pains of childhood)","

"]],"raynaud-phenomenon":[[52673,"Raynaud phenomenon","

Raynaud phenomenon

Primary

Secondary

Etiology

  • Idiopathic response to cold or stress
  • Risk factors include CVD, smoking
  • Vasoconstriction due to vascular pathology
  • Causes: autoimmune disease (eg, systemic sclerosis), drugs (eg, amphetamines), trauma (eg, frostbite)

Clinical
presentation

  • Young; predominantly female
  • Symmetric attacks
  • Normal examination & laboratory results
  • Older (>40); male & female
  • Asymmetric attacks
  • Examination/laboratory results: tissue injury (eg, digital ulcers), abnormal nail fold capillaries, autoimmune antibodies (eg, ANA)

Management

  • Nonpharmacologic: warming techniques, smoking cessation, stress reduction
  • Medication: CCB (first-line), PDE-5 inhibitor (second-line)
  • Evaluate & treat underlying disorder
  • Same medications as for primary RP
  • Consider aspirin if increased risk for digital ulceration

ANA = antinuclear antibody; CCB = calcium channel blocker; CVD = cardiovascular disease; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; PDE-5 = phosphodiesterase type 5; RP = Raynaud phenomenon.

"]],"avascular-necrosis-of-bone":[[52715,"Avascular necrosis","

  • Alcohol abuse

Laboratory findings

  • Normal white blood cell count

Radiologic imaging

  • Crescent sign seen in advanced stage
  • MRI is most sensitive modality

CRP = C-reactive protein; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

"]],"wrist-and-hand-injuries":[[60858,"Clenched-fist bite injury (fight bite)","

Clenched-fist bite injury (fight bite)

Mechanism

  • Puncture through thin soft tissue overlying MCP joint
  • Enclosed bacterial proliferation under extensor tendon & within joint capsule

Pathogens

  • Oral flora (eg, Eikenella corrodens, beta-lactamase–producing anaerobes)

  • Antibiotics (eg, ampicillin-sulbactam [IV], amoxicillin-clavulanate [PO])

"]],"vasculitides--polyarteritis-nodosa":[[60880,"Polyarteritis nodosa","

Polyarteritis nodosa

  • Constitutional: fever, weight loss, malaise
  • Skin: nodules, livedo reticularis, ulcers, purpura

  • Musculoskeletal: myalgias, arthritis

  • Negative ANCA & ANA

  • Tissue biopsy: nongranulomatous transmural inflammation

Natural course

  • Growth until physeal closure (skeletal maturity)
"]],"common-skin-disorders--rosacea":[[118629,"Treatment of rosacea","

Treatment of rosacea

General measures

  • Avoid sun, hot/spicy foods, alcohol
  • Gentle cleansers & emollients

Papules/pustules

  • Mild/moderate: topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, ivermectin
  • Moderate/severe: oral tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline

Telangiectasia

  • Laser therapy

Facial erythema

  • Topical brimonidine, oxymetazoline
  • Laser therapy

Phymatous changes

  • Oral isotretinoin
  • Laser therapy, surgery

Ocular manifestations

  • Ophthalmology consultation
  • Lid scrubs, topical or systemic antibiotic therapy

"]],"vasculitides-continued--small-vessel-vasculitis":[[120316,"ANCA-associated vasculitis","

ANCA-associated vasculitis

ANCA pattern

Histopathology

Organ involvement

 

GPA

  • Mainly c-ANCA (anti-proteinase-3)
  • Neutrophils, granulomas & fibrinoid necrosis
  • Necrotizing sinusitis
  • Cavitary lung lesions & DAH
  • RPGN
 

EGPA

  
  • Mainly p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase)
  • Eosinophils, granulomas & fibrinoid necrosis
  • Allergic sinusitis & polyps
  • Asthma
  • Broadest involvement (eg, RPGN, myocarditis, cutaneous nodules, mononeuritis multiplex)

MPA

  • Neutrophils & fibrinoid necrosis (no granulomas)
  • RPGN
  • DAH

ANCA = antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies; DAH = diffuse alveolar hemorrhage; EGPA = eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; GPA = granulomatosis with polyangiitis; MPA = microscopic polyangiitis; RPGN = rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

"]],"achondroplasia":[[127086,"Achondroplasia","

Achondroplasia

Pathogenesis

De novo or autosomal dominant FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation → decreased endochondral ossification (skeletal dysplasia)

Clinical features

Short stature with rhizomelia (proximal limb shortening)

Craniofacial abnormalities:

  • Macrocephaly with frontal bossing
  • Midface hypoplasia

Normal cognition

Diagnosis

Molecular genetic testing

FGFR3 = fibroblast growth factor receptor 3.

"]],"cutaneous-ulcers":[[127477,"Clinical characteristics of common lower extremity ulcers","

Clinical characteristics of common lower extremity ulcers

Ulcer type

Common locations

Clinical features

Associated findings

Arterial (ischemic)

Tips of toes, lateral malleoli, heels

  • Painful (worse at night, with elevation)
  • Pale or necrotic base
  • Punched-out edges
  • Diminished or absent pulses
  • Prolonged capillary refill
  • Cool, shiny, hairless skin

Venous (stasis)

Medial lower leg  (above medial malleolus)

  • Moderately painful (better with elevation)
  • Shallow, irregular border
  • Serous drainage
  • Intact pulses
  • Hyperpigmented, thickened skin/stasis dermatitis
  • Edema
  • Varicosities

Neuropathic

Feet, under bony prominences (eg, metatarsal head)

  • Painless
  • Well-defined, punched-out edges
  • Surrounding callus
  • Intact pulses
  • Dry, cracked skin
  • Loss of protective sensation
"]],"igg4-related-disease":[[132165,"IgG4-related disease","

IgG4-related disease

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic generalized lymphadenopathy
  • Autoimmune pancreatitis, sclerosing cholangitis
  • Thyroid disease (eg, Riedel thyroiditis, fibrous Hashimoto)
  • Retroperitoneal fibrosis
  • Bilateral salivary &/or lacrimal gland involvement

Diagnosis

  • Elevated IgG4 levels (nonspecific, markers of disease severity)
  • Biopsy with characteristic triad: IgG4-positive lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis

Management

  • Immunosuppression with glucocorticoids (rapid improvement)
"]]};

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["endo"] = {"syndrome-of-inappropriate-antidiuretic-hormone-secretion":[[31070,"Classification of hyponatremia","

Classification of hyponatremia

Serum osmolality

ECV

Urine findings

Causes

Hypotonic (<275 mOsm/kg)

Hypovolemic

UNa <40 mEq/L

  • Nonrenal salt loss (eg, vomiting, diarrhea)

UNa >40 mEq/L

  • Renal salt loss (eg, diuretics, primary adrenal insufficiency)

Euvolemic

UOsm <100 mOsm/kg

  • Primary polydipsia
  • Malnutrition (eg, beer potomania)

UOsm >100 mOsm/kg & UNa >40 mEq/L

  • SIADH*

Hypervolemic

Variable

  • Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome

Isotonic

Variable

  • Pseudohyponatremia (eg, paraproteinemia, hyperlipidemia)

Hypertonic (>295 mOsm/kg)

  • Translocational hyponatremia (eg, hyperglycemia, exogenous solutes such as mannitol)

*Hypothyroidism & secondary adrenal insufficiency should be ruled out.

ECV = extracellular volume; SIADH = syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; UNa = urine sodium; UOsm = urine osmolality.

"], [34700,"Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone","

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone

Etiologies

  • CNS disturbance (eg, stroke, hemorrhage, trauma)
  • Medications (eg, carbamazepine, SSRIs, NSAIDs)
  • Lung disease (eg, pneumonia)
  • Ectopic ADH secretion (eg, small cell lung cancer)
  • Pain &/or nausea

Clinical
features

  • Mild/moderate hyponatremia: nausea, forgetfulness
  • Severe hyponatremia: seizures, coma
  • Euvolemia (eg, moist mucous membranes, no edema, no JVD)

Laboratory
findings

  • Hyponatremia
  • Serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg H2O (hypotonic)
  • Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg H2O
  • Urine sodium >40 mEq/L

Management

  • Fluid restriction ± salt tablets
  • Hypertonic (3%) saline for severe hyponatremia

ADH = antidiuretic hormone; JVD = jugular venous distension; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

"], [79876,"Common causes of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion","

Common causes of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

  • CNS disruptions (eg, stroke, infection, trauma, neurosurgery)
  • Malignancies (eg, small cell lung carcinoma)
  • Drugs (eg, desmopressin, chlorpropamide, carbamazepine)
  • Pulmonary disorders (eg, pneumonia, tuberculosis, ventilator use)
"], [106529,"Thiazide-induced hyponatremia","

Thiazide-induced hyponatremia

Pathogenesis

  • ↓ Water excretion (ADH-dependent & ADH-independent mechanisms)
  • ↑ Water intake (natural tendency to polydipsia)

Risk factors & presentation

  • Advanced age (mean age >75), female, low BMI
  • Typically within few weeks of therapy or after acute event (eg, diarrhea)
  • Patients often euvolemic with subtle symptoms (eg, confusion)

Treatment

  • Discontinue thiazide

"], [119899,"Major considerations influencing selection of pharmacotherapy in T2DM","

Major considerations influencing selection of pharmacotherapy in T2DM

Weight

  • GLP-1 RA (± GIP): weight loss (followed by SGLT-2i & metformin)
  • Insulin, sulfonylureas, TZDs: weight gain

ASCVD

  • Metformin: primary prevention (reduced CVD events, mortality)
  • GLP-1 RA, SGLT-2i: secondary prevention in patients with ASCVD (reduced stroke, CVD events, mortality)

Heart failure

  • SGLT-2i: secondary prevention in patients with ASCVD (reduced heart failure hospitalizations, mortality)
  • TZDs: higher risk of heart failure

Nephropathy & kidney disease

  • SGLT-2i: reduction in DKD progression (most benefits for GFR >45 mL/min/1.73 m2)
  • GLP-1 RA: possible renoprotection in patients with ASCVD
  • Metformin: renoprotective with tight glycemic control

Nonalcoholic hepatic steatosis

  • TZDs: reduction in progression of disease; may not be feasible due to adverse effects (eg, heart failure, fluid retention)

Chronic kidney disease (nondialysis)

  • Sulfonylureas (short-acting), DPP-4 inhibitors, insulin & potentially GLP-1 RA: appropriate for safety & glycemic control (rather than organ-specific benefits)
  • SGLT-2: selective use may have renoprotective benefits (but minimal effects on glycemic control)
  • Avoid metformin

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; CVD = cardiovascular disease; DKD = diabetic kidney disease; DPP-4 = dipeptidyl peptidase-4; GFR = glomerular filtration rate; GIP RA = glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide receptor agonists; GLP-1 RA = glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists; SGLT-2i = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor; T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus; TZD = thiazolidinediones.

"], [119914,"SGLT-2 inhibitors","

SGLT-2 inhibitors

Mechanism of action

  • Increase urinary excretion of glucose (block SGLT-2 in proximal tubule, reducing glucose reabsorption)
  • Induce osmotic diuresis, leading to weight loss
  • Induce natriuresis, leading to decreased extracellular volume, reduced cardiac preload/afterload

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • Reduced progression of proteinuria & nephropathy
  • Reduced cardiovascular morbidity & mortality
  • Reduced heart failure hospitalizations
  • Moderate weight loss

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Genitourinary infections
  • Euglycemic ketoacidosis in states that increase glucagon secretion (eg, fasting, illness)
  • Decreased effectiveness with impaired renal function
  • Orthostatic hypotension

Precautions & contraindications

  • Concomitant diuretic use (may require dose reduction or discontinuation)
  • Severely reduced GFR (<30-45 mL/min/1.73 m2)
  • DKA

DKA = diabetic ketoacidosis; GFR = glomerular filtration; SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2.

Diabetic ketoacidosis

Patient characteristics

  • Young age
  • Brittle type 1 diabetes mellitus
  • May be initial manifestation of diabetes

Clinical symptoms

  • Acute to subacute onset
    • Initial: polydipsia/polyuria, blurred vision, weight loss

"], [87381,"Management of diabetic ketoacidosis","

Management of diabetic ketoacidosis

Fluids

  • Initial: give isotonic intravenous fluids
  • Subsequent:
    • Continue isotonic fluids if serum Na+ <135 mEq/L
    • Switch to half normal saline if serum Na+ ≥135 mEq/L
    • Add dextrose when serum glucose <200 mg/dL

Insulin

  • Reduce insulin infusion rate when serum glucose <200 mg/dL
  • Hold insulin infusion if serum K+ <3.3 mEq/L
  • Switch to subcutaneous insulin on DKA resolution*

Potassium

  • Give replacement when serum K+ <5.3 mEq/L**

Bicarbonate

  • Consider replacement for severe DKA with blood pH ≤6.9

*Normalization of anion gap & patient able to eat.

**Due to total body potassium depletion and risk of insulin-induced hypokalemia.

DKA = diabetic ketoacidosis.

Major considerations influencing selection of pharmacotherapy in T2DM

Weight

  • GLP-1 RA, SGLT-2i, metformin associated with weight loss
  • Insulin, sulfonylureas, TZDs associated with weight gain

ASCVD

  • Metformin: primary prevention (reduced CVD events, mortality)
  • GLP-1 RA, SGLT-2i: secondary prevention in patients with ASCVD (reduced stroke, CVD events, mortality)

Heart failure

  • SGLT-2i: secondary prevention in patients with known ASCVD (reduced hospitalizations, mortality) 
  • TZDs: higher risk for heart failure

Nephropathy and kidney disease

"]],"hyperthyroidism--graves-disease":[[80896,"Neonatal Graves disease","

Neonatal Graves disease

Pathophysiology

  • Transplacental passage of maternal TSH receptor–stimulating antibodies (due to maternal Graves disease)
  • Antibodies bind to infant's TSH receptors & cause excessive thyroid hormone release → neonatal thyrotoxicosis

Clinical features

  • Tachycardia & irritability
  • Warm, moist skin
  • Low birth weight or preterm birth
  • ± Goiter, stare

Diagnosis

  • Maternal & neonatal TSH receptor–stimulating antibodies
  • ↓ TSH, ↑ free thyroxine

Treatment & outcome

  • Methimazole plus β blocker
  • Usually self-resolves within months (due to clearance of maternal antibodies)
"], [96214,"Choice of treatment in Graves disease","

Choice of treatment in Graves disease

Antithyroid drugs

  • Preferred in patients with limited life expectancy
  • May induce remission in mild hyperthyroidism
  • May be used as pretreatment prior to radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy (eg, high-risk patient, severe hyperthyroidism)

Radioactive iodine

  • Acceptable option for moderate hyperthyroidism
  • May initially worsen ophthalmopathy & hyperthyroid symptoms (increases TRAb)
  • Leads to permanent hypothyroidism over time

Thyroidectomy

  • Preferred in patients with very large goiter, obstructive symptoms, or ophthalmopathy
  • Potential complications from injury to parathyroids (eg, hypocalcemia, hypoparathyroidism) &/or laryngeal or vagus nerve (eg, hoarseness)

TRAb = thyrotropin receptor antibodies.

Clinical features of thyroid storm

Precipitating factors

  • Thyroid or nonthyroidal surgery
  • Acute illness (eg, trauma, infection), childbirth
  • Acute iodine load (eg, iodine contrast)

Clinical presentation

  • Fever as high as 40-41.1 C (104-106 F)
  • Tachycardia, hypertension, congestive heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias (eg, atrial fibrillation)
  • Agitation, delirium, seizure, coma
  • Goiter, lid lag, tremor, warm & moist skin

Treatment

  • β Blocker (eg, propranolol) to ↓ adrenergic manifestations
  • PTU followed by iodine solution (SSKI) to ↓ hormone synthesis & release

  • Identify trigger & treat, provide supportive care

PTU = propylthiouracil; SSKI = potassium iodide.

"], [119906,"Sulfonylureas","

Sulfonylureas

Mechanism of action

  • Directly stimulate pancreatic beta cells to produce insulin
  • Glucose-independent effect

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • Moderate-high A1c reduction (~1%-2%)
  • Rapid glucose-lowering effects
  • Low cost

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Hypoglycemia (older, frail populations)
  • Weight gain (due to increased insulin secretion)
  • Possible CVD risk (eg, increased heart failure)
  • No mortality benefits

Precautions & contraindications

  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Sulfonamide allergy
  • Hypoglycemia (more liberal A1c target advised)

A1c = hemoglobin A1c; CVD = cardiovascular disease.

"]],"hyperparathyroidism--primary-hyperparathyroidism":[[114906,"Primary hyperparathyroidism surgical indications","

Primary hyperparathyroidism surgical indications

Parathyroidectomy is indicated for patients with ≥1 of the following*:

  • Symptoms of hypercalcemia
  • Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above upper limit of normal
  • Age <50
  • Bone mineral density T-score less than −2.5 or prior vertebral fracture on imaging
  • eGFR <60 mL/min
  • 24-hour urinary calcium >250-300 mg or evidence of nephrocalcinosis on imaging

*Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia should be excluded prior to surgery.

eGFR = estimated glomerular filtration rate.

"]],"type-1-vs-type-2-diabetes-mellitus--type-2":[[119797,"Modifiable risk factors for development of T2DM","

Modifiable risk factors for development of T2DM

Obesity

  • Visceral fat (central adiposity) appears to drive risk for insulin resistance
  • Decreases insulin sensitivity, increases circulation of inflammatory cytokines

Dietary factors

  • Sugary beverages and heavy consumption of foods high in saturated fat (eg, red meats) 
  • Low fruit, vegetable, and fiber intake

Sleep deprivation

  • Impairs insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism

Sedentary behavior

  • Associated with intramuscular lipid accumulation and insulin resistance

Mood disorders (eg, depression)

  • Associated with increased baseline cortisol, chronic inflammation, visceral fat 
  • Influences lifestyle behaviors associated with T2DM risk

T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus.

"], [119798,"Medical conditions associated with increased risk of T2DM","

Medical conditions associated with increased risk of T2DM

Disorders increasing systemic inflammation or insulin resistance

  • Cardiovascular diseases 
  • Metabolic syndrome*
  • Polycystic ovarian syndrome
  • Cushing syndrome
  • Chronic kidney disease 

Disorders impairing pancreatic function

  • Hemochromatosis
  • Pancreatic insufficiency 

Diseases requiring chronic use of drugs, causing diabetes

  • HIV (antiretrovirals)
  • Psychosis (atypical antipsychotics)
  • Rheumatic disorders (glucocorticoids, certain immunosuppressants [eg, tacrolimus])
  • Certain cancers (immune checkpoint inhibitors)

*Drugs associated with treatment (eg, statins for hyperlipidemia, thiazides for hypertension) are also associated with increased risk for T2DM.

T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus.

"]],"adrenal-insufficiency--secondary-and-tertiary-adrenal-insufficiency":[[119801,"No risk","

Risk of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal suppression with chronic glucocorticoid therapy

No risk
(No perioperative stress-dose steroids required)

  • Daily morning dose of prednisone <5 mg (or its equivalent) for any period
  • Any dose of any glucocorticoid for <3 weeks
  • Prednisone 10 mg (or its equivalent) every other day

Intermediate or unknown risk
(Preoperative evaluation of HPA axis recommended)

  • Daily morning dose of prednisone 5-20 mg (or its equivalent) for >3 weeks
  • Daily evening doses of prednisone <5 mg (may disrupt diurnal variation)
  • Prior longer duration or higher doses of glucocorticoids in the past year
  • Inhaled glucocorticoids for >3 weeks, or ≥3 intraarticular or spinal glucocorticoid injections within past 3 months

High risk
(Stress-dose glucocorticoids recommended during perioperative period)

  • Daily prednisone ≥20 mg (or its equivalent) for >3 weeks
  • Any patient taking glucocorticoids who has Cushingoid features (eg, buffalo hump, central obesity, moon face, weight gain)
"]],"diabetes-mellitus-therapy-continued--metformin":[[119904,"Biguanides (eg, metformin)","

Biguanides (eg, metformin)

Mechanism of action

  • Reduce hepatic gluconeogenesis by inhibiting mitochondrial enzymes
  • Increase insulin sensitivity by upregulating AMPK
  • Reduce lipolysis & free fatty acid concentrations

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • Moderate-high A1c reduction (~1%-2%)
  • Mild weight loss
  • Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease & mortality
  • Lower cost, wide availability

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Diarrhea, bloating (avoid by titrating dose)
  • Lactic acidosis (rare risk), B12 deficiency (longstanding use)

Precautions & contraindications

  • Conditions predisposing to lactic acidosis:
    • Severe infection
    • Renal failure, decompensated heart failure
    • Alcohol use disorder
  • Decreased fluid intake (consider temporary discontinuation)

A1c = hemoglobin A1c; AMPK = AMP-activated protein kinase.

"]],"diabetes-mellitus-therapy-continued--pioglitazone":[[119910,"Thiazolidinediones","

Thiazolidinediones

Mechanism of action

  • Increase insulin sensitivity by activating PPAR-γ
  • Upregulate genes involved in glucose transport & fatty acid oxidation

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • Low A1c reduction (~0.5%-1%)
  • Possible reduction in NASH progression
  • No risk for hypoglycemia

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Weight gain & fluid retention
  • Possible increase in CVD risk (eg, heart failure) in high-risk patients
  • Peripheral edema, macular edema
  • Fracture

Precautions & contraindications

  • Heart failure
  • Macular edema
  • Osteoporosis
  • Severe liver disease (not NASH)

CVD = cardiovascular disease; NASH = nonalcoholic steatohepatitis; PPAR = peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor.

"]],"diabetes-mellitus-therapy-continued--dpp-4-inhibitors":[[119911,"DPP-4 inhibitors","

DPP-4 inhibitors

Mechanism of action

  • Inhibit enzyme responsible for degradation of GLP-1
  • Indirectly potentiate GLP-1 effects
    • Decreased gut motility
    • Increased glucose-dependent pancreatic insulin secretion
  • Modest A1c reduction (~1%)

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • No risk for hypoglycemia

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Decreased effectiveness compared to GLP-1 RA due to indirect effects (weight neutral, no ASCVD benefits)
  • Possible increased risk for heart failure (saxagliptin)
  • Adverse effects (eg, nasopharyngitis, pancreatitis)

Precautions & contraindications

  • Pancreatitis

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; DPP-4 = dipeptidyl peptidase-4; GLP-1 RA = glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist.

"]],"diabetes-mellitus-therapy-continued--glp-1-analogs":[[119912,"GLP-1 receptor agonists","

GLP-1 receptor agonists

Mechanism of action

  • Mimic incretin effects of GLP-1
  • Increases pancreatic insulin release in response to oral food intake (glucose-dependent effect)
  • Slow gut motility, increased satiety
  • Additive effects when combined with GIP RA

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • High A1c reduction (~2%)
  • Weight loss
  • No associated hypoglycemia
  • Secondary prevention of ASCVD, mortality, possible renoprotection
  • Potential alternative if insulin cannot be used (T2DM only)

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Significant gastrointestinal distress (gastroparesis, pancreatitis)
  • Possible retinopathy (eg, semaglutide)
  • Evidence of primary prevention of ASCVD/mortality lacking

Precautions & contraindications

  • Medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2A/2B
  • History of gastroparesis or pancreatitis
  • Severe kidney impairment (<30-45 mL/min/1.73 m2)

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; GIP RA = glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide receptor agonist; GLP-1 = glucagon-like peptide 1; MEN = multiple endocrine neoplasia; T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus.

"]],"appetite-regulation":[[121550,"Hypothalamic centers and effects on appetite","

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["renal"] = {"pyelonephritis":[[31274,"Pyelonephritis in pregnancy","

Pyelonephritis in pregnancy

Risk factors

  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Age <20

Common
pathogens

  • Escherichia coli (most common)
  • Klebsiella
  • Enterobacter
  • Group B Streptococcus

Complications

  • Preterm labor
  • Low birth weight
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome

Treatment

  • Intravenous antibiotics
  • Supportive therapy
"], [60028,"Renal abscess","

Renal abscess

Risk factors

  • Pyelonephritis, complicated UTI
  • Renal calculi
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Anatomic abnormality (eg, tumor, PKD)
  • Pregnancy

Clinical

features

  • Fever, chills
  • Flank &/or abdominal pain
  • No improvement after 48-72 hr of broad-spectrum antibiotics

Diagnosis

  • Renal ultrasound
  • CT scan of abdomen

Treatment

  • Intravenous antibiotics
  • +/− Drainage

PKD = polycystic kidney disease; UTI = urinary tract infection.

"]],"acute-cystitis":[[33450,"Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome)","

Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome)

Epidemiology

  • More common in women
  • Associated with psychiatric & pain disorders (eg, fibromyalgia)

Clinical presentation

  • Bladder pain with filling, relief with voiding
  • ↑ Urinary frequency, urgency
  • Dyspareunia

Diagnosis

  • Bladder pain with no other cause for ≥6 weeks
  • Normal urinalysis

Treatment

  • Not curative; focus is on improving quality of life
  • Behavioral modification, avoidance of triggers, physical therapy
  • Amitriptyline, pentosan polysulfate sodium
  • Analgesics for acute exacerbations
"], [82103,"Urine dipstick results in","

Urine dipstick results in urinary tract infection

Result

Pathophysiology

Clinical significance

Leukocyte esterase

  • Released by lysed neutrophils/macrophages
  • Marker of white blood cells

Nitrites*

  • Produced by conversion of urinary nitrate into nitrite by nitrate reductase
  • Marker of nitrate reductase–producing bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus mirabilis)

pH

  • Alkaline urine (pH >8) due to ammonia produced from hydrolysis of urea by urease
  • Marker of urease-producing bacteria (eg, Proteus mirabilis)

*The absence of nitrites does not exclude these bacteria.

"], [91455,"Acute cystitis","

Acute cystitis

Microbiology

  • Escherichia coli (most common)
  • Other gram-negative pathogens (eg, Proteus spp., Klebsiella spp.)
  • Staphylococcus saprophyticus

Clinical features

  • Dysuria
  • Increased urinary frequency and/or urgency
  • Suprapubic tenderness

Diagnosis

  • Urinalysis with pyuria (WBC > 10 cells/mm3), bacteria & positive leukocyte esterase and/or nitrites
  • Urine culture for organism identification & susceptibility

Empiric treatment

Oral antibiotics

  • Nitrofurantoin* 100 mg BID × 5 days
  • Fosfomycin 3 grams × 1 dose
  • Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim DS 1 tablet BID × 3 days (if no sulfa allergy)
*Contraindicated if creatinine clearance is < 60 mL/min.

DS = double-strength; WBC = white blood cells.

"]],"renal-cyst-disorders--simple-vs-complex-renal-cysts":[[35217,"Characteristics of renal cysts","

Characteristics of renal cysts

Simple renal cyst

Malignant cystic mass

Thin, smooth, regular wall

Thick, irregular wall

Unilocular

Multilocular

No septae

Multiple septae, occasionally thick & calcified

Homogenous content

Heterogenous content (solid & cystic)

Absence of contrast enhancement on CT/MRI

Presence of contrast enhancement on CT/MRI

Usually asymptomatic

May cause pain, hematuria, or hypertension

No follow-up needed

Requires follow-up imaging & urological evaluation for malignancy

"]],"acute-tubular-necrosis":[[37199,"Laboratory features of rhabdomyolysis","

Laboratory features of rhabdomyolysis

Muscle
enzymes

  • Elevated CK (often >10,000 U/L)

Urine tests

  • Red to brown urine with positive blood but no RBCs (myoglobinuria)

Electrolytes

  • Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia & hyperuricemia due to intracellular electrolyte release
  • Hypocalcemia & dehydration due to influx of calcium & intravascular fluid into injured muscles

Creatinine

  • AKI due to tubular injury from myoglobinuria
  • FENa can be falsely low

AKI = acute kidney injury; CK = creatine kinase; FENa = fractional excretion of sodium; RBCs = red blood cells.

"], [38385,"Contrast-associated acute kidney injury","

Contrast-associated acute kidney injury

Presentation

  • Highest risk with arterial iodinated contrast (eg, coronary angiogram)
  • Creatinine elevation 24-48 hr after contrast exposure, gradually returning to baseline within 3-7 days
  • Clinical diagnosis based on timing & trajectory above (ie, biopsy rarely needed)

Risk factors

  • Preexisting chronic kidney disease (especially diabetic nephropathy)
  • Decreased kidney perfusion (eg, NSAIDs, hypovolemia, venous congestion)
  • High contrast load

Pathophysiology

  • Prerenal vasoconstriction & direct tubular cytotoxicity
  • Prerenal state (eg, FeNa <1%) with concurrent necrosis (eg, muddy brown casts)

Prevention

  • Optimize kidney perfusion (eg, intravenous saline, avoidance of NSAIDs)
  • Minimize contrast load

FeNa = fractional excretion of sodium; NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

"], [49988,"Rhabdomyolysis","

Rhabdomyolysis

Etiology

Skeletal muscle lysis/necrosis due to:

  • Crush injury or prolonged immobilization
  • Intense muscle activity (eg, seizure, exertion)
  • Drug/medication toxicity (eg, statins)

Clinical features

  • Muscle pain & weakness
  • Dark urine (myoglobinuria/pigmenturia)
  • + Blood on urinalysis & no RBCs on microscopy
  • ↑ Serum K & PO4, ↓ serum Ca, ↑ AST > ALT
  • Acute kidney injury

Diagnosis

  • Serum creatine kinase >1,000 U/L
  • Consistent clinical features

Management

  • Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation
  • Sodium bicarbonate in some cases

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; RBCs = red blood cells.

"]],"electrolyte-disturbances--potassium":[[38457,"Medication-induced hyperkalemia","

Medication-induced hyperkalemia

Medication

Mechanism

ACE inhibitors & ARBs

↓ Aldosterone secretion (↓ AT II production; block AT II receptor)

NSAIDs

↓ Renin secretion → ↓ aldosterone

↓ Renal perfusion → ↓ distal Na+ delivery →  ↓ ENaC activity

Potassium-sparing
diuretics

Inhibit ENaC (eg, amiloride) or aldosterone receptor (eg, spironolactone)

Heparin

↓ Aldosterone production

Trimethoprim

Inhibits ENaC (similar to amiloride)

Cyclosporine

Blocks aldosterone activity

Nonselective
β-blockers

Interfere with β2-mediated intracellular K+ uptake

Digoxin

Inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase

Succinylcholine

Causes extracellular leakage of K+ through acetylcholine receptors

ARBs = angiotensin II receptor blockers; AT = angiotensin; ENaC = epithelial sodium channel; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

"]],"renovascular-disease":[[42060,"Renal artery stenosis","

Renal artery stenosis

Etiology

  • Atherosclerotic narrowing of the renal artery (>90% of cases)
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia (younger women)

Risk factors

  • Other atherosclerotic disease (eg, CAD, carotid stenosis)
  • Smoking, diabetes, hypertension

Presentation

  • Refractory hypertension
  • Recurrent flash pulmonary edema
  • Abdominal bruits
  • Acute kidney injury after initiation of ACE inhibitor

Pathology

  • Gross: Shrunken, atrophic kidney
  • Microscopic: Crowded glomeruli, tubular atrophy, interstitial
    fibrosis, focal inflammatory infiltrates

CAD = coronary artery disease.

"]],"kidney-stones":[[42288,"Risk & prevention of kidney stones","

Risk & prevention of kidney stones

Stone type

Risk factors

Prevention

Calcium stones

(oxalate, phosphate)

  • Hypercalciuria (eg, hyperparathyroidism)
  • Hyperoxaluria (eg, malabsorption,
    low-calcium diet)
  • Hypocitraturia (eg, distal RTA)
  • Diet: ↑ sodium, ↑ protein, ↑ oxalate, 
    ↓ calcium
  • Reduce sodium, animal protein, oxalate intake
  • Increase potassium intake; moderate calcium intake
  • Thiazide diuretics

Uric acid

  • Gout
  • Myeloproliferative disorders
  • Urine alkalinization
  • Allopurinol

Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite)

  • Recurrent upper urinary infection
    (eg, Klebsiella, Proteus)
  • Stone removal
  • Suppressive antibiotics

All types

  • Dehydration
  • Increase fluid intake

RTA = renal tubular acidosis.

"]],"electrolyte-disturbances--magnesium":[[42295,"Magnesium toxicity","

Magnesium toxicity

Clinical
features

  • Mild: nausea, flushing, headache, hyporeflexia
  • Moderate: areflexia, hypocalcemia, somnolence
  • Severe: respiratory paralysis, cardiac arrest

Treatment

  • Stop magnesium therapy
  • Give IV calcium gluconate bolus
"]],"acid-base-physiology--metabolic-acidosis":[[42521,"Anion gap metabolic acidosis","

Anion gap metabolic acidosis

Calculation

Anion gap = sodium − (chloride + bicarbonate)
(normal: 10-14 mEq/L)

Common causes
(mnemonic: MUDPILES)

  • Methanol
  • Uremia
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis
  • Propylene glycol/paraldehyde
  • Isoniazid/iron

"]],"acid-base-physiology--metabolic-alkalosis":[[59288,"Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis","

Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis

Common etiologies

  • Gastric suction or severe vomiting
  • Loop or thiazide diuretic overuse

Pathophysiology

  • Gastric or renal H+ losses initiate alkalosis
  • Volume depletion activates RAAS
  • ↑ Renal K+ & H+ losses cause hypokalemia & worsen alkalosis
  • Relatively greater loss of Cl− than Na+ → profound Cl− depletion
  • ↓ Cl− impairs renal HCO3− excretion to perpetuate alkalosis

Management

  • Remove or treat initiating factor
  • Cl− replenishment with normal saline corrects alkalosis

RAAS = renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

"]],"hydronephrosis":[[77848,"Urinary tract obstruction","

Urinary tract obstruction

Common
etiologies

Clinical
presentation

"]],"nephrotic-syndrome--diabetic-glomerulonephropathy":[[80594,"Typical features of diabetic kidney disease","

Typical features of diabetic kidney disease

Major findings

  • Persistent albuminuria (>3 months duration)
  • Initial hyperfiltration followed by progressive decline in GFR
  • Hypertension usually present

Typical course

  • Gradual onset
    • ≥5 years after type 1 DM diagnosis
    • May be present at diagnosis in type 2 DM
  • Slow progression

Atypical features

Consider renal biopsy & additional evaluation if any of the following is present:

  • Early onset (<5 years after type 1 DM diagnosis)
  • Rapid progression:
    • >5-10× increase in albuminuria in <1-2 years
    • >5 mL/min/1.73 m2 decline in GFR per year
  • Active urinary sediment (eg, white or red blood cell casts)
  • Comorbid conditions associated with glomerulonephritis (eg, SLE)

DM = diabetes mellitus; GFR = glomerular filtration rate; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.

"], [119805,"Characteristics warranting further work-up* in diagnosis of DKD","

Characteristics warranting further work-up* in diagnosis of DKD

  • Active urinary sediment (eg, red blood cell casts, dysmorphic red blood cells, white blood cell casts)
  • Rapidly declining renal function and/or acute, severe rise in proteinuria (eg, over <1-2 years)
  • Initial presentation of severely increased albuminuria <5 years after onset of T1DM
  • Comorbid autoimmune disorder suggesting possible alternate etiology (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus)
  • Significant urinary symptoms (eg, postvoid dribbling, dysuria)

*Renal biopsy, ultrasonography.

DKD = diabetic kidney disease; T1DM = type 1 diabetes mellitus.

"]],"nephrotic-syndrome":[[92943,"Complications of nephrotic syndrome*","

Complications of nephrotic syndrome*

Mechanism

Hypercoagulability
(↑ thromboembolism risk)

  • Urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins (eg, antithrombin III)
  • Hepatic synthesis of prothrombotic proteins (eg, fibrinogen)

Hyperlipidemia
(↑ atherosclerosis risk)

  • Hepatic synthesis of lipoproteins

Infection
(particularly encapsulated bacteria)

  • Urinary loss of immunoglobulins & opsonizing factors

Protein malnutrition

  • Negative nitrogen balance

Intravascular volume depletion

  • Low oncotic pressure

*Nephrotic syndrome results from glomerular filtration barrier (eg, podocyte) injury that leads to heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia & peripheral edema.

"]],"nephrotic-syndrome--membranous-nephropathy":[[93754,"Membranous nephropathy","

  • Primary: testing for anti-PLA2R antibodies**
  • Secondary: testing for underlying disease (eg, cancer screening, virus testing, ANA testing); kidney biopsy

  • Supportive measures for all (eg, ACE inhibitor, diuretic)
  • Primary:
    • Low risk: observation (spontaneous remission common)
    • Moderate to high risk: immunosuppression
  • Secondary: treatment of underlying disease, discontinuation of culprit medication

*Generalized edema, heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) & hypoalbuminemia.

**Kidney biopsy not needed when anti-PLA2R antibodies are present, kidney function is normal & evidence of secondary disease is absent.

Renal cell carcinoma

Epidemiology

  • Males > females, age ≥60

Clinical

manifestations

  • Asymptomatic (incidental finding)
  • Hematuria
  • Flank pain
  • Palpable abdominal mass
  • Left-sided varicocele that does not compress
  • Paraneoplastic syndromes (eg, polycythemia, ↑ calcium)

Risk factors

  • Smoking, obesity, hypertension
  • Toxins (eg, asbestos, trichloroethylene)
  • Genetic disorders (eg, von Hippel-Lindau disease, sickle cell anemia)
  • Acquired polycystic kidney disease
  • Analgesics (eg, aspirin, acetaminophen)
  • Hepatitis C

Diagnosis and

treatment

  • Abdominal CT scan
  • Partial or complete nephrectomy (for histology)

Effects on glomerular filtration rate (GFR) & renal blood flow (RBF)

Arteriole tone change

GFR

RBF

Mechanism

Example

Afferent constriction

↓

↓

Less blood enters glomerulus → ↓ GHP → ↓ filtration

SNS

Efferent constriction

↑ (mild)

↓ (severe)

↓

Mild constriction ↑ GFR by ↑ GHP, but severe constriction ↓ RBF so much that GFR eventually drops

Angiotensin II*

Afferent dilation

↑

↑

More blood enters glomerulus → ↑ GHP → ↑ filtration

Prostaglandins (eg, PGE2), ANP

Efferent dilation

↓

↑

Blood exits glomerulus more easily → ↓ GHP → ↓ filtration

Nitric oxide**

* At low levels, there is preferential efferent arteriole constriction, increasing GFR.  At high levels, both afferent & efferent arterioles are constricted, decreasing GFR.
** Specific effects on GFR and RBF can vary depending on balance with other vasoconstrictors.

ANP = atrial natriuretic peptide; GHP = glomerular hydrostatic pressure; SNS = sympathetic nervous system.

"], [37670,"Nocturnal asthma–like symptoms","

Nocturnal asthma–like symptoms

True nocturnal
asthma

  • Symptoms usually 2:00 to 4:00 AM
  • Awakenings with cough & wheezing
  • Responds to albuterol or step-up in asthma therapy

Gastroesophageal
reflux disease

  • Frequent regurgitation symptoms (worse at night)
  • Awakenings with heartburn
  • Possible cough & wheezing
  • Responds to trial of proton pump inhibitor

Obstructive
sleep apnea

  • Difficulty maintaining sleep & daytime sleepiness
  • Awakenings with gasping & choking sensation
  • Goes away on awakening

Upper airway
cough syndrome

  • Daytime rhinorrhea or allergic symptoms
  • Awakenings with cough
  • Responds to intranasal corticosteroids
"], [41998,"Common triggers of asthma","

Common triggers of asthma

Inhaled allergens

  • Animal dander
  • Dust mites & cockroaches
  • Pollens & molds

Respiratory irritants

  • Cigarette smoke & air pollutants
  • Perfumes

Medications

  • Aspirin/NSAIDs
  • Nonselective ꞵ blockers

Other

  • Upper respiratory tract infection
  • Exercise & cold, dry air
  • Gastroesophageal reflux disease

NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

"], [77698,"Fatal asthma: risk factors","

Fatal asthma: risk factors

Patient history

  • Prior respiratory failure: NIPPV, intubation, ICU admission
  • Poor asthma control: ↑ inhaler use, frequent oral corticosteroids or acute care visits

Clinical status (impending respiratory failure)

  • Examination: respirations >30/min, SaO2 ≤90%, accessory muscle use, AMS, "silent chest"
  • ABG: ↑ or inappropriately normal PaCO2 relative to WOB
  • Peak flow: ≤50% of baseline

ABG = arterial blood gas; AMS = altered mental status; ICU = intensive care unit; NIPPV = noninvasive positive pressure ventilation; SaO2 = arterial saturation of oxygen; WOB = work of breathing.

"], [94400,"Asthma risk factors","

Asthma risk factors

Perinatal

  • Family history of asthma*
  • Prematurity

Childhood

  • Atopy* (eg, eczema, allergies)
  • RSV in infancy
  • Air pollution, secondhand smoke

Adolescence/adulthood

  • Obesity
  • Active smoking
  • Occupational exposures
    (eg, pesticides, cleaning products)

*Significant risk factor.

RSV = respiratory syncytial virus.

"]],"pleural-effusions--exudate":[[31497,"Parapneumonic effusions","

Parapneumonic effusions

Uncomplicated

Complicated

Etiology

Sterile exudate in pleural space

Bacterial invasion of pleural space

Radiologic
appearance

Small to moderate & free flowing

Moderate to large, free flowing
or loculated

Pleural fluid characteristics

  • pH ≥7.2
  • Glucose ≥60 mg/dL
  • WBCs ≤50,000/mm3
  • LDH ≤1,000 units/L
  • pH <7.2
  • Glucose <60 mg/dL
  • WBCs >50,000/mm3
  • LDH >1,000 units/L

Pleural fluid
Gram stain & culture

Negative

Positive or negative*

Treatment

Antibiotics

Antibiotics & drainage

*Gram stain & culture are often falsely negative due to low bacterial count.  Both are typically positive in empyema, which represents advanced progression of a complicated effusion.

LDH = lactate dehydrogenase; WBC = white blood cell.

"], [33472,"Pleural effusion glucose concentration","

Pleural effusion glucose concentration

Low*
(pleural fluid/serum glucose ratio <0.5)

  • Tuberculosis
  • Malignancy
  • Complicated parapneumonic
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Esophageal rupture

High
(pleural fluid/serum glucose ratio ~1)

  • Transudative effusions
  • Uncomplicated parapneumonic
  • Other infection (eg, viral)
  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Post–coronary artery bypass grafting

*Likely due to high pleural fluid glucose consumption by inflammatory, malignant &/or bacterial cells.

"]],"methemoglobin":[[31706,"Clinical presentation of methemoglobinemia","

Clinical presentation of methemoglobinemia

History

  • Exposure to oxidizing substances (eg, dapsone, nitrites,
    local/topical anesthetic)

Clinical examination

  • Cyanosis
  • Pulse oximetry saturation ~85%
  • Dark chocolate–colored blood

Laboratory findings

  • Saturation gap (>5% difference between oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry & ABG)
  • Normal PaO2

ABG = arterial blood gas.

"], [58954,"Acquired methemoglobinemia","

Acquired methemoglobinemia

Precipitating factors

  • Dapsone
  • Local/topical anesthetics (eg, benzocaine, teething medications)
  • Nitrates/nitrites (eg, drinking ground water)

Pathophysiology

  • Oxidation of heme iron from Fe2+ to Fe3+
  • Fe3+ unable to bind oxygen
  • Oxygen affinity of other hemes increased → left shift → decreased tissue oxygen delivery

Clinical manifestations

  • Cyanosis (not improved with supplemental O2)
  • Chocolate-brown blood (no color change on exposure to air/oxygen)
  • Pulse oximetry inaccurate → reads near 85% due to absorption wavelength

Management

  • Methylene blue
"]],"cyanide-vs-carbon-monoxide-poisoning--carbon-monoxide":[[31861,"Carbon monoxide poisoning","

Carbon monoxide poisoning

Epidemiology

  • Smoke inhalation
  • Defective heating systems
  • Gas motors operating in poorly ventilated areas

Manifestations

Mild-moderate

  • Headache, confusion
  • Malaise, dizziness, nausea

Severe

  • Seizure, syncope, coma
  • Myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias

Diagnosis

  • ABG: carboxyhemoglobin level
  • ECG ± cardiac enzymes

Treatment

  • High-flow 100% oxygen
  • Intubation/hyperbaric oxygen (severe)

ABG = arterial blood gas.

"], [57363,"Carbon monoxide poisoning","

Carbon monoxide poisoning

Epidemiology

  • Smoke inhalation
  • Defective heating systems
  • Gas motors operating in poorly ventilated areas

Manifestations

  • Mild to moderate
    • Headache, confusion
    • Malaise, dizziness, nausea
  • Severe
    • Seizure, syncope, coma
    • Myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias

Diagnosis

  • ABG: carboxyhemoglobin level
  • ECG ± cardiac enzymes

Treatment

  • High-flow 100% oxygen
  • Intubation/hyperbaric oxygen (severe)

ABG = arterial blood gas.

"]],"sleep-apnea--obstructive-sleep-apnea":[[32918,"STOP-Bang survey for obstructive sleep apnea","

STOP-Bang survey for obstructive sleep apnea

1 point for each characteristic present

  • Snoring
  • Excessive daytime tiredness
  • Observed apneas or choking/gasping
  • High blood pressure
  • BMI >35 kg/m2
  • Age >50
  • Neck size: men >17 in (43.2 cm), women >16 in (40.6 cm)
  • Male gender

Scoring: 0-2 points: low risk; 3-4 points: intermediate risk; ≥5 points: high risk.

"], [34760,"Clinical characteristics of obstructive sleep apnea","

Clinical characteristics of obstructive sleep apnea

Symptoms/signs

  • Insomnia, nonrestorative sleep, daytime somnolence
  • Witnessed apneas ± snoring
  • Mood changes, cognitive deficits, impaired concentration, fatigue
  • Morning headaches
Potential sequelae
  • Resistant hypertension
  • Angina pectoris
  • Cardiac dysrhythmias
  • Pulmonary hypertension & cor pulmonale
  • Polycythemia
  • Decreased libido & impotence
Diagnosis
  • Polysomnography
"], [55545,"Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea","

Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea

Pathophysiology

  • Adenotonsillar hypertrophy

Clinical manifestations

  • Night symptoms
    • Loud snoring, pauses in breathing, gasping
    • Enuresis, parasomnias (eg, sleepwalking, sleep terrors)
  • Day symptoms
    • Inappropriate naps or falling asleep during school
    • Irritability, inattention, learning problems, behavioral problems
    • Mouth breathing, nasal speech

Complications

  • Poor growth (ie, failure to thrive)
  • Poor school performance
  • Cardiopulmonary (eg, hypertension, structural heart changes)

Management

  • Tonsillectomy & adenoidectomy
"], [57140,"Obstructive sleep apnea","

Obstructive sleep apnea

Pathophysiology

  • Relaxation of pharyngeal muscles, leading to closure of airway
  • Loud snoring with periods of apnea

Symptoms

  • Daytime somnolence
  • Nonrestorative sleep with frequent awakenings
  • Morning headaches
  • Affective & cognitive symptoms

Sequelae

  • Systemic hypertension
  • Pulmonary hypertension & right heart failure
"]],"pleural-effusions":[[33396,"Exudative & transudative pleural effusions","

Exudative & transudative pleural effusions

Exudate

Transudate

Light criteria

Pleural protein/serum protein >0.5

OR

Pleural LDH/serum LDH >0.6

OR

Pleural LDH >2/3 upper limit of normal of serum LDH

Exudate criteria not met

Pathophysiology

Inflammatory disruption of vascular permeability

Change in hydrostatic or oncotic pressure

Common causes

  • Infection (eg, TB, pneumonia)
  • Malignancy
  • Rheumatologic disease (eg, RA, SLE)
  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Pancreatitis
  • Post-CABG
  • Heart failure
  • Cirrhosis (hepatic hydrothorax)
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Constrictive pericarditis

CABG = coronary artery bypass grafting; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase; RA = rheumatoid arthritis; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus; TB = tuberculosis.

"], [63261,"Empyema","

Empyema

Etiology

  • Bacterial invasion of pleural space resulting in fibrinopurulent consolidation
  • Usually due to progression of a complicated parapneumonic effusion

Common
organisms

  • Oral anaerobic bacteria (likely most common)
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus

Clinical
features

  • Symptoms of pneumonia (eg, fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain)
  • Insidious presentation (eg, 1-2 weeks or more), weight loss
  • Laboratory evidence of inflammation (eg, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis)

Management*

  • Chest tube drainage when possible
  • Intrapleural fibrinolytic drugs (eg, tPA/DNase) may assist drainage
  • Surgical decortication for highly fibrotic, loculated effusions

*In addition to antibiotics.

tPA/DNase = tissue plasminogen activator/recombinant deoxyribonuclease.

"]],"pulmonary-emboli":[[34582,"+3 points","

Modified Wells criteria for pretest probability
of pulmonary embolism

+3 points

  • Clinical signs of DVT
  • Alternate diagnosis less likely than PE

+1.5 points

  • Previous PE or DVT
  • Heart rate >100/min
  • Recent surgery or immobilization

+1 point

  • Hemoptysis
  • Cancer

Total score

  • ≤4 = PE unlikely
  • >4 = PE likely

DVT = deep vein thrombosis; PE = pulmonary embolism.

"], [87336,"Pulmonary embolism management","

Pulmonary embolism management

Classification

Definition

Typical management

Low risk

  • No RV dysfunction
 
  • No hypotension (SBP ≥90 mm Hg)
  • Anticoagulation unless contraindicated

Submassive

  • RV dysfunction (dilation &/or hypokinesis)
    • Higher risk: elevated biomarkers (troponin I &/or BNP)
 
  • No hypotension
  • Individualized strategies ranging from anticoagulation to tailored (eg, catheter-directed) thrombolysis if higher risk

Massive

  • RV dysfunction
 
  • Hypotension (SBP <90 mm Hg)
  • Systemic thrombolysis &/or embolectomy

BNP = B-type natriuretic peptide; RV = right ventricle; SBP = systolic blood pressure.

"]],"sarcoidosis":[[34697,"Manifestations of sarcoidosis","

Manifestations of sarcoidosis

Pulmonary

  • Bilateral hilar adenopathy
  • Interstitial infiltrates

Cutaneous

  • Papular, nodular, or plaquelike lesions
  • Erythema nodosum

Ophthalmologic

  • Anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis or iritis)
  • Posterior uveitis
  • Keratoconjunctivitis sicca

Reticuloendothelial

  • Peripheral lymphadenopathy
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Splenomegaly

Musculoskeletal

  • Acute polyarthritis (especially ankles)
  • Chronic arthritis

Cardiovascular

  • Atrioventricular block
  • Dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy

CNS/endocrine

  • Facial nerve palsy
  • Central diabetes insipidus
  • Hypercalcemia

Löfgren syndrome

  • Erythema nodosum
  • Hilar adenopathy
  • Migratory polyarthralgia
  • Fever
"], [97708,"Sarcoidosis organ involvement & recommended treatment","

Sarcoidosis organ involvement & recommended treatment

System

Indications for systemic corticosteroids

Indications for additional therapies

Lungs

  • Abnormal PFT
  • Dyspnea
  • Cough or wheezing (ICS)

Skin

  • Disfiguring plaques or nodules
  • Lupus pernio
  • Erythema nodosum (NSAIDs)

Musculoskeletal

  • Arthritis
  • Myositis & myopathy
  • Arthralgias (NSAIDs)

Cardiac

  • Infiltrative cardiomyopathy
  • Conduction system disease
  • Dysrhythmias (ICD, pacemaker)

CNS

  • Neuropathy (eg, facial nerve [CN VII] palsy)
  • Encephalopathy
  • Hypopituitarism (hormone replacement)

Eyes

  • Uveitis

Other

  • Symptomatic hypercalcemia

Any organ-threatening disease unresponsive to corticosteroids

  • MTX, anti-TNF-α agents

ICS = inhaled corticosteroid; MTX = methotrexate; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; PFT = pulmonary function test; TNF-α = tumor necrosis factor-alpha.

"], [119640,"Pulmonary sarcoidosis staging","

Pulmonary sarcoidosis staging

Stage

"], [132938,"Venous vs arterial air embolism","

Feature

Venous air embolism (VAE)

Arterial air embolism (AAE)

  • Arterial system → end-organ ischemia (brain, heart)

  • High-flow O2

Classification

  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO group 1)

  • Due to chronic thromboembolic disease (group 4)

"]],"obstructive-lung-diseases--chronic-obstructive-pulmonary-disease":[[37449,"Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease","

Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Precipitants

  • Infectious (70%): respiratory viruses (eg, rhinovirus) & commensal bacteria (eg, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae)
  • Noninfectious (30%): sterile inflammation (underlying disease), pulmonary embolism, inhaled irritants

Pathophysiology
& presentation

  • Bronchial inflammation: systemic response (eg, fever, leukocytosis) usually absent
  • Cardinal symptoms: ↑ dyspnea, ↑ sputum volume, ↑ sputum purulence
  • ↑ WOB (hyperinflation) & impaired gas exchange (hypoxemia [↓ V/Q], hypercapnia [↑ VD])

Management

  • Maximize expiratory flow: inhaled bronchodilators
  • Reduce airway inflammation: systemic glucocorticoids
  • Treat underlying triggers: ± antibiotics* &/or antivirals (influenza, COVID-19)
  • Maintain adequate oxygenation: SpO2 target 88%-92%
  • Maintain adequate ventilation: NIPPV or invasive mechanical ventilation

*Antibiotics generally indicated if (1) there is increased sputum purulence + ≥1 other cardinal symptoms or (2) patient requires hospitalization.

NIPPV = noninvasive positive pressure ventilation; VD = alveolar dead space ventilation; V/Q = ventilation/perfusion ratio; WOB = work of breathing.

"], [93058,"Management of stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease","

Management of stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Nonpharmacologic

  • Smoking cessation*
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation*
  • Vaccination (influenza*, pneumococcal, COVID-19)
  • Long-term oxygen therapy* if SaO2 ≤88% at rest
  • Nocturnal noninvasive ventilation if daytime hypercapnia*

Surgical

  • Lung volume reduction or lung transplantation for advanced disease*

Medications

  • Bronchodilators (LAMA, LABA) ± ICS
  • Long-term macrolide (eg, azithromycin 3× weekly)**
  • PDE4 inhibitor (eg, roflumilast)**

"], [69013,"Acute respiratory distress syndrome: pathogenesis & diagnosis","

Acute respiratory distress syndrome: pathogenesis & diagnosis

Risk factors &
pathogenesis

  • Direct (eg, pneumonia, inhalation) or indirect (eg, sepsis, pancreatitis, trauma) lung injury
  • Inflammatory cell activation & ↑ permeability ↔ fluid & cytokine leakage into alveoli

Pathophysiology

  • ↓ Lung compliance (alveolar flooding) → ↑ work of breathing
  • Severe V/Q mismatch (intrapulmonary shunt) → severe hypoxemia
  • ↑ Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → ↑ RV afterload & acute PHTN

Diagnosis

  • New bilateral alveolar opacities within 1 week of inciting insult
  • Edema not explained by cardiac failure or volume overload
  • Hypoxemia with PaO2/FiO2 ≤300
PHTN = pulmonary hypertension; RV = right ventricular; V/Q = ventilation/perfusion.
"], [69591,"Acute respiratory distress syndrome: management & prognosis","

Acute respiratory distress syndrome: management & prognosis

Mechanical ventilation

  • Lung protection: limit alveolar distending volume (VT 6 mL/kg) & pressure (Pplat ≤30 cm H2O)
  • Ventilation: tolerate permissive hypercapnia (ie, ↑ PaCO2 & ↓ pH acceptable) to avoid excessive VT
  • Oxygenation: set lowest feasible FiO2 (goal SpO2 92%-96%) to avoid O2 toxicity

Supportive care

  • Treat underlying etiology: source control (eg, sepsis)
  • Prevent iatrogenic harm: negative fluid balance, timely extubation (eg, minimize sedation)
  • ± Corticosteroids: select patients with moderate-to-severe early ARDS

Prognosis

  • Mortality rate: 40% in hospital, death mostly due to multiorgan failure
  • Morbidity rate: 50% with chronic cognitive impairment & physical debility, 25% with chronic pulmonary dysfunction (restriction & ↓ DLCO)

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; DLCO = diffusion capacity of lung for carbon monoxide; Pplat = plateau pressure; SpO2 = oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry; VT = tidal volume.
