"]],"alveolar-gas-equation":[[92554,"Alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient calculation: worked example","

Alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient calculation: worked example

48-year-old woman with emphysema
ABGs: pH 7.34, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, PaO2 50 mm Hg

Step 1

Calculate PiO2

  • PiO2 is the inspired oxygen that reaches the alveoli
  • Determined by atmospheric pressure (Patm), water vapor (PH2O) & FiO2 (21% at room air)

►Patient's PiO2 = (Patm − PH2O) × (FiO2) = (760 − 47) × (0.21) = 150 mm Hg

Step 2

Calculate PAO2

  • PAO2 is the oxygen in the alveolar airspace after admixture with CO2
  • Each molecule of O2 occupies the same space as 0.8 molecules of CO2

►Patient's PAO2 = PiO2 − PaCO2 / 0.8 = 150 − 60 / 0.8 = 150 − 75 = 75 mm Hg

Step 3

Calculate A-a gradient

  • Difference between PAO2 (calculated above) & PaO2 (from ABG analysis)
  • Elevated by a damaged alveolar membrane (eg, emphysema) or by right-to-left shunt

►Patient's A-a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2 = 75 − 50 = 25 mm Hg

Step 4

Compare to normal

  • Small A-a gradient is normal due to physiologic right-to-left shunting (eg, bronchial arteries)
  • Expected A-a gradient ~ age / 3 = 48 / 3 = 16 mm Hg

►Patient's A-a gradient is elevated (25 > 16)

ABG = arterial blood gas.

"]],"pancoast-tumor":[[96228,"Pancoast (superior pulmonary sulcus) tumors","

Pancoast (superior pulmonary sulcus) tumors

Anatomy

  • Lung apex: characteristic symptoms from invasion of nearby structures
  • Peripheral lung: pulmonary symptoms (eg, cough, hemoptysis) usually late findings

Clinical features (invaded structures)

  • Pancoast syndrome
    • Shoulder pain (brachial plexus, ribs &/or pleura)
    • Horner syndrome* (sympathetic chain)
    • Hand weakness/atrophy (brachial plexus)
  • Other findings
    • Potential emergencies**: paraplegia (spinal cord), face/arm edema (SVC)
    • Hoarseness (RLN), hemidiaphragm paresis (phrenic nerve), supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (metastasis)

Pathology

  • <5% of all lung cancers: non–small cell (95%), small cell (5%)

*Ptosis, miosis & anhidrosis.

**Typically require immediate evaluation/management.

RLN = recurrent laryngeal nerve; SVC = superior vena cava.

"]],"atelectasis":[[97699,"Acute opacified hemithorax (unilateral whiteout)","

Acute opacified hemithorax (unilateral whiteout)

Trachea pulled toward
opacified side

Trachea midline

Trachea pushed away from
opacified side

Total lung atelectasis*
(eg, mainstem bronchial obstruction or intubation)

Extensive consolidation
(eg, pneumonia in all lobes
of 1 lung)

Massive pleural effusion
(eg, empyema, hemothorax)

  • Mainstem obstruction (eg, mucus plug) causes ipsilateral atelectasis
  • Mainstem intubation causes contralateral atelectasis
  • Alveoli fill with pus/debris, but no force is exerted on mediastinum
  • Pleural fluid displaces mediastinal structures to opposite side

*Trachea may remain midline early in the course of atelectasis.

"], [126101,"Atelectasis","

Atelectasis

Etiologies

Pathophysiology

Obstructive (resorptive)

  • Mucus plugging
  • Endobronchial mass
  • Hypoinflation

Obstruction or collapse of bronchus, leading to absent ventilation & resorption of alveolar gas

Compression

  • Pleural masses
  • Ascites or severe obesity
  • Chest wall trauma

Extrinsic compression of lung tissue by pleurae, chest wall, or abdomen

Relaxation (passive)

  • Pneumothorax
  • Pleural effusion

Separation of lung from chest wall, allowing natural inward recoil.

Adhesive

  • Neonatal RDS
  • ARDS
  • Drowning

Depletion or inactivation of surfactant, allowing alveolar walls to cling together due to surface tension

ARDS = adult respiratory distress syndrome; RDS = respiratory distress syndrome.

"]],"mediastinal-pathology--mediastinitis":[[104650,"Acute postoperative mediastinitis","

Acute postoperative mediastinitis

Etiology/epidemiology

  • Direct microbial contamination of operative site
  • Complicates 1%-2% of cardiothoracic operations involving sternotomy

Clinical presentation

  • 1-2 weeks after the operation
  • Sepsis (ie, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis)
  • Signs of sternal wound infection (eg, drainage, tenderness)
  • Chest x-ray: ± localized mediastinal fluid or air

Diagnosis

  • Characteristic clinical presentation
  • Surgical exploration revealing pus in mediastinum

Management

  • Intravenous antibiotics & surgical debridement
"]],"pneumothorax--tension-pneumothorax":[[119950,"Tension pneumothorax","

Tension pneumothorax

Clinical presentation

  • Tracheal deviation to opposite side
  • Hyper-expanded chest with decreased movement with respiration
  • Increased percussion note
  • Elevated central venous pressure (CVP)*

Management

  • Emergency needle thoracostomy in the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line

*CVP may be decreased in hypovolemic shock

"]],"lung-malformations":[[132004,"Congenital lung malformations","

Congenital lung malformations

Pathogenesis

Clinical presentation

Bronchopulmonary anomalies

Bronchogenic cyst

Foregut duplication (embryonic stage)

  • Typically asymptomatic
  • Recurrent childhood respiratory infections (eg, postobstructive pneumonia)
  • Rare malignant transformation
  • Airway obstruction (eg, hyperinflation or atelectasis)

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation

Defective branching morphogenesis (pseudoglandular stage)

Pulmonary hypoplasia

Impaired alveolar development (any stage) due to compression (or oligohydramnios)

  • Severe respiratory failure
  • Persistent pulmonary hypertension (underdeveloped vasculature)

Congenital lobar emphysema

Bronchial "ball valve" obstruction from another developmental lesion

  • Increased work of breathing (eg, nasal flaring, retractions)
  • Unilateral hyperinflation (eg, hyperresonance)

Vascular anomalies

Bronchopulmonary sequestration

Systemically perfused region of lung tissue disconnected from the main respiratory tree

  • Typically asymptomatic
  • Recurrent respiratory infections due to lack of drainage

Pulmonary artery defects

Pulmonary artery atresia, stenosis, or slings

  • Atresia: Pulmonary hypertension (eg, atretic vascular bed)
  • Slings: Tracheal or esophageal compression

Anomalous pulmonary venous return

Anastomoses of pulmonary veins to right atrium or vena cavae (instead of left atrium)

  • Partial: Noncyanotic at birth but progression to right heart failure
  • Total: Cyanotic at birth

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations

Direct connection between pulmonary artery and vein, bypassing capillaries

  • Paradoxical emboli
  • Brain abscess
  • Hypoxia (right-to-left shunting)
"]]};

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["repro"] = {"_more":[[31082,"Fetal growth restriction","

Fetal growth restriction

Symmetric

Asymmetric

Definition

  • Ultrasonographically estimated fetal weight <10th percentile or birth weight <3rd percentile for gestational age

Onset

  • 1st trimester
  • 2nd/3rd trimester

Etiology

  • Chromosomal abnormalities
  • Congenital infection
  • Uteroplacental insufficiency
  • Maternal malnutrition

 Clinical
features

  • Global growth lag
  • Head-sparing growth lag

Management

  • Regular nonstress testing
  • Weekly biophysical profiles
  • Serial umbilical artery Doppler sonography
  • Serial growth ultrasonography
"], [31879,"Low back pain during pregnancy","

Low back pain during pregnancy

Etiology

  • Enlarged uterus → exaggerated lordosis
  • Joint/ligament laxity from ↑ progesterone/relaxin
  • Weak abdominal muscles → decreased lumbar support

Risk factors

  • Excessive weight gain
  • Chronic back pain  
  • Back pain in prior pregnancy
  • Multiparity

Imaging

  • Not indicated

Management

  • Behavioral modifications
  • Heating pads
  • Analgesics  
"], [32003,"Prenatal testing","

Prenatal testing

Test

Timing (weeks)

Advantages

Disadvantages

First-trimester combined test*

9-13

Early screening

Not diagnostic

Cell-free fetal DNA

≥10

High sensitivity & specificity for aneuploidy

Not diagnostic

Chorionic villus sampling

10-13

Definitive karyotypic diagnosis

Invasive; risk for spontaneous abortion

Second-trimester quadruple screen**

15-22

Screens for neural tube defects & aneuploidy

Not diagnostic

Amniocentesis

15-20

Definitive karyotypic diagnosis

Invasive; risk for membrane rupture, fetal injury & pregnancy loss

Second-trimester ultrasonography

18-20

Measures fetal growth, evaluates fetal anatomy, confirms placenta position

Cannot identify all abnormalities; some findings are of uncertain significance

*Pregnancy-associated plasma protein, β-hCG, nuchal translucency.

**Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein, estriol, β-hCG, inhibin A.

"], [32437,"Urethral diverticulum","

Urethral diverticulum

Definition

  • Urethral mucosa herniated
    into surrounding tissue

Clinical features

  • Dysuria
  • Postvoid dribbling
  • Dyspareunia
  • Anterior vaginal wall mass

Diagnostic testing

  • Urinalysis
  • Urine culture
  • MRI of the pelvis
  • Transvaginal ultrasonography
"], [32488,"Septic abortion","

Septic abortion

Risk factors

  • Elective abortion
  • Spontaneous abortion
  • Pregnancy with intrauterine device in situ

Clinical presentation

  • Fever
  • Lower abdominal pain
  • Purulent vaginal discharge
  • Boggy, tender uterus
  • Dilated cervix

Complications

  • Myometrial infection/necrosis
  • Sepsis
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Death

Management

  • Blood & endometrial cultures
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Suction curettage
  • Hysterectomy
"], [32531,"","

Indications for prophylactic administration of anti-D
immunoglobulin for Rh D-negative patients*

  • At 28-32 weeks gestation
  • <72 hours after delivery of Rh D-positive infant
  • <72 hours after spontaneous abortion
  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Threatened abortion
  • Hydatidiform mole
  • Chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis
  • Abdominal trauma
  • 2nd- & 3rd-trimester bleeding
  • External cephalic version  

*Antepartum prophylaxis is not indicated if the father is Rh D-negative.

"], [32823,"Intrauterine fetal demise","

Intrauterine fetal demise

Definition

  • Absent fetal cardiac activity at ≥20 weeks gestation

Risk factors

  • Aneuploidy
  • Fetal or placental anomalies
  • Fetal growth restriction
  • Congenital infection
  • Substance use (eg, tobacco, cocaine)
  • Maternal conditions (eg, hypertension, diabetes mellitus)

Evaluation

Fetal

  • Autopsy
  • Gross & microscopic examination of placenta & umbilical cord
  • Karyotype/genetic studies

Maternal

  • Kleihauer-Betke test
  • Antiphospholipid antibodies
  • Coagulation studies*

Management

20-23 weeks

  • Dilation & evacuation OR vaginal delivery**

≥24 weeks

  • Vaginal delivery**

Complications

Coagulopathy after several weeks of fetal retention

*For history of recurrent pregnancy loss, family or personal history of venous thrombosis, or fetal growth restriction.

**Cesarean delivery by maternal choice if history of prior classical cesarean/myomectomy.

"], [33165,"Vesicovaginal fistula","

Vesicovaginal fistula

Risk factors

  • Pelvic surgery
  • Pelvic irradiation
  • Prolonged labor/childbirth trauma
  • Genitourinary malignancy

Clinical features

  • Painless, continuous urine leakage from the vagina

Diagnostic studies

  • Physical examination
  • Dye testing
  • Cystourethroscopy
"], [33315,"Amniotic fluid embolism","

Amniotic fluid embolism

Risk factors

  • Advanced maternal age
  • Gravida ≥5 (live births or stillbirths)
  • Cesarean or instrumental delivery
  • Placenta previa or abruption
  • Preeclampsia

Clinical presentation

  • Shock
  • Hypoxemic respiratory failure
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
  • Coma or seizures

Treatment

  • Respiratory & hemodynamic support
  • ± Transfusion
"], [33869,"Maternal serum α-fetoprotein screening","

Maternal serum α-fetoprotein screening

↑ MSAFP

↓ MSAFP

  • Open neural tube defects (eg, anencephaly, open spina bifida)
  • Ventral wall defects (eg, omphalocele, gastroschisis)
  • Multiple gestation
  • Aneuploidies (eg, trisomy 18 & 21)

MSAFP = maternal serum α-fetoprotein.

"], [35359,"Management of shoulder dystocia (BE CALM)","

Management of shoulder dystocia (BE CALM)

B

Breathe; do not push

E

Elevate legs & flex hips, thighs against abdomen(McRoberts)

C

Call for help

A

Applysuprapubic pressure

L

EnLarge vaginal opening with episiotomy

M

Maneuvers:

  • Deliver posterior arm
  • Rotate posterior shoulder (Woods screw): apply pressure to anterior aspect of the posterior shoulder
  • Adduct posterior fetal shoulder (Rubin): apply pressure to the posterior aspect of the posterior shoulder
  • Mother on hands & knees: "all fours" (Gaskin)
  • Replace fetal head into pelvis for cesarean delivery (Zavanelli)
"], [36642,"Intraamniotic infection (chorioamnionitis)","

Intraamniotic infection (chorioamnionitis)

Risk factors

  • Prolonged rupture of membranes (>18 hr)
  • Preterm prelabor rupture of membranes
  • Prolonged labor
  • Internal fetal/uterine monitoring devices
  • Repetitive vaginal examinations
  • Presence of genital tract pathogens

Diagnosis

Maternal fever PLUS ≥1 of the following:

  • Fetal tachycardia (>160/min)
  • Maternal leukocytosis
  • Purulent amniotic fluid

Management

  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Delivery

Complications

  • Maternal: postpartum hemorrhage, endometritis
  • Neonatal: preterm birth, pneumonia, encephalopathy
"], [37609,"GTPAL system for obstetric history notation","

GTPAL system for obstetric history notation

G

Gravidity

The number of times a person has been pregnant, regardless of pregnancy outcome

T

Term

The number of births at 37 weeks 0 days gestation & beyond

P

Preterm

The number of births at 20 weeks 0 days to 36 weeks 6 days gestation

A

Abortions

The number of pregnancies ending before 20 weeks 0 days gestation; these may be spontaneous (miscarriage) or induced abortions

L

Living

The number of currently living children

"], [38355,"Management of erectile dysfunction in cardiovascular disease","

Management of erectile dysfunction in cardiovascular disease

CV risk level

Recommendation

Low risk

  • No CV disease & <3 CV risk factors*
  • Prior MI with successful revascularization

No CV evaluation necessary; PDE-5 inhibitor may be initiated if no contraindication

Intermediate risk

  • ≥3 CV risk factors
  • Stable angina or noncardiac atherosclerosis
  • Past MI without revascularization

Additional evaluation (eg, exercise or chemical stress test) prior to initiating PDE-5 inhibitor

High risk

  • Unstable or refractory angina
  • Recent MI (<2 weeks) without revascularization

Defer sexual activity & refer to cardiology

*Risk factors include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, smoking, obesity & sedentary lifestyle.

CV = cardiovascular; MI = myocardial infarction; PDE = phosphodiesterase.

"], [38440,"Operative vaginal delivery","

Operative vaginal delivery

Indications

  • Fetal distress
  • Maternal cardiac or neurologic disorders prohibiting Valsalva maneuver
  • Prolonged 2nd stage of labor

Contraindications

  • Suspected cephalopelvic disproportion
  • Fetal connective tissue, skeletal, or bleeding disorder
  • <34 weeks gestation

Requirements

  • Fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes
  • Engaged fetal head with known station/presentation
  • Empty maternal bladder
  • Anesthesia

Complications

  • Vacuum: neonatal brachial plexus injury, cephalohematoma, retinal hemorrhage
  • Forceps: neonatal facial nerve/ocular injury, maternal trauma
"], [38816,"Hyperemesis gravidarum","

Hyperemesis gravidarum

Risk factors

  • Hydatidiform mole
  • Multifetal gestation
  • History of hyperemesis gravidarum

Clinical features

  • Severe, persistent vomiting
  • >5% loss of prepregnancy weight
  • Dehydration
  • Orthostatic hypotension

Laboratory abnormalities

  • Ketonuria
  • Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
  • Hypokalemia
  • Hemoconcentration

Treatment

  • Admission to hospital
  • Antiemetics & intravenous fluids
"], [39521,"Infertility","

Infertility

Etiology

Diagnostic test

Male factor

  • Semen analysis

Ovulatory function

  • Midluteal phase (day 21) progesterone level

Ovarian reserve

  • Day 3 FSH & estradiol levels
  • Clomiphene citrate challenge test
  • Antral follicle count
  • Antimüllerian hormone

Fallopian tube patency

  • Hysterosalpingogram

Uterine cavity evaluation

  • Sonohysterogram
"], [39690,"Types of spontaneous abortion","

Types of spontaneous abortion

Type

Clinical features

Cervix

Missed

  • Asymptomatic, decreased pregnancy symptoms

Closed

Inevitable

  • Bleeding, cramping, tissue visible in lower uterus

Open

Incomplete

  • Bleeding, cramping, tissue within vagina/cervix

Open

Complete

  • Resolution of passage of clots/tissue & cramping

Closed

Septic

  • Fever, uterine tenderness, purulent discharge

Usually open

"], [39791,"Shoulder dystocia","

Shoulder dystocia

Definition

  • Failure of usual obstetric maneuvers to deliver fetal shoulders

Risk factors

  • Fetal macrosomia
  • Maternal obesity
  • Excessive pregnancy weight gain
  • Diabetes mellitus (gestational, types 1 & 2)
  • Postterm pregnancy

Warning signs

  • Protracted labor
  • Retraction of fetal head into perineum after delivery (turtle sign)

Management

  • McRoberts maneuver
  • Suprapubic pressure
  • ± Episiotomy
  • Posterior arm delivery
  • Woods corkscrew or Rubin maneuver
  • Gaskin maneuver
  • Zavanelli maneuver
"], [40285,"Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy","

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

Clinical features

  • Development in 3rd trimester
  • Generalized pruritus
  • Pruritus worse on hands & feet
  • No associated rash
  • Right upper quadrant pain

Laboratory abnormalities

  • ↑ Total bile acids (≥10 µmol/L)
  • ↑ Liver transaminases (typically <2× normal, rarely >1,000 U/L)
  • ± ↑ Total & direct bilirubin

Pretest probability of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

1 point

Thrombosis

"], [54138,"Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia","

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Clinical features

Heparin exposure ≥5 days & any of the following:

  • Drop in platelet count by >50%
  • Arterial or venous thrombosis
  • Necrotic skin lesions at heparin injection site
  • Anaphylactoid reaction after heparin

Diagnosis

  • Serotonin release assay

Treatment

  • Stop all heparin products
  • Start nonheparin medication
"], [79879,"Clinical features of type 2 heparin-induced thrombocytopenia","

Clinical features of type 2 heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Clinical signs

Suspected with heparin exposure >5 days & any of the following:

  • Platelet count reduction >50% from baseline
  • Arterial or venous thrombosis
  • Necrotic skin lesions at heparin injection sites
  • Acute systemic (anaphylactoid) reactions after heparin

Diagnostic evaluation

  • Serotonin release assay: gold standard confirmatory test
  • Start treatment in suspected cases prior to confirmatory tests

Therapy

  • Stop all heparin products
  • Start a direct thrombin inhibitor (eg, argatroban) or fondaparinux (synthetic pentasaccharide)

  • <3%

  • Usually >20,000/mm3

outcome

Major causes

  • Severe traumatic injury
  • Malignancy
  • Obstetric complications

  • Bleeding & organ damage (eg, kidneys, lungs)

Laboratory findings

  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Prolonged PT & PTT
  • ↓ Fibrinogen
  • ↑ D-dimer
  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes)

"]],"heme-synthesis-porphyrias-and-lead-poisoning--acute-intermittent-porphyria":[[58046,"Acute intermittent porphyria","

Acute intermittent porphyria

Etiology

  • Autosomal dominant disorder with low penetrance
  • Reduced activity of porphobilinogen deaminase

Exacerbating factors

  • Medications (eg, cytochrome P-450 inducers, progesterone)
  • Physiologic stress (eg, fasting, surgery, illness)
  • Alcohol, tobacco

Manifestations

  • Abdominal pain
  • Peripheral neuropathy most pronounced in the proximal upper extremities
  • Autonomic dysfunction (eg, tachycardia, diaphoresis, hypertension)
  • Neuropsychiatric (eg, hallucinations, anxiety, psychosis)
  • Red-tinged urine that oxidizes with light/air exposure

Laboratory findings

  • Elevated serum & urinary PBG, ALA, porphyrins
  • ± Hyponatremia, elevated transaminases

Management

  • Glucose & hemin (heme analogue)

ALA = aminolevulinic acid; PBG = porphobilinogen.

"]],"extrinsic-hemolytic-anemias--drug-induced-hemolytic-anemia":[[59785,"Drug-induced, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia","

Drug-induced, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia

Pathogenesis

  • Drug coats erythrocytes → IgG binding → splenic destruction of RBCs (extravascular hemolysis)
  • Drug triggers immune complexes → complement-mediated destruction of RBCs (intravascular hemolysis)

Manifestations

  • Sudden onset (within hours of exposure)
  • Anemia: fatigue, pallor, dyspnea
  • Hemolysis: jaundice, dark urine, abdominal or back pain
    • ↑ Reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin & LDH
    • ↓ Haptoglobin
    • Spherocytes on peripheral blood smear
    • + Direct Coombs test (anti-IgG, anti-C3)

Treatment

  • Discontinue offending drug
  • Transfusion (if severe)
  • ± Glucocorticoids, IVIG

IVIG = intravenous immunoglobulin; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase; RBCs = red blood cells.

"]],"nonhemolytic-normocytic-anemias--anemia-of-chronic-disease":[[60023,"Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation)","

Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation)

Pathogenesis

  • ↑ Inflammatory cytokines (eg, hepcidin)
  • Inhibition of ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages
  • ↓ Iron absorption and ↑ iron sequestration
  • Reduced circulating iron → impaired erythropoiesis

Common
etiologies

  • Malignancy
  • Chronic infection
  • Rheumatic disease
  • Obesity
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Heart failure

Laboratory
findings

  • Normocytic/slightly microcytic anemia
  • ↓ Serum iron, iron-binding capacity, reticulocyte count
  • ↑ Bone marrow iron
  • Lower than expected erythropoietin for degree of anemia

Treatment

  • Treat underlying condition causing inflammation
"]],"hodgkin-lymphoma":[[60193,"Hodgkin lymphoma","

Hodgkin lymphoma

Epidemiology

  • Bimodal peak incidence: age 15-35 & >60
  • Association with EBV in the immunosuppressed

Manifestations

  • Painless lymphadenopathy
  • Mediastinal mass
  • B symptoms (ie, fever, sweats, weight loss)
  • Pruritus

Diagnosis

  • Lymph node biopsy
  • Reed-Sternberg cells on histology

Staging

  • Positron emission tomography/CT scan

EBV = Epstein-Barr virus.

"]],"chromosomal-translocations":[[73273,"Chromosomal translocations associated with hematologic malignancies","

Chromosomal translocations associated with hematologic malignancies

Malignancy

Pathogenesis

Acute promyelocytic
leukemia

t(15;17) involving PML & RARA → PML-RARα oncoprotein → myeloid differentiation inhibited

  • RARα: nuclear receptor involved in myeloid differentiation
  • PML: fusion forms receptor with dominant negative activity

Burkitt
lymphoma

t(8;14) involving MYC & IGH → MYC overexpression → cell growth

  • MYC: transcription factor regulating cell growth
  • IGH: immunoglobulin heavy chain (high expression in B cells)

Chronic myeloid
leukemia

t(9;22) involving ABL1 & BCR → BCR-ABL1 oncoprotein → cell proliferation

  • ABL1: nonreceptor tyrosine kinase
  • BCR: fusion leads to activation

Follicular
lymphoma

t(14;18) involving IGH & BCL2 → BCL2 overexpression → apoptosis evasion

  • BCL2: antiapoptotic protein

Mantle cell
lymphoma

t(11;14) involving CCND1 & IGH → cyclin D1 overexpression → cell cycle progression

  • Cyclin D1: regulates cell cycle
"]],"myeloproliferative-neoplasms":[[79865,"Chronic myeloproliferative disorders","

Chronic myeloproliferative disorders

Disorder

Diagnostic features

Mutation

Chronic myelogenous leukemia

Constitutional symptoms (eg, fatigue, weight loss, excessive sweating), splenomegaly & leukocytosis with marked left shift (eg, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, band forms)

Philadelphia chromosome t(9:22)

BCR-ABL fusion protein

Essential thrombocytosis

Hemorrhagic & thrombotic symptoms (eg, easy bruising, microangiopathic occlusion), thrombocytosis & megakaryocytic hyperplasia

JAK2

Primary myelofibrosis

Severe fatigue, splenomegaly (often causing early satiety/abdominal discomfort), hepatomegaly, anemia & bone marrow fibrosis

"]],"extrinsic-hemolytic-anemias--autoimmune-hemolytic-anemia":[[79875,"Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)","

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)

Warm agglutinin AIHA

Cold agglutinin AIHA

Etiology

  • Drugs (eg, penicillin)
  • Viral infections
  • Autoimmune (eg, SLE)
  • Immunodeficiency states
    • Lymphoproliferative (eg, CLL)
  • Infections (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection & infectious mononucleosis)
  • Lymphoproliferative diseases

Clinical presentation

  • Asymptomatic to life-threatening anemia
  • Direct Coombs positive with anti-IgG, anti-C3, or both
  • Symptoms of anemia
  • Livedo reticularis & acral cyanosis with cold exposure that disappear with warming
  • Direct Coombs positive with anti-C3 or anti-IgM, but usually not IgG

Treatment

  • Corticosteroids
  • Splenectomy for refractory disease
  • Avoidance of cold temperatures
  • Rituximab ± fludarabine

Complications

  • Venous thromboembolism
  • Lymphoproliferative disorders
  • Ischemia & peripheral gangrene
  • Lymphoproliferative disorders

CLL = chronic lymphocytic leukemia; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.

"]],"leukemias--chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia-small-lymphocytic-lymphoma":[[81531,"Chronic lymphocytic leukemia","

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Clinical features

  • Lymphadenopathy (cervical, supraclavicular, axillary)
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Mild thrombocytopenia & anemia
  • Often asymptomatic

Diagnosis

  • Severe lymphocytosis & smudge cells
  • Flow cytometry
  • Lymph node & bone marrow biopsy not generally needed

Prognosis

  • Median survival 10 years
  • Worse prognosis with:
    • Multiple chain lymphadenopathy
    • Hepatosplenomegaly
    • Anemia & thrombocytopenia

Complications

  • Infection
  • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  • Secondary malignancies (eg, Richter syndrome)

Hereditary thrombophilias*

Factor V Leiden

  • Most common in white patients
  • Activated protein C resistance

Prothrombin mutation

  • 2nd most common in white patients
  • ↑ Prothrombin levels

Antithrombin deficiency

  • Inherited form is rare
  • Acquired: DIC, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome

Protein C or S deficiency

  • ↓ Inactivation of factors Va & VIIIa
  • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis (protein C only)

*Typically autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.

DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation.

"]],"heme-synthesis-porphyrias-and-lead-poisoning--porphyria-cutanea-tarda":[[81838,"Porphyria cutanea tarda","

Porphyria cutanea tarda

Clinical presentation

  • Blisters, bullae, scarring, hypopigmentation/hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed skin (eg, back of hands, forearms, face)
  • Scarring & calcification similar to scleroderma

Associated conditions

  • Hepatitis C
  • HIV
  • Excessive alcohol consumption
  • Estrogen use
  • Smoking

Diagnostic testing

  • Mildly elevated liver enzymes & iron overload
  • Elevated plasma or urine porphyrin levels
"]],"leukopenias--neutropenia":[[82009,"Congenital causes of isolated* neutropenia","

Congenital causes of isolated* neutropenia

Condition

Pathogenesis

Features

Benign familial neutropenia

  • Single nucleotide polymorphism
  • Asymptomatic (mild neutropenia)
  • Most commonly patients of African descent

Cyclic neutropenia

  • Mutations encoding neutrophil elastase
  • Episodic (q21 days) neutropenia → recurrent mucositis/fever starting in early childhood
  • Treatment: G-CSF

Severe congenital neutropenia**

  • Persistent/severe neutropenia → recurrent & severe infections starting in early infancy
  • Treatment: G-CSF

*Bone marrow disorders (eg, leukemia, aplastic anemia) & hypersplenism usually cause multiple cytopenia.

**Most cases due to elastase mutation but can be caused by other mutations.

G-CSF = granulocyte colony-stimulating factor.

"]],"warfarin":[[91639,"Select warfarin interactions","

Examples

(↑ INR)

CYP450 2C9 inhibition

Amiodarone, azole antifungals (eg, fluconazole), metronidazole, SMX/TMP

Alteration of intestinal flora

Some antibiotics (eg, quinolones, tetracyclines)

(↓ INR)

CYP450 2C9 induction

Carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John's wort

↑ Vitamin K ingestion

Green leafy vegetables

Inhibition of platelet function

NSAIDs (eg, ibuprofen, aspirin), P2Y12 inhibitors (eg, clopidogrel, ticagrelor)

Unknown mechanism

*The 5Gs are garlic, ginger, ginkgo, ginseng & glucosamine.

CYP450 = cytochrome P450; SMX/TMP = sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim.

"]],"thrombotic-microangiopathies--thrombotic-thrombocytopenic-purpura":[[92407,"Thrombocytic thrombocytopenic purpura","

Thrombocytic thrombocytopenic purpura

Pathophysiology

  • Plasma enzyme deficiency → disseminated microvascular
    thrombosis (clotting)
  • Increased use of clotting factors → bleeding
  • Acquired (autoantibody) or hereditary

Clinical
manifestations

  • Fever
  • Hemolytic anemia (eg, jaundice, pallor)
  • Thrombocytopenia (eg, petechial rash, purpura)
  • Renal failure
  • Neurologic impairment (coma, convulsions, paralysis)

Laboratory
abnormalities

  • Hemolytic anemia (↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin, schistocytes)
  • Thrombocytopenia

Management

  • Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis)
  • Bleeding precautions

LDH = lactate dehydrogenase.

"]],"alkylating-agents--nitrogen-mustards":[[105388,"Select adverse effects of cyclophosphamide & ifosfamide","

Select adverse effects of cyclophosphamide & ifosfamide

Adverse effect

Monitoring

Prevention

Hemorrhagic cystitis

  • Evidence of hematuria (visual and/or RBCs on urinalysis)
  • Lower urinary tract symptoms (eg, urinary urgency, painful urination)
  • Adequate hydration
  • Mesna*

Myelosuppression

  • Anemia: Hgb/Hct & symptoms (eg, weakness)
  • Neutropenia: WBCs & symptoms (eg, fever)
  • Thrombocytopenia: platelets & symptoms (eg, bleeding)
  • G-CSF for neutropenia

Nausea & vomiting

  • Patient symptoms (eg, vomiting episodes, hydration status)
  • Electrolytes (eg, potassium, magnesium, sodium)
  • Antiemetics (eg, NK1 RA,
    5-HT3 RA, dexamethasone)
  • IV/PO hydration

Neurotoxicity
(ifosfamide only)

  • Symptoms (eg, encephalopathy, cerebellar dysfunction)
  • Methylene blue

*With high doses (eg, > 1 gram/m2) of cyclophosphamide & all doses of ifosfamide.

5-HT3 RA = serotonin receptor antagonist; G-CSF = granulocyte colony-stimulating factor; Hct = hematocrit; Hgb = hemoglobin; NK1 RA = neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist.

"]],"macrocytic-anemias--megaloblastic-anemia":[[116692,"Causes","

Vitamin B12 deficiency

Causes

  • Pernicious anemia (antibodies to intrinsic factor)
  • Drug-induced (eg, long-term metformin or PPI use)
  • Low intake or ↓ absorption (eg, gastric bypass, Crohn's disease)
  • Alcohol use disorder

Signs & symptoms

  • Fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, pallor, glossitis
  • Neurologic dysfunction
    • Peripheral neuropathy
    • Cognitive impairment
    • Psychiatric symptoms

Laboratory findings

  • ↓ Hgb, RBCs, reticulocyte count
  • ↑ MCV (> 100 fL), methylmalonic acid, homocysteine
  • ↓ Serum vitamin B12

Treatment

  • Cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12)
    • Parenteral (SC or IM injection)*
    • Nasal spray
    • Tablets

*Preferred for pernicious anemia, severe deficiency, or neurologic symptoms.

Hgb = hemoglobin; IM = intramuscular; MCV = mean corpuscular volume; PPI = proton pump inhibitor; RBC = red blood cell; SC = subcutaneous.

"]],"blood-transfusion-therapy--packed-rbcs":[[119863,"Indications for specialized red blood cell treatments","

Indications for specialized red blood cell treatments

Irradiated

  • Bone marrow transplant recipients
  • Acquired or congenital cellular immunodeficiency
  • Blood components donated by first- or second-degree relatives

Leukoreduced

  • Chronically transfused patients
  • CMV seronegative at-risk patients (eg, patients with AIDS, transplant recipients)
  • Potential transplant recipients
  • Previous febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction

Washed

  • IgA deficiency
  • Complement-dependent autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  • Continued allergic reactions (eg, hives) with red blood cell transfusion despite antihistamine treatment
"]],"rbc-morphology":[[120035,"Common RBC abnormalities seen on peripheral smear","

Common RBC abnormalities seen on peripheral smear

Type

Appearance

Common associated conditions

Bite cell

  • "Bites" secondary to phagocytes extracting denatured hemoglobin (Heinz bodies) precipitates
  • α-thalassemia
  • G6PD deficiency

Schistocyte

(helmet cell)

  • RBC fragments
  • DIC, TTP/HUS, traumatic hemolysis

Spherocyte

  • Spheroidal RBC, absent central pallor
  • Hereditary spherocytosis
  • Autoimmune hemolysis

Target cell

  • Red blood cell with "bull's eye" extra hemoglobin drop in center
  • Thalassemia
  • HbC disease
  • Postsplenectomy states
  • Liver disease (especially obstructive)

Teardrop cell

  • Teardrop shaped RBC
  • Extramedullary hematopoiesis (eg, myelofibrosis, major thalassemia)

Basophilic stippling

  • Blue granules of various sizes in RBC cytoplasm
  • Represent ribosomal precipitates
  • Thalassemias & iron deficiency
  • Alcohol abuse
  • Lead & heavy metal poisoning

Howell-Jolly bodies

  • Retained RBC nuclear remnants normally removed by spleen
  • Usually single, round, dark, purple-red & peripheral in location
  • Asplenia or splenic hypofunction (eg, sickle cell disease)

DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation; G6PD = glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; HbC = hemoglobin C; HUS = hemolytic uremic syndrome; RBC = red blood cell; TTP = thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

"]],"platelet-disorders":[[121058,"Common causes of thrombocytopenia","

Common causes of thrombocytopenia

Decreased production

  • Bone marrow disorders
    • Infections (eg, EBV, hepatitis C, HIV)*
    • Bone marrow failure (eg, infiltrative neoplasms, aplastic anemia)
    • Therapy (eg, chemotherapy, radiation)
    • Nutritional deficiency (eg, folate, vitamin B12)
  • Inherited platelet disorders (eg, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Fanconi anemia)
  • Liver disease (reduced TPO synthesis)

Increased destruction

  • Immune-mediated (eg, ITP, drug-induced thrombocytopenia, HIT)
  • Non–immune-mediated (eg, TTP, HUS, DIC, mechanical heart valves, ECMO)

Sequestration

  • Hypersplenism (eg, from portal hypertension, lymphoproliferation)
  • Placental sequestration during pregnancy

Dilution

  • Plasma expansion during pregnancy (ie, gestational thrombocytopenia)
  • Volume resuscitation, massive RBC transfusions
  • Postoperative

*Viral infections such as HIV may also contribute to autoantibody-induced platelet destruction.

DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation; EBV = Epstein-Barr virus; ECMO = extracorporeal membrane oxygenation; HIT = heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; HUS = hemolytic uremic syndrome; ITP = immune thrombocytopenia; RBC = red blood cell; TPO = thrombopoietin; TTP = thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["cvs"] = {"myocarditis":[[31110,"Viral myocarditis","

Viral myocarditis

Clinical presentation

  • Commonly asymptomatic & resolves without detection
  • Heart failure that may progress to DCM*
  • Chest pain, ventricular arrhythmia with risk of SCD
  •  Relatively young adults usually affected (eg, age <55)
  • ± Viral prodrome (eg, fever, malaise, myalgia)

Diagnosis

  • ECG: nonspecific findings
  • Laboratory: mild to moderate serum troponin elevation
  • Echocardiography: 4-chamber dilation with diffuse hypokinesis
  • Cardiac MRI: epicardial or midwall enhancement
  • Biopsy: lymphocytic infiltration, viral DNA or RNA**

Treatment

  • Supportive care to allow time for recovery
  • HFrEF medications (eg, diuretic, ACE inhibitor, β blocker)
  • Temporary ventricular assist device, if needed
  • Heart transplant if no recovery

*Most common symptomatic presentation.

**Endomyocardial biopsy is rarely required for diagnosis.

DCM = dilated cardiomyopathy; HFrEF = heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; SCD = sudden cardiac death.

"], [97495,"Causes of myocarditis*","

Causes of myocarditis*

Infectious

  • Viral (eg, coxsackievirus, adenovirus)**
  • Protozoal (eg, Chagas disease)
  • Spirochetal (eg, Lyme disease)
  • Rickettsial (eg, RMSF)
  • Fungal (eg, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis)
  • Mycobacterial (ie, tuberculosis)
  • Helminthic (eg, strongyloidiasis, trichinosis)
  • Bacterial toxins (eg, diphtheria)

Noninfectious

  • Rheumatologic disorders (eg, sarcoidosis, SLE)
  • Medication hypersensitivity (eg, antibiotics, clozapine)

*Some etiologies may cause persistent contractile dysfunction that can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy.

**Most common cause.

RMSF = Rocky Mountain spotted fever; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.

"]],"syncope":[[31410,"Vasovagal & situational syncope","

Vasovagal & situational syncope

Triggers

  • Pain,* anxiety,* emotional stress, heat, prolonged standing
  • Situational: cough,* micturition,* defecation, eating, hair-combing*

Clinical
presentation

  • Prodrome (eg, warmth, pallor, nausea, diaphoresis)
  • Rapid recovery of consciousness (eg, <1-2 min)

Diagnosis

  • Mainly based on clinical history of event
  • Upright tilt table testing sometimes indicated in uncertain cases

Treatment

  • Reassurance & avoidance of triggers
  • Counterpressure techniques for recurrent episodes

*Particularly common triggers in the pediatric population.

"], [57146,"Clues to etiology of syncope","

Clues to etiology of syncope

Reflex syncope

Vasovagal

  • Trigger (eg, emotional stress, prolonged standing)
  • Prodrome (eg, nausea, sweating, warmth)

Situational

  • Occurs with micturition, defecation, swallowing, or coughing

Carotid hypersensitivity

  • Tactile stimulation of carotid sinus while standing
  • Advanced age, carotid atherosclerosis

Orthostatic syncope

Medications

  • Vasodilators (eg, α-1 blockers, antihypertensives)
  • Inotropic/chronotropic blockade (eg, β blockers)

Hypovolemia

  • History consistent with volume loss

Autonomic dysfunction

  • Advanced age
  • Predisposing disease (eg, DM, Parkinson)

Cardiac syncope

LV outflow obstruction

  • Syncope with exertion
  • Systolic ejection murmur

Ventricular tachycardia

  • No warning symptoms
  • Cardiomyopathy or ischemic HD (monomorphic)
  • QT-interval prolongation (polymorphic)

Conduction impairment*

  • Preceding fatigue or lightheadedness
  • ECG abnormalities (eg, sinus pauses, dropped QRS complexes)

*Sick sinus syndrome or advanced atrioventricular block.

DM = diabetes mellitus; HD = heart disease; LV = left ventricular.

"], [57751,"Medication-induced orthostasis","

Medication-induced orthostasis

Mechanism

Examples

α1 blockade–mediated vasodilation

  • Terazosin, prazosin, doxazosin
  • Antipsychotics (eg, risperidone)
  • Antihistamines, TCAs

Other vasodilation

  • ACE inhibitors & ARBs
  • Dihydropyridine CCBs
  • Hydralazine, nitrates
  • Phosphodiesterase inhibitors

Volume depletion

  • Diuretics
  • SGLT-2 inhibitors

Sympathetic blockade

  • β blockers
  • Clonidine

ARBs = angiotensin II receptor blockers; CCBs = calcium channel blockers;
SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2; TCAs = tricyclic antidepressants.

"], [72184,"Diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension","

Diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension

Within 2-5 min of standing
from a supine position

  • ≥20 mm Hg ↓ in systolic blood pressure
    OR
  • ≥10 mm Hg ↓ in diastolic blood pressure
"]],"infective-endocarditis":[[31456,"Bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis","

Bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis

High-risk cardiac
conditions

  • Prosthetic heart valve
  • Previous valve repair using prosthetic material
  • Previous infective endocarditis
  • Unrepaired cyanotic CHD
  • Repaired CHD with residual shunt or defect
  • Valvular disease in transplanted heart

Indicated
procedures

  • Dental work with gingival manipulation
  • Respiratory tract procedure with incision or biopsy

Antibiotic
choice*

  • Amoxicillin (first-line)
  • Cephalexin, azithromycin, or doxycycline (if PCN allergy)

*Antibiotics are targeted at viridans group Streptococcus coverage.

CHD = congenital heart disease; PCN = penicillin.

"], [65526,"Common surgical indications in infectious endocarditis","

Common surgical indications in infectious endocarditis

  • Acute heart failure (eg, aortic/mitral valve regurgitation)
  • Extension of infection (eg, abscess, fistula, heart block)
  • Difficult-to-eradicate organism (eg, fungus, MDR pathogen)
  • Persistent bacteremia on antibiotics
  • Large vegetation/persistent septic emboli

MDR = multidrug-resistant.

"]],"acute-coronary-syndrome-treatments":[[31561,"Acute management of acute coronary syndrome","

Acute management of acute coronary syndrome

(STEMI, NSTEMI, or unstable angina)

Nitrates

  • Rapid chest pain relief
  • Caution with hypotension (eg, RV infarction)

Beta blocker

  • Cardioselective (eg, metoprolol, atenolol)
  • Decreases myocardial O2 demand to limit infarct size
  • Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock & bradycardia

Antiplatelet therapy

  • Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (eg, prasugrel, clopidogrel)*
  • Reduces platelet activity

Anticoagulation

  • Unfractionated heparin, bivalirudin, or enoxaparin
  • Limits thrombus expansion

Statin therapy

  • High potency (eg, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin)
  • Stabilizes atherosclerotic plaque

Coronary reperfusion

STEMI

  • PCI <90 min from first medical contact
  • Fibrinolytics (eg, alteplase) if PCI is unavailable

NSTEMI or unstable angina

  • Coronary angiography often within 24 hr

*In patients with NSTEMI or unstable angina, P2Y12 inhibitor therapy is often held until after coronary angiography in case the atherosclerotic coronary anatomy indicates the need for coronary artery bypass grafting.

NSTEMI = non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction; PCI = percutaneous coronary intervention; RV = right ventricular; STEMI = ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction.

"], [84525,"Medical management following myocardial infarction","

Medical management following myocardial infarction

Medication

Indication

Dual antiplatelet therapy
(low-dose aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor)

  • All patients (regardless of stent placement)
  • Low-dose aspirin continued indefinitely
  • P2Y12 inhibitor continued for 12 months

Beta blocker
(eg, metoprolol, carvedilol)

  • All patients, continued indefinitely
  • Reduces myocardial oxygen demand, decreases arrhythmia risk & inhibits remodeling

ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker

  • All patients, continued indefinitely for reduced LVEF
  • Inhibits post-MI remodeling

High-intensity statin
(eg, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin)

  • All patients, continued indefinitely
  • Stabilizes atherosclerotic plaque & reduces recurrent MI

Mineralocorticoid antagonist
(eg, spironolactone)

  • Reduced LVEF with symptoms or comorbid DM
  • Inhibits post-MI remodeling

DM = diabetes mellitus; LVEF = left ventricular ejection fraction; MI = myocardial infarction.

"], [91392,"Absolute contraindications","

Contraindications to fibrinolytic therapy for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction

Absolute contraindications

  • History of intracranial hemorrhage
  • History of ischemic stroke within 3 months
  • Presence of cerebrovascular malformation or intracranial malignancy
  • Suspected aortic dissection
  • Bleeding diathesis or active bleeding (except menses)
  • Major closed head or facial trauma within past 3 months

Relative contraindications

  • Blood pressure >180/110 mm Hg
  • History of ischemic stroke >3 months prior
  • Prolonged CPR or major surgery within past 3 weeks
  • Internal bleeding within past 2-4 weeks
  • Current warfarin use with INR >1.7
CPR = cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
"]],"acute-pericarditis":[[31628,"Acute pericarditis","

Acute pericarditis

Etiology

  • Viral or idiopathic
  • Autoimmune disease (eg, SLE)
  • Uremia (acute or chronic kidney failure)
  • Post myocardial infarction
    • Early: peri-infarction pericarditis
    • Late: Dressler syndrome

Clinical features & diagnosis

  • Pleuritic chest pain (↓ when sitting) ± fever
  • Pericardial friction rub (highly specific)
  • ECG: diffuse ST-segment elevation & PR-segment depression
  • Echocardiography: pericardial effusion

Treatment

  • NSAIDs & colchicine for viral or idiopathic etiology
  • Variable for other etiologies

NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.

"], [80023,"Etiologies of pericarditis","

Etiologies of pericarditis

Infection

Viral (most common), bacterial

Iatrogenic

Surgery, trauma, radiation & drug-related

Connective tissue disease

Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus

Cardiac

Dressler syndrome (post myocardial infarction), usually 1-6 weeks after myocardial infarction

Uremic

Serum BUN usually >60 mg/dL, but degree of pericarditis does not always correlate with degree of elevation

Malignancy

Can be due to cancer (eg, lung, breast, Hodgkin lymphoma) or treatment (eg, radiation, chemotherapy)

BUN = blood urea nitrogen.

"]],"myocardial-infarction-complications--true-ventricular-aneurysm":[[31871,"Left ventricular aneurysm","

Left ventricular aneurysm

Etiology

  • Scar tissue deposition following transmural MI

Clinical presentation

  • Several months following MI
  • Heart failure & angina
  • Ventricular arrhythmia (eg, ventricular tachycardia)
  • Systemic embolization (eg, stroke)

Diagnosis

  • ECG: Persistent ST elevation, deep Q waves
  • Echocardiograph: Thin and dyskinetic myocardial wall

 MI = myocardial infarction. 

"]],"antianginal-therapy":[[31989,"Pharmacologic management of chronic stable angina","

Pharmacologic management of chronic stable angina

Beta blockers

  • First-line therapy
  • ↓ Myocardial contractility & heart rate

Nondihydropyridine CCBs

  • Alternate to beta blocker
  • ↓ Myocardial contractility & heart rate

Dihydropyridine CCBs

  • Added to beta blocker when needed
  • ↓ Afterload via systemic arterial dilation

Nitrates

  • Short-acting to abort acute symptoms
  • Long-acting added for persistent angina
  • ↓ Preload via dilation of capacitance veins

Ranolazine

  • Alternate therapy for refractory angina
  • ↓ Myocardial calcium influx

CCBs = calcium channel blockers.

"]],"coronary-artery-disease--angina":[[32005,"Vasospastic angina","

Vasospastic angina

Pathogenesis

  • Hyperreactivity of coronary smooth muscle

Clinical
presentation

  • Young patients (age <50)
  • Smoking (minimal other CAD risk factors)
  • Recurrent chest discomfort
    • Occurs at rest or during sleep
    • Spontaneous resolution ≤15 min

Diagnosis

  • Ambulatory ECG: ST-segment elevation
  • Coronary angiography: no CAD

Treatment

  • Calcium channel blocker (preventive)
  • Sublingual nitroglycerin (abortive)

CAD = coronary artery disease.

"], [46853,"Vasospastic angina","

Vasospastic angina

Pathogenesis

  • Hyperreactivity of coronary smooth muscle due to endothelial dysfunction & autonomic imbalance

Clinical presentation

  • Young age (<50)
  • Minimal CAD risk factors (other than smoking)
  • Recurrent chest discomfort
    • At rest or during sleep
    • Spontaneous resolution ≤15 min

Diagnosis

  • ECG: ST-segment elevation during episode
  • Coronary angiography: no CAD

CAD = coronary artery disease.

"], [53633,"Differential diagnosis & features of chest pain","

Differential diagnosis & features of chest pain

Coronary artery
disease

  • Substernal
  • Precipitated by exertion
  • Relieved by rest or nitroglycerin

Pulmonary/pleuritic
(pleurisy, pneumonia,
pericarditis, PE)

  • Sharp/stabbing pain
  • Worse with inspiration
  • Pericarditis: worse when lying flat

Aortic
(dissection,
intramural hematoma)

  • Abrupt (maximal at onset), severe "tearing" pain
  • May radiate to back
  • Hypertension and/or inherited aortopathy

Esophageal

  • Substernal, may refer to neck
  • Associated with regurgitation
  • Provoked by recumbent position
  • Nonexertional, relieved by antacids

Chest wall/
musculoskeletal

  • Persistent pain
  • Worse with movement or change in position
  • Often follows repetitive activity

PE = pulmonary embolism.

"], [120281,"Classic features of stable anginal chest pain","

Classic features of stable anginal chest pain

Location & associated symptoms

  • Substernal
  • May radiate to arms, neck, lower jaw, or epigastrium

"], [54553,"Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy","

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Pathophysiology

  • Genetic mutations affecting cardiac sarcomere proteins
  • Autosomal dominant inheritance
  • Variable phenotypic penetrance

Clinical features

  • Many patients are asymptomatic
  • Exertional dyspnea, fatigue, angina, light-headedness, syncope
  • Systolic ejection murmur accentuated by ↓ LV blood volume
  • Diastolic dysfunction with audible S4
  • ↑ Risk of atrial fibrillation & ventricular tachycardia

Diagnosis

  • ECG: left axis deviation, abnormalities of depolarization (eg, Q waves) or repolarization (eg, inverted T waves)
  • Echocardiography: septal LV hypertrophy, dynamic LVOT obstruction, LA dilation

Management

  • Beta blocker or nondihydropyridine CCB (↑ LV blood volume)
  • Avoidance of dehydration & vasodilators (↓ LV blood volume)
  • ICD placement if substantially increased risk for SCD
  • Septal ablation, cardiac transplantation

CCB = calcium channel blocker; ICD = implantable cardiac defibrillator; LA = left atrial; LV = left ventricular; LVOT = LV outflow tract; SCD = sudden cardiac death.

"], [119967,"Ezetimibe","

Ezetimibe

Mechanism of action

  • ↓ Dietary cholesterol absorption by blocking NPC1L1 enterocyte transporter
  • ↓ Cholesterol delivery to liver, which ↑ LDL-R expression

Physiologic effects

  • ↓ LDL cholesterol, synergistic effects with statins
  • Small effect on TGs
  • Possible ↓ ASCVD in high-risk patients (when used with statin); no clear primary prevention benefits

Indications

  • Treatment intensification in high-risk patients (eg, prior MI) with persistently elevated LDL despite statin

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Gastrointestinal distress
  • Hepatotoxicity, myopathy (eg, when used with statins)
  • Possible ↑ risk of gallstones (eg, when used with fibrates)

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; MI = myocardial infarction; NPC1L1 = Niemann-Pick C1-like 1; PCSK9i = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor; TG = triglycerides.

"], [89466,"Sepsis & septic shock","

Sepsis & septic shock

Definitions & pathophysiology

  • Sepsis: infection + ≥2 organ system dysfunction (eg, encephalopathy, ARDS, DIC)
  • Septic shock: sepsis + refractory hypotension (ie, vasopressors) + ↑ lactate (hypoperfusion)

Work-up &
management

  • First 1-3 hr: cultures, empiric antibiotics & crystalloid (eg, lactated Ringer) resuscitation
  • Evaluate: infection source, sequential organ dysfunction
  • Organ protection: MAP >65 mm Hg, low tidal volume ventilation, glucose control
 

Prognosis

  • Mortality predictors: sequential organ failure (~15%/system), ↑↑ lactic acidosis (≥4 mmol/L)
  • Late mortality: mainly nosocomial infections (postseptic immune paralysis)
  • PICS: cognitive, emotional & physical impairments in most survivors

  • No visible change

4-12 hours

  • Wavy fibers with narrow, elongated myocytes

12-24 hours

  • Myocyte hypereosinophilia with pyknotic (shrunken) nuclei

1-3 days

  • Coagulation necrosis (loss of nuclei & striations)
  • Prominent neutrophilic infiltrate

3-7 days

  • Disintegration of dead neutrophils & myofibers
  • Macrophage infiltration at border areas

7-10 days

  • Robust phagocytosis of dead cells by macrophages
  • Beginning formation of granulation tissue at margins

10-14 days

  • Well-developed granulation tissue with neovascularization

2-8 weeks

  • Progressive collagen deposition & scar formation

Extra (gallop) heart sounds

Associated disorders*

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia

"]],"congenital-heart-diseases--d-transposition-of-great-arteries":[[68555,"Transposition of the great arteries","

Transposition of the great arteries

Anatomy

  • Parallel (separate) systemic & pulmonary circuits
    • Right ventricle → aorta
    • Left ventricle → pulmonary artery
  • Deoxygenated blood is delivered to the systemic circulation
  • Mixing shunt (eg, VSD, PDA) must be present for viability

Clinical features

  • Cyanosis at or shortly after birth
  • Tachypnea & tachycardia
  • Murmur typically absent at birth due to low velocity shunting

Diagnosis

  • Chest x-ray: narrow mediastinum ± cardiomegaly ("egg on a string")
  • Hyperoxia test: little to no ↑ in arterial oxygenation with 100% O2
  • Echocardiography typically confirmatory

Initial management

  • Promote mixing of oxygenated & deoxygenated blood
    • Prostaglandin infusion (maintains PDA)
    • Atrial septostomy (maintains PFO)

PDA = patent ductus arteriosus; PFO = patent foramen ovale; VSD = ventricular septal defect.

Type of defect

Left heart obstruction

  • Allow blood flow from pulmonary artery to systemic circulation
  • Severe hypoplastic left heart
  • Critical aortic coarctation
  • Critical aortic stenosis

Parallel circulation

  • Allow mixing of oxygenated & deoxygenated blood
  • Transposition of great arteries

RVOT = right ventricular outflow tract obstruction; ToF = tetralogy of Fallot; VSD = ventricular septal defect.

"]],"congenital-heart-diseases--tetralogy-of-fallot":[[68606,"Tetralogy of Fallot","

Tetralogy of Fallot

Pathophysiology

  • Embryonic deviation of infundibular septum creates 4 defects:
    • RVOT obstruction
    • Ventricular septal defect
    • Overriding aorta
    • Concentric RVH (secondary to RVOT obstruction)

Clinical presentation

  • Based on severity of RVOT obstruction:
    • Severe: profound neonatal cyanosis & hypoxemia
    • Moderate: tet spells in infancy/childhood
    • Mild: heart failure in childhood/adulthood
  • RVOT obstruction is dynamic (eg, worsens with feeding or crying)
  • Squatting can improve cyanosis via increased systemic afterload

Clinical findings

  • Harsh systolic ejection murmur at LUSB (RVOT obstruction)
  • Soft or absent pulmonic component of S2
  • Chest x-ray: boot-shaped heart caused by RVH

LUSB = left upper sternal border; RVH = right ventricular hypertrophy; RVOT = right ventricular outflow tract.

"]],"antiarrhythmics-beta-blockers-class-ii":[[87785,"Beta blocker toxicity","

Beta blocker toxicity

Mechanism

  • Excessive adrenergic blockade → ↓↓ intracellular cAMP

Clinical
presentation

  • Beta 1 blockade–mediated effects:
    • Cardiac suppression with bradycardia & hypotension*
    • Confusion due to cerebral hypoperfusion
  • Beta 2 blockade–mediated effects:
    • Bronchospasm
    • Hypoglycemia (impaired gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis)
    • Confusion & seizures due to hypoglycemia**

Diagnosis

  • ECG: sinus node dysfunction, atrioventricular block
  • Consistent clinical presentation (drug levels not useful)

Treatment

  • Intravenous fluids for hypotension & atropine for bradycardia
  • Glucagon to directly counteract toxicity (↑ intracellular cAMP)
  • Calcium gluconate sometimes given to ↑ blood pressure

*Beta 1 blockade–mediated effects are predominant with cardioselective beta blockers (eg, metoprolol), whereas all effects are seen with nonselective beta blockers (eg, propranolol).

**Lipid-soluble beta blockers (eg, propranolol) can also cause confusion & seizures via direct CNS effects.

"]],"wide-complex-tachycardias--ventricular-tachycardia":[[90258,"Monomorphic nonsustained ventricular tachycardia","

Monomorphic nonsustained ventricular tachycardia

Identification

  • ≥3 consecutive ventricular beats (wide QRS complex)
  • Rate >100/min & duration <30 sec

Predisposing conditions

  • Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
  • Ischemic heart disease
  • Other cardiomyopathy (eg, HCM)

Precipitating factors

  • Serum electrolyte abnormalities (eg, ↓ K, ↓ Mg)
  • Hypoxemia or acute myocardial ischemia
  • Elevated sympathetic tone (eg, sepsis)

Management

  • Address precipitating factors (eg, replace electrolytes)
  • Consider adding (or increasing dose of) beta blockade

HCM = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

"]],"cardiomyopathies--dilated-cardiomyopathy":[[95026,"Alcohol-induced cardiomyopathy","

Alcohol-induced cardiomyopathy

Pathophysiology

  • Direct toxicity of ethanol leads to contractile dysfunction
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy eventually develops

Clinical presentation

  • History of heavy & prolonged alcohol use
  • Symptomatic HFrEF (eg, dyspnea, volume overload)
  • Laboratory evidence of heavy alcohol use (eg, AST/ALT >2:1)

Diagnosis

  • Consistent clinical presentation
  • Exclusion of other causes of HFrEF (eg, ischemic heart disease)

Management

  • Complete alcohol abstinence (may reverse cardiomyopathy)
  • Standard treatment of persistent HFrEF (eg, ARNI, diuretic)

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; ARNI = angiotensin receptor blocker-neprilysin inhibitor; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; HFrEF = heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

"], [97423,"Dilated cardiomyopathy","

Dilated cardiomyopathy

Pathophysiology

  • Myocardial contractile dysfunction → ventricular dilation
  • Heart failure & myocardial fibrosis can eventually develop*
  • May be preceded by myocarditis (myocardial inflammation)

Notable causes

  • Infection (eg, viral, Chagas disease)
  • Toxins (eg, alcohol, cocaine)
  • Medications (eg, anthracyclines, anti-HER2 agents)
  • Inherited (eg, classic familial, Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
  • Rheumatologic/infiltrative (eg, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis)
  • Nutritional deficiency (eg, thiamine, selenium)
  • Other (eg, idiopathic, peripartum, tachycardia induced)

*Cardiomyopathy may be reversible if disease process is halted before substantial fibrosis develops.

"]],"heart-murmurs--mitral-tricuspid-regurgitation":[[100471,"Chronic mitral regurgitation","

Chronic mitral regurgitation

Etiology

  • Myxomatous degeneration leading to mitral valve prolapse
    • Usually occurs as an isolated valvular process
    • Connective tissue syndrome (eg, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos)
  • Rheumatic heart disease
  • Sequelae of prior infective endocarditis

Clinical features

  • Systolic murmur best heard at cardiac apex
  • LV dilation develops when severe (S3, laterally displaced PMI)
  • Atrial fibrillation is common due to left atrial dilation

Management

  • Medications to reduce afterload (eg, ACE inhibitor)
  • Surgical repair or replacement for severe disease

LV = left ventricular; PMI = point of maximal impulse.

"]],"aortic-aneurysm--thoracic-aortic-aneurysm":[[102632,"Thoracic aortic aneurysm","

Thoracic aortic aneurysm

Risk factors

  • Advanced age (>60), smoking, HTN
  • Connective tissue disease (eg, Marfan syndrome)
  • Family history, bicuspid aortic valve

Clinical
presentation

  • Usually asymptomatic & discovered incidentally
  • Subacute symptoms due to expansion:
    • Vague chest/back pain
    • Compression of structures (eg, hoarseness, dysphagia)
  • Symptoms indicate imminent risk of dissection/rupture

Imaging

  • CXR may show widened mediastinum, enlarged aortic knob
  • Chest CT or MR angiography for diagnostic confirmation

CXR = chest x-ray; HTN = hypertension.

"]],"lipid-lowering-agents-continued":[[119966,"Statins (eg, simvastatin)","

Statins (eg, simvastatin)

Mechanism of action

  • Inhibits HMG CoA reductase to ↓ cholesterol & VLDL synthesis
  • Results in ↑ LDL-R expression and ↑ LDL clearance

Effects

  • Main: ↓ LDL cholesterol
  • Secondary: ↑ HDL, ↓ TG (modest)
  • ↓ CVD events & mortality

Indications

  • First-line treatment for primary & secondary ASCVD prevention
  • ASCVD risk >20% & age <75: high-intensity statin
  • ASCVD risk 7.5-10% &/or age >75: moderate-intensity statin
  • Synergistic effects with PCSK9i (in high-risk patients)

Adverse effects

  • Myalgias, myopathy
  • Transaminitis/hepatic inflammation
  • Increase in risk of T2DM (small)
  • Possible cognitive effects (mild)

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; CVD = cardiovascular disease; HDL = high-density lipoprotein; HMG CoA = 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; PCSK9i = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor; T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus; TG = triglycerides.

"], [119968,"PCSK9 inhibitors","

PCSK9 inhibitors(eg, evolucumab)

Mechanism of action

  • Blocks binding of PCSK9 to LDL-R to ↓ LDL-R degradation
  • Net effect is ↑ LDL receptor availability & LDL clearance

Physiologic effects

  • ↓ LDL cholesterol, synergistic effects with statins
  • ↓ CVD events in high-risk patients

Indications

  • Adjunct treatment to statin if persistent dyslipidemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, or very high CVD risk

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • High cost; administered as injection
  • Side effects: rare myopathy, injection site reaction

CVD = cardiovascular disease; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9.

"], [119977,"Omega-3 fatty acids","

Omega-3 fatty acids

Mechanism of action

  • ↓ Hepatic VLDL synthesis
  • ↑ LPL activity (increased metabolism of circulating TGs)
  • ↑ PPAR-α activity → beta-oxidation of FFAs

Physiologic effects

  • ↓ TG, ↑ HDL
  • Effective for secondary ASCVD prevention in patients with high TGs
  • No clear effect for primary ASCVD prevention

Indications

  • First-line treatment of moderate-to-severe hyperTG (eg, >500 mg/dL) with ↑ ASCVD risk

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Often requires very high dose for effectiveness
  • May raise LDL, risk of atrial fibrillation

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; FFA = free fatty acid;  HDL = high-density lipoprotein; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PPAR-α = peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha; TG = triglycerides; VLDL = very low density lipoprotein.

"], [119980,"Fibrates (eg, gemfibrozil)","

Fibrates (eg, gemfibrozil)

Mechanism of action

  • Stimulate lipoprotein lipase activity (↑ TG lipolysis)
  • ↑ FFA uptake, ↓ TG levels
  • Also ↓ bile acid synthesis → reducing dietary cholesterol solubility

Physiologic effects

  • ↓ LDL cholesterol, synergistic effects with statins
  • ↑ HDL

Indications

  • Hypertriglyceridemia (>500 mg/dL) → reduce risk of pancreatitis
  • No clear evidence of ↓ ASCVD risk for primary prevention

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Myopathy (especially when used with statins)
  • Gallstone precipitation (due to ↓ bile acids)

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; FFA = free fatty acid; HDL = high-density lipoprotein receptor; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; TG = triglyceride.

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["gi"] = {"appendicitis":[[31284,"Acute appendicitis","

Acute appendicitis

Clinical
presentation

  • Nausea, vomiting, anorexia
  • Initially: diffuse abdominal pain (visceral pain)
  • Later: localized RLQ pain (somatic pain)
  • Mild leukocytosis

Examination

  • McBurney point tenderness
  • Psoas sign: pain with right hip extension
  • Obturator sign: pain with right hip internal rotation
  • Rovsing sign: RLQ pain with LLQ palpation

Diagnosis

  • Clinical presentation
  • CT scan or ultrasonography

Treatment

  • Surgical appendectomy

LLQ = left lower quadrant; RLQ = right lower quadrant.

"], [57369,"Modified Alvarado score","

Modified Alvarado score

Points
(each)

Clinical feature

1

  • Migratory RLQ pain
  • Anorexia
  • Nausea or vomiting
  • Fever >37.5 C (>99.5 F)
  • RLQ rebound tenderness

2

  • RLQ tenderness
  • Leukocytes >10,000/mm3

9

Total possible score

0-3: appendicitis unlikely

 ≥4: evaluate for appendicitis

RLQ = right lower quadrant.

"], [82008,"Examination signs of appendicitis","

Examination signs of appendicitis

Sign

Findings

Significance

Peritoneal signs

  • Rebound tenderness
  • Involuntary guarding
  • Abdominal rigidity
  • Acute increase in pain after removing the hand from applying pressure
  • Tensing of abdominal wall muscles during palpation of abdomen
  • Persistent tension of abdominal wall muscles

Peritoneal irritation (rupture or impending rupture)

Psoas sign

  • RLQ pain with extension of right thigh

Abscess adjacent to psoas or retrocecal appendix

Obturator sign

  • RLQ pain with internal rotation of right thigh

Pelvic appendix or abscess

Rovsing's sign

  • RLQ pain with LLQ palpation & retropulsion of colonic contents

Acute appendicitis

Rectal tenderness

  • Right pelvic pain during rectal examination, especially with pressure on the right rectal wall

Pelvic appendix or abscess

"]],"other-intestinal-disorders--small-bowel-obstruction":[[31523,"Small bowel obstruction","

Small bowel obstruction

Clinical presentation

  • Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting
  • Inability to pass flatus or stool if complete (no obstipation if partial)
  • Hyperactive → absent bowel sounds
  • Distended & tympanitic abdomen

Diagnosis

  • Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels on plain film or CT scan
  • Partial: air in colon
  • Complete: transition point (abrupt cutoff), no air in colon

Complications

  • Ischemia/necrosis (strangulation)
  • Bowel perforation

Management

  • Bowel rest, nasogastric tube suction, intravenous fluids
  • Surgical exploration for signs of complications
"], [116583,"Small bowel obstruction","

Small bowel obstruction

Etiology

  • Most commonly due to adhesions (scar tissue)
  • Tumors, masses, or complicated hernias

Clinical presentation

  • Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting
  • Inability to pass flatus or stool if complete (no obstipation if partial)
  • Hyperactive → absent bowel sounds
  • Distended & tympanitic abdomen

Diagnosis

  • Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels on plain film or CT scan

Management

  • Bowel rest, nasogastric tube suction, intravenous fluids
  • Surgical exploration for signs of complications
"]],"wilson-disease":[[32077,"Wilson disease","

Wilson disease

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal recessive mutation of ATP7B → hepatic copper accumulation → leak from damaged hepatocytes → deposits in tissues (eg, basal ganglia, cornea)

Clinical
findings

  • Hepatic (acute liver failure, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis)
  • Neurologic (parkinsonism, gait disturbance, dysarthria)
  • Psychiatric (depression, personality changes, psychosis)

Diagnosis

  • ↓ Ceruloplasmin & ↑ urinary copper excretion
  • Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination
  • ↑ Copper content on liver biopsy

Treatment

  • Chelators (eg, D-penicillamine, trientine)
  • Zinc (interferes with copper absorption)
"]],"other-esophageal-pathologies--gastroesophageal-reflux-disease":[[32162,"Gastroesophageal reflux disease","

Gastroesophageal reflux disease

Pathophysiology

  • Decreased tone or excessive transient relaxations of LES
  • Anatomic disruption to gastroesophageal junction (eg, hiatal hernia)
  • ↑ Risk with obesity, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol intake

Manifestations

  • Regurgitation of acidic material in mouth
  • Heartburn
  • Odynophagia (often indicates reflux esophagitis)
  • Extraesophageal manifestations: cough, hoarseness, wheezing

Complications

  • Esophageal: erosive esophagitis, Barrett esophagus, strictures
  • Extraesophageal: asthma exacerbation, laryngitis

Initial treatment

  • Lifestyle (eg, weight loss) & dietary changes
  • H2R blocker or PPI

H2R = histamine 2 receptor; LES = lower esophageal sphincter; PPI = proton pump inhibitor.

"]],"reye-syndrome":[[32373,"Reye syndrome","

Reye syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Aspirin use in children during viral infection (eg, influenza, varicella)
  • Microvesicular fat deposits in the liver
  • Cerebral edema

Clinical features

  • Acute liver failure
    • Hepatomegaly without jaundice
  • Rapidly progressive encephalopathy
    • Vomiting, lethargy, seizure, coma

Laboratory findings

  • ↑ AST, ALT, ammonia
  • ↑ PT, INR, PTT
  • ↓ Glucose
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Normal bilirubin

Treatment

  • Supportive

ALT = alanine aminotransferase (SGPT); AST = aspartate aminotransferase (SGOT).

"], [69965,"Reye syndrome","

Reye syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Aspirin use in children during viral infection (eg, influenza, varicella)
  • Mitochondrial toxicity → impaired fatty acid metabolism
  • Microvesicular fat deposits in the liver
  • Hepatic dysfunction → hyperammonemia
  • Diffuse astrocyte swelling (ie, cerebral edema)

Clinical features

  • Acute liver failure
    • Hepatomegaly
    • Elevated transaminases; coagulopathy
  • Rapidly progressive encephalopathy
    • Vomiting, lethargy, seizures, coma

Treatment

  • Supportive
"]],"cholelithiasis-and-related-pathologies--acute-cholangitis":[[32550,"Acute cholangitis","

Acute cholangitis

Etiology

  • Ascending infection due to biliary obstruction

Clinical
presentation

  • Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain (Charcot triad)
  • ± Hypotension, AMS (Reynolds pentad)

Diagnosis

  • Cholestatic liver function abnormalities
    • ↑ Direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase
    • Mildly ↑ aminotransferases
  • Biliary dilation on abdominal ultrasonography or CT scan

Treatment

  • Antibiotic coverage of enteric bacteria
  • Biliary drainage by ERCP within 24-48 hr

AMS = altered mental status; ERCP = endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography;
RUQ = right upper quadrant.

"], [59284,"Acute cholangitis","

Acute cholangitis

Etiology

  • Ascending infection due to biliary obstruction
    • Obstructive gallstone
    • Malignancy (eg, cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic head cancer)
    • Stricture (eg, primary sclerosing cholangitis)
    • Biliary stent blockage

Clinical
presentation

  • Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain (Charcot triad)
  • ± Hypotension, altered mental status (Reynolds pentad)

Laboratory
results

  • Cholestatic liver function test
    • ↑ Alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin
    • ± Mildly elevated transaminases
  • Leukocytosis

Imaging

  • Biliary dilation on abdominal imaging

RUQ = right upper quadrant.

"]],"intussusception":[[32943,"Intussusception","

Intussusception

Pathogenesis &
epidemiology

  • Telescoping of one bowel segment into adjacent segment (most often ileocecal)
  • Bowel edema → ischemia & necrosis
  • Age 6 months to 3 years most common

Risk factors

  • Hypertrophy of intestinal Peyer patches (eg, recent viral illness)
  • Pathologic lead point (eg, Meckel diverticulum, HSP, intestinal tumor)

Clinical
presentation

  • Sudden, intermittent abdominal pain & vomiting
  • Sausage-shaped mass in right abdomen
  • Currant jelly stools
  • Lethargy or altered mental status

Diagnosis &
management

  • Ultrasonography: target sign 
  • Nonoperative enema reduction* (eg, air, saline, iodine-contrast)
  • Surgical intervention for failed enema reduction or signs of peritonitis
*Diagnostic & therapeutic.

HSP = Henoch-Schönlein purpura. 

"]],"hirschsprung-disease":[[33644,"Hirschsprung disease","

Hirschsprung disease

Pathophysiology

  • Failed neural crest cell migration to distal colon
  • Absent parasympathetic ganglia → chronic rectosigmoid contraction

Clinical presentation

  • Neonates: delayed passage of meconium, bilious emesis
  • Children: chronic constipation, failure to thrive

Examination findings

  • Distended abdomen
  • Tight anal sphincter & absent stool in rectal vault
  • Forceful stool expulsion on rectal examination (squirt sign)

Evaluation

  • Contrast enema: narrow rectosigmoid area with dilated proximal colon
  • Anorectal manometry: impaired relaxation of internal anal sphincter
  • Rectal suction biopsy (diagnostic): absent submucosal ganglion

Treatment

  • Surgical resection of aganglionic segment
"], [61178,"Delayed passage of meconium","

Delayed passage of meconium

Hirschsprung disease

Meconium ileus

Pathophysiology

  • Failure of neural crest cell migration
  • Obstruction by inspissated stool

Level of obstruction

  • Rectosigmoid
  • Ileum

Rectal examination

  • Increased tone
  • Positive squirt sign*
  • Normal tone
  • Negative squirt sign*

Meconium consistency

  • Normal
  • Inspissated

Imaging

  • Dilated proximal colon ± small bowel
  • Narrow rectosigmoid
  • Dilated small bowel
  • Microcolon

Associated disorder

  • Down syndrome
  • Cystic fibrosis

*Expulsion of gas/stool on rectal examination.

"], [64752,"Hirschsprung disease","

Hirschsprung disease

Pathophysiology

  • Failure of neural crest cell migration caudally to distal colon
  • Absent parasympathetic ganglia in affected submucosal & myenteric plexuses
  • Chronically contracted colonic segment

Clinical features

  • Delayed passage of meconium in neonates
  • Chronic constipation
  • Abdominal distension

Evaluation

  • Contrast enema: narrow rectosigmoid area with dilated proximal colon
  • Rectal suction biopsy (diagnostic): absent submucosal ganglia
"], [120022,"Differential diagnosis of delayed passage of meconium","

Differential diagnosis of delayed passage of meconium

Diagnosis

Level of obstruction

Meconium consistency

Meconium plug syndrome

Descending colon

Normal

Meconium ileus

Terminal ileum
