Hirschsprung disease

Rectosigmoid

Normal

"]],"diverticula-of-the-gi-tract--diverticulosis":[[34305,"Diverticular bleeding","

Diverticular bleeding

Etiology

  • Arterial erosion due to colonic mucosal outcropping

Clinical
presentation

  • Painless hematochezia in patients age >40
  • Bleeding often self-limited but can recur

Diagnosis

  • Colonoscopy or tagged red blood cell scan

Treatment

  • Intravenous volume replacement
  • Endoscopic therapy or angiographic embolization
  • Colonic resection for persistent bleeding
"]],"other-intestinal-disorders--small-intestinal-bacterial-overgrowth":[[34493,"Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth","

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

Pathogenesis

  • ↑ Colonic bacteria (eg, Bacteroides, Escherichia) in small intestine
  • ↑ Bacterial carbohydrate fermentation (eg, flatulence, bloating)
  • ↓ Vitamin B12 (bacterial consumption)
  • ↑ Folate, vitamin K (bacterial synthesis)
  • Mucosal injury/inflammation → malabsorption (eg, fat)

Risk factors

  • Anatomic abnormalities (eg, strictures, Roux-en-Y)
  • Motility disorders (eg, scleroderma)
  • Immunodeficiency (eg, IgA)
  • Gastric hypochlorhydria (PPI use)

Clinical manifestations

  • Diarrhea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal pain
  • Severe: steatorrhea, nutritional deficiencies (vitamins A, D, E, B12)

Treatment

  • Antibiotics (eg, rifaxmin), dietary changes (eg, low carbohydrate)

PPI= proton pump inhibitor.

"]],"other-esophageal-pathologies--mallory-weiss-syndrome":[[34588,"Mallory-Weiss tear","

Mallory-Weiss tear

Etiology

  • Sudden increase in abdominal pressure (eg, forceful retching)
  • Mucosal tear in esophagus or stomach (submucosal arterial or venous plexus bleeding)
  • Risk factors: hiatal hernia, alcoholism

Clinical presentation

  • Vomiting, retching
  • Hematemesis
  • Epigastric pain

Diagnosis

  • Longitudinal laceration on endoscopy

Treatment

  • Most heal spontaneously
  • Endoscopic therapy for persistent bleeding
"], [36360,"Characteristics of gastroesophageal mural injury","

Characteristics of gastroesophageal mural injury

Etiology

Mallory-Weiss syndrome

Boerhaave syndrome

  • Forceful retching
  • Mucosal tear
  • Submucosal venous or arterial plexus bleeding
  • Forceful retching
  • Transmural tear
  • Spillage of esophageal air/fluid into surrounding tissues

Clinical presentation

  • Epigastric/back pain
  • Hematemesis (bright red or coffee-grounds appearance)
  • Possible hypovolemia
  • Chest/back/epigastric pain
  • Crepitus, crunching sound (Hamman sign)
  • Odynophagia, dyspnea, fever, sepsis

Studies

  • Upper GI endoscopy confirms diagnosis (& can treat persistent bleeding)
  • X-ray of the chest: pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, pleural effusion
  • Esophagography or CT scan with water-soluble contrast confirms diagnosis

Management

  • Acid suppression
  • Most heal spontaneously
  • Acid suppression, antibiotics, NPO
  • Emergency surgical consultation

GI = gastrointestinal.

"]],"acid-suppression-therapy":[[34849,"Indications for stress ulcer prophylaxis","

Indications for stress ulcer prophylaxis

Any 1 factor

  • Coagulopathy: platelets <50,000/mm3, INR >1.5,
    PTT >2x normal control
  • Mechanical ventilation >48 hr
  • GI bleeding or ulceration in last 12 months
  • Head trauma, spinal cord injury, major burn

≥2 factors

  • Glucocorticoid therapy
  • >1 week ICU stay
  • Occult GI bleeding >6 days
  • Sepsis

GI = gastrointestinal; ICU = intensive care unit.

"]],"_more":[[34875,"Rectovaginal fistula","

Rectovaginal fistula

Risk factors

  • Pelvic radiation
  • Obstetric trauma
  • Pelvic surgery
  • Colon cancer
  • Diverticulitis
  • Crohn disease

Clinical features

  • Uncontrollable passage of gas &/or feces from the vagina

Diagnostic studies

  • Physical examination
  • Fistulography
  • MRI
  • Endosonography
"], [35858,"Differential diagnosis of delayed gastric emptying","

Differential diagnosis of delayed gastric emptying

Mechanism

Common etiologies

Diagnostic tests

Intrinsic obstruction

  • Peptic ulcer stricture
  • Gastric malignancy
  • Bezoar/foreign body
  • Gastric volvulus
  • Small bowel mass
  • Upper endoscopy ± CT/MR enterography or barium follow-through to rule out small bowel pathology

Extrinsic obstruction

  • Malignancy
  • Superior mesenteric artery syndrome

Impaired motility

(eg, gastroparesis)

  • Medication (eg, anticholinergics)
  • Autonomic neuropathy (eg, diabetic)
  • Nerve injury (eg, postsurgical)
  • Idiopathic (postviral)
  • Nuclear gastric emptying study
  • Gastroduodenal manometry
"], [36550,"Causes of fecal incontinence","

Causes of fecal incontinence

Trauma

  • Operative vaginal delivery, obstetric laceration
  • Surgery (hemorrhoidectomy, anorectal surgery)

Neurologic

  • Diabetic neuropathy
  • Multiple sclerosis
  • Spinal cord injury
  • Dementia

Chronic disease

  • Constipation
  • Hemorrhoids, rectal prolapse
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Infiltrative disease (cancer, systemic sclerosis)
  • Pelvic irradiation
"], [38224,"Gastroparesis","

Gastroparesis

Causes

  • Diabetes mellitus (autonomic neuropathy)
  • Medications (eg, opioids, anticholinergic drugs)
  • Traumatic/postsurgical injury (ie, vagus nerve injury)
  • Neurologic (eg, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury)
  • Idiopathic/postviral

Clinical features

  • Nausea & vomiting, epigastric abdominal pain
  • Early satiety, bloating, weight loss
  • Labile glucose (diabetes mellitus)
  • Epigastric distension & succussion splash

Diagnosis

  • Exclude obstruction: upper endoscopy ± CT/MR enterography
  • Assess motility: nuclear gastric emptying study

Treatment

  • Frequent small meals (low fat, soluble fiber only)
  • Promotility drugs (eg, metoclopramide, erythromycin)
  • Gastric electrical stimulation &/or jejunal feeding tube (refractory symptoms)
"], [46917,"Food protein","

Food protein–induced allergic proctocolitis

Pathophysiology

  • Non–IgE-mediated reaction
  • Eosinophilic inflammation of rectosigmoid colon
  • Common triggers: cow's milk & soy proteins

Risk factors

  • Eczema
  • Family history of food allergies

Clinical features

  • Age 2-8 weeks (up to 6 months)
  • Well-appearing
  • Blood- &/or mucus-streaked stools (positive Hemoccult test)

Diagnosis & treatment

  • Clinical diagnosis confirmed by symptom resolution after protein elimination
    • Breastfed infants: restrict dairy (± soy) from maternal diet
    • Formula-fed infants: switch to hydrolyzed formula

Prognosis

  • Tolerance of offending protein by age 1
"], [47889,"Anorectal fistula (fistula in ano)","

Anorectal fistula (fistula in ano)

Causes

  • Perianal abscess
  • Crohn disease
  • Malignancy, radiation proctitis
  • Infection (eg, lymphogranuloma venereum)

Clinical manifestations

  • Perirectal pain, discharge
  • Inflammatory papule/pustule
  • Palpable fistula tract

Management

  • Assess extent of fistula
    • Gentle probe

"], [63794,"Management of necrotizing enterocolitis","

interventions

  • Nasogastric decompression
  • Blood cultures & empiric antibiotics
  • Intravenous fluid repletion

"]],"diverticula-of-the-gi-tract":[[41620,"Diverticular disease","

Etiology

  • Diverticulosis: ↑ intraluminal pressure causing herniation

  • Diverticular bleeding: painless hematochezia
  • Diverticulitis: left lower quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, fever

Risk
factors

  • Diet high in red meat & fat & low in fiber
  • Obesity, physical inactivity, smoking
"]],"alpha1-antitrypsin-deficiency":[[42498,"Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency","

Etiology

  • Autosomal codominant inheritance
  • ↓ Alpha-1 antitrypsin leads to unchecked elastase activity

Clinical presentation

  • Early-onset (age ≤45) panacinar emphysema
  • Basilar lung areas predominantly affected
  • Smoking accelerates disease
  • Associated liver dysfunction or cirrhosis 

Diagnosis

  • Obstructive pattern on PFT: ↓ FEV1/FVC ratio, ↓ DLCO
  • ↓ Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level & genetic testing

DLCO = diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide; PFT = pulmonary function testing.

"]],"meckel-diverticulum":[[45286,"Meckel diverticulum","

Meckel diverticulum

Pathogenesis

  • Persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
  • Often contains ectopic gastric mucosa → intestinal ulceration & bleeding

Epidemiology

Rule of 2s:

  • Presentation often by age 2 (but can occur at any age)
  • Usually <2 inches long
  • Location within 2 feet of ileocecal valve

  • May be asymptomatic (incidental finding)
  • Painless rectal bleeding ± iron deficiency anemia
  • Acute abdominal pain due to complications:
    • Intussusception (recurrent, atypical)
    • Diverticulitis (mimics appendicitis)
    • Bowel obstruction, perforation (peritoneal signs)

  • Technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan detects gastric mucosa

"]],"cholelithiasis-and-related-pathologies--cholecystitis":[[48855,"Emphysematous cholecystitis","

Emphysematous cholecystitis

Risk factors

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Vascular compromise
  • Immunosuppression

Clinical
presentation

  • Fever, right upper quadrant pain, nausea/vomiting
  • Crepitus in abdominal wall adjacent to gallbladder

Diagnosis

  • Air-fluid levels in gallbladder, gas in gallbladder wall
  • Cultures with gas-forming Clostridium, Escherichia coli
  • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, mildly elevated aminotransferases

Treatment

  • Emergency cholecystectomy
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics with Clostridium coverage
    (eg, piperacillin-tazobactam)
"], [55445,"Acute calculous","

Acute calculous cholecystitis

Risk factors

  • Obesity
  • Female sex
  • Age >40
  • Pregnancy

Clinical
features

  • Fever
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • RUQ/epigastric pain
  • Murphy sign (pain with gallbladder palpation)

Diagnosis

  • RUQ ultrasonography: thickened gallbladder,
    sludge, gallstones
  • HIDA scan: nonvisualization of gallbladder

Management

  • NPO, intravenous fluids
  • Antibiotics
  • Cholecystectomy (<72 hr)

RUQ = right upper quadrant.

"]],"other-esophageal-pathologies--esophageal-perforation":[[49014,"Esophageal perforation","

Esophageal perforation

Etiology

  • Instrumentation (eg, endoscopy), trauma
  • Effort rupture (Boerhaave syndrome)
  • Esophagitis (infectious/drug-induced/caustic)

Clinical presentation

  • Chest/back &/or epigastric pain, systemic signs (eg, fever)
  • Crepitus, Hamman sign (crunching sound on auscultation)
  • Pleural effusion with atypical (eg, green) fluid

Diagnosis

  • X-ray or CT scan of chest: widened mediastinum, pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax, pleural effusion
  • CT scan: esophageal wall thickening, mediastinal fluid collection
  • Esophagography with water-soluble contrast: leak from perforation

Management

  • NPO, IV antibiotics & proton pump inhibitors
  • Emergency surgical consultation
IV = intravenous.
"]],"irritable-bowel-syndrome":[[49427,"Clinical features of irritable bowel syndrome","

Clinical features of irritable bowel syndrome

Rome IV diagnostic criteria

Recurrent abdominal pain/discomfort ≥1 days/week for past 3 months & ≥2 of the following:

  • Related to defecation (improves or worsens)
  • Change in stool frequency
  • Change in stool form

Alarm features

  • Older age of onset (≥50)
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Nocturnal diarrhea (ie, fasting state)
  • Worsening pain
  • Unintended weight loss
  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • Elevated C-reactive protein
  • Positive fecal lactoferrin or calprotectin
  • Family history of early colon cancer or IBD
IBD = inflammatory bowel disease.
"], [94341,"Pharmacologic management","

Pharmacologic management of IBS

Abdominal pain

  • First line: antispasmodic therapy (eg, hyoscyamine) as needed
  • Second line: tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline)*

Diarrhea

  • First line: soluble fiber (eg, psyllium), loperamide
  • Second line: bile acid sequestrants (eg, cholestyramine), serotonin-3 receptor antagonists (eg, alosetron)

Constipation

  • First line: soluble fiber (eg, psyllium), osmotic laxatives (eg, PEG)
  • Second line: lubiprostone, guanylate cyclase agonists (eg, linaclotide), sodium/hydrogen exchanger 3 inhibitor (eg, tenapanor) 

*Preferred for IBS with diarrhea; avoid with constipation.

IBS = irritable bowel syndrome; PEG = polyethylene glycol.

"], [126884,"Rome IV criteria for functional constipation","

Rome IV criteria for functional constipation

  • Symptoms present ≥6 months, with full criteria ≥3 months
  • ≥2 present for ≥25% of bowel movements
    • Straining with defecation
    • Lumpy or hard stool
    • Sensation of incomplete evacuation
    • Sensation of anorectal obstruction
    • Manual maneuvers required for defecation (eg, digital evacuation)
    • <3 bowel movements/week
  • Loose stools rare unless laxatives are used
  • Does not meet criteria for irritable bowel disorder
"]],"pancreatitis--chronic-pancreatitis":[[49748,"Overview of chronic pancreatitis","

Overview of chronic pancreatitis

Etiology

  • Alcohol use
  • Cystic fibrosis (common in children)
  • Ductal obstruction (eg, malignancy, stones)
  • Autoimmune

Clinical presentation

  • Chronic epigastric pain with intermittent pain-free intervals
  • Malabsorption: steatorrhea, weight loss
  • Diabetes mellitus

Laboratory results/imaging

  • Amylase/lipase can be normal & nondiagnostic
  • CT scan or MRCP can show calcifications, dilated ducts & enlarged pancreas

Treatment

  • Pain management
  • Alcohol & smoking cessation
  • Frequent, small meals
  • Pancreatic enzyme supplements

MRCP = magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography.

"]],"budd-chiari-syndrome":[[49844,"Budd-Chiari syndrome","

Budd-Chiari syndrome

Etiology

  • Hepatic venous outflow obstruction
  • Usually due to:
    • Myeloproliferative disorder (eg, PV)
    • Malignancy (eg, hepatocellular carcinoma)
    • Oral contraception use/pregnancy

Manifestations

  • Acute
    • Jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding
    • Prolonged INR/PTT; elevated transaminases
  • Subacute/chronic
    • Vague, progressive abdominal pain
    • Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites
    • Mild/moderate elevation in bilirubin, transaminases

Diagnosis

  • Abdominal Doppler ultrasonography: ↓ hepatic vein flow
  • Investigation for underlying disorders (eg, JAK2 testing for PV)

PV = polycythemia vera.

"]],"hernias-continued--diaphragmatic-hernia":[[49909,"Congenital diaphragmatic hernia","

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

Pathogenesis

  • Incomplete fusion of pleuroperitoneal folds
  • Herniation of bowel into chest → pulmonary hypoplasia & hypertension

Clinical
features

  • Respiratory distress (within hours of birth)
  • Absent breath sounds ipsilateral to defect
  • Concave abdomen; barrel-shaped chest

Diagnosis

  • Chest x-ray: intrathoracic bowel loops, displaced cardiac silhouette

Management

  • Endotracheal intubation
  • Gastric decompression (eg, nasogastric tube)
  • Surgical correction
"]],"hernias-continued":[[49919,"Groin hernias","

Groin hernias

Type

Classic presentation

Pathophysiology

Anatomy

Indirect inguinal

Male infants

Patent processus vaginalis

  • Originates lateral to inferior epigastric vessels
  • Protrudes through the deep inguinal ring into inguinal canal
  • May extend into the scrotum (following spermatic cord)

Direct inguinal

Older men

Weakness of transversalis fascia

  • Protrudes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels into Hesselbach's triangle
  • May pass through superficial inguinal ring
  • No direct route into the scrotum

Femoral

Women

Widening of the femoral ring

  • Emerges inferior to inguinal ligament
  • Protrudes through the femoral ring into the femoral canal
"], [98897,"Groin hernias","

Groin hernias

Epidemiology

  • Inguinal: more common in male patients
  • Femoral: more common in female patients; more likely to become incarcerated/strangulated (~40%)

Clinical features

  • Uncomplicated (reducible): ↑ groin bulge with ↑ abdominal pressure (eg, cough) ± discomfort
  • Incarcerated (nonreducible): moderate to severe groin pain & swelling
  • Strangulated (nonreducible & ischemic): severe groin pain & swelling, vomiting, fever ± peritonitis

Diagnosis

  • Clinical diagnosis; confirmatory testing typically not required
  • If diagnosis unclear: ultrasonography (preferred), CT scan, or MRI of the groin

Management

  • Watchful waiting considered for male patients with asymptomatic inguinal hernias
  • Elective surgical repair: symptomatic groin hernias; femoral hernias
  • Urgent or immediate surgical repair: incarcerated or strangulated hernias
"]],"hernias":[[50309,"Incisional hernia","

Incisional hernia

Pathogenesis

  • Breakdown of prior fascial closure

Risk factors

  • Obesity
  • Tobacco smoking
  • Poor wound healing (eg, immunosuppression, malnutrition)
  • Vertical or midline incision
  • Surgical site infection

Clinical features

  • Abdominal mass that enlarges with Valsalva maneuver
  • Palpable fascial edges in patients who are not obese
  • Possible delayed presentation (months to years)

Diagnosis

  • Clinical
  • CT scan of abdomen
"]],"malrotation":[[50573,"Malrotation with midgut volvulus","

Malrotation with midgut volvulus

Pathogenesis

  • Failure of normal embryonic gut rotation
  • Narrow mesenteric base allows for ↑ small bowel mobility
  • Twisting of small bowel around superior mesenteric artery → gut ischemia & necrosis

Clinical
features

  • Most common in infancy (usually age <1 month)
  • Acute: bilious emesis, abdominal distension
  • Chronic: intermittent abdominal pain & vomiting, failure to thrive 
  • Untreated: hematochezia, peritonitis & shock

Diagnosis

  • Abdominal x-ray: ± dilated bowel, air-fluid levels, pneumoperitoneum
  • Upper gastrointestinal series (gold standard): ligament of Treitz on right; corkscrew, or bird's-beak, duodenum

Treatment

  • Emergency laparotomy (to relieve volvulus)
  • Ladd procedure (to reposition malrotated bowel)
"]],"inflammatory-bowel-diseases":[[51005,"Inflammatory bowel disease subtype characteristics","

"]],"biliary-atresia":[[51803,"Biliary atresia","

Biliary atresia

Pathogenesis

  • Extrahepatic bile duct fibrosis → obstruction of bile (& bilirubin) flow from liver to intestines

Clinical
findings

  • Asymptomatic at birth
  • Infants age 2-8 weeks:
    • Jaundice, acholic stools, dark urine
    • Hepatomegaly

Diagnostic

  • Direct hyperbilirubinemia
  • Ultrasonography:
    • Absent/abnormal gallbladder &/or CBD
  • Liver biopsy:
    • Intrahepatic bile duct proliferation
    • Portal tract inflammation & edema
    • Fibrosis
  • Intraoperative cholangiography (gold standard):
    • Biliary obstruction

  • Surgical hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai procedure)
  • Liver transplant

CBD = common bile duct.

"]],"antacids--calcium-carbonate":[[52312,"Milk-alkali syndrome","

Milk-alkali syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Excessive intake of calcium & absorbable alkali
  • Renal vasoconstriction & decreased GFR
  • Renal loss of sodium & water, reabsorption of bicarbonate

Symptoms

  • Nausea, vomiting, constipation
  • Polyuria, polydipsia
  • Neuropsychiatric symptoms

Laboratory
findings

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Acute kidney injury
  • Suppressed PTH

Treatment

  • Discontinuation of causative agent
  • Isotonic saline followed by furosemide

GFR = glomerular filtration rate; PTH = parathyroid hormone.

Retroperitoneal abdominal organs

  • Esophagus

"]],"achalasia":[[54343,"Achalasia","

Achalasia

Pathophysiology

  • Inflammatory degeneration of inhibitory ganglions of the myenteric plexus

Clinical
presentation

  • Chronic dysphagia to solids & liquids, regurgitation
  • Heartburn, weight loss

Diagnosis

  • Manometry: incomplete LES relaxation, ↓ peristalsis of distal esophagus
  • Barium esophagography: smooth "bird-beak" narrowing at gastroesophageal junction
  • Upper endoscopy to exclude malignancy

  • Myotomy or pneumatic balloon dilation
  • Botulinum toxin injection, nitrates & CCB

CCB = calcium channel blocker; LES = lower esophageal sphincter.

"]],"pectinate-line--anal-fissure":[[55263,"Anal fissures","

Anal fissures

Etiology

  • Local trauma (eg, constipation, prolonged diarrhea, anal sex)
  • Inflammatory bowel disease (eg, Crohn disease)
  • Malignancy

Clinical
presentation

  • Pain with bowel movements
  • Bright red blood on toilet paper or stool surface
  • Most common at posterior anal midline
  • Chronic fissure may have skin tag at distal end

Treatment

  • High-fiber diet & adequate fluid intake
  • Stool softeners
  • Sitz baths
  • Topical anesthetics & vasodilators (eg, nifedipine, nitroglycerin)
"]],"cholelithiasis-and-related-pathologies":[[55446,"Management of gallstones","

Management of gallstones

Gallstones without symptoms

  • No treatment required in most patients

Gallstones with typical biliary colic symptoms

  • Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
  • Possible ursodeoxycholic acid in poor surgical candidates

Complicated gallstone disease*

  • Cholecystectomy within 72 hr

*Acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, gallstone pancreatitis.

"]],"biliary-tract-disease--primary-sclerosing-cholangitis":[[55618,"Primary sclerosing cholangitis","

Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic initially; fatigue & pruritus with progressive disease
  • Associated with IBD, particularly ulcerative colitis

Laboratory & imaging results

  • Cholestasis (↑ ALP, GGT, bilirubin)
  • Multifocal strictures/dilation of bile ducts on MRCP

Complications

  • Cholangitis, cholangiocarcinoma, colon cancer
  • Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies

ALP = alkaline phosphatase; GGT = γ-glutamyl transferase; IBD = inflammatory bowel disease; MRCP = MR cholangiopancreatography.

"]],"anticonstipation-drugs":[[57637,"Anticonstipation agents","

Anticonstipation agents

Bulk-forming laxatives
(eg, fiber supplements)

  • Binds luminal water to decrease consistency of stool
  • Adverse effects: flatulence, abdominal distension

Osmotic laxatives
(eg, polyethylene glycol, magnesium hydroxide, lactulose)

  • Osmotically active agent that draws water into the lumen
  • Adverse effects: electrolyte disturbances, bloating

Surfactant
(eg, docusate)

  • Decreases stool surface tension, enabling water to enter stool
  • Adverse effects: rare

Stimulant laxatives
(eg, bisacodyl, senna)

  • Activates enteric nerves in myenteric plexus to stimulate peristalsis
  • Adverse effects: abdominal cramping, electrolyte disturbances

Chloride channel agonist
(eg, lubiprostone)

  • Causes chloride efflux into intestinal lumen, which is followed by sodium and water
  • Adverse effects: headache, nausea

Peripherally acting µ-opioid
receptor antagonists
(eg, methylnaltrexone)

  • Counteracts inhibitory effect of opioids on peristalsis
  • Adverse effects: rare (does not cause opiate withdrawal)

*All constipation medications can cause diarrhea at high doses.

"], [72157,"Opioid-induced constipation management","

Opioid-induced constipation management

Nonpharmacologic
interventions

  • Increased fluids
  • Increased dietary fiber
  • Increased exercise
  • Early ambulation (postsurgical)

Pharmacotherapy

  • Osmotic laxatives (eg, polyethylene glycol, lactulose)
  • Contact cathartics or stimulant laxatives (eg, senna, bisacodyl)
  • Hard stools: stool softeners (eg, docusate)
  • Refractory: methylnaltrexone or lubiprostone
"]],"autoimmune-hepatitis":[[58707,"Autoimmune liver disease","

Autoimmune
hepatitis

Primary biliary
cholangitis

Primary sclerosing
cholangitis

Epidemiology

  • Female > male
  • Female >> male
  • Male > female

Associations

  • Other autoimmune disorders
  • Other autoimmune disorders

Liver injury
pattern

  • Hepatocellular (↑ transaminases)
  • Cholestatic (↑ alkaline phosphatase)
  • Cholestatic (↑ alkaline phosphatase)

Antibodies

"]],"serum-markers-of-liver-pathology":[[58712,"Patterns of liver injury","

Patterns of liver injury

Hepatocellular

Cholestatic

  • AST & ALT >> alkaline phosphatase
  • ↑ Bilirubin
  • Alkaline phosphatase >> AST & ALT
  • ↑ Bilirubin
  • ↑ Gamma-glutamyl transferase

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate transaminase.

"]],"cholangiocarcinoma":[[58717,"Cholangiocarcinoma","

Cholangiocarcinoma

Risk factors

  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis (90% of patients), cirrhosis, liver fluke infection (eg, southwest Asia)

Clinical & laboratory findings

  • Often clinically silent until advanced; may have jaundice, weight loss, RUQ pain
  • Cholestasis (↑↑ alkaline phosphatase, hyperbilirubinemia)
  • Elevated CA 19-9

Imaging

  • Unexplained extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (eg, ductal dilation but no gallstones or pancreatic mass on ultrasonography, CT scan)
  • Intrahepatic mass (~20% of cancers)

Histology

  • Adenocarcinoma with cuboidal or columnar cells with prominent nucleoli arranged in glandular structures
  • + Mucin production, + desmoplastic response
CA 19-9 = cancer-associated antigen 19-9; RUQ = right upper quadrant.
"]],"volvulus":[[58826,"Sigmoid volvulus","

Sigmoid volvulus

Risk factors

  • Sigmoid colon redundancy (eg, dilation/elongation from chronic constipation)
  • Colonic dysmotility (eg, underlying neurologic disorder)

Presentation

  • Slowly progressive abdominal discomfort/distension ± obstructive symptoms (eg, nausea, emesis, obstipation)
  • Abdomen distended & tympanitic to percussion

Imaging

  • X-ray: dilated, inverted, U-shaped loop of colon (coffee bean sign)
  • CT scan: dilated sigmoid colon, mesenteric twisting (whirl sign)

Management

  • Endoscopic detorsion (eg, flexible sigmoidoscopy) & elective sigmoid colectomy
  • Emergency sigmoid colectomy if perforation/peritonitis present
"]],"tracheoesophageal-anomalies":[[59520,"VACTERL association","

VACTERL association

V: vertebral anomaly

A: anorectal malformation

C: cardiovascular anomaly

T: tracheoesophageal fistula

E: esophageal atresia

R: renal &/or radial anomaly

L: limb defect

"], [60020,"Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia","

Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia

Pathogenesis

  • Defective division of foregut into esophagus & trachea
  • Most commonly results in proximal esophageal pouch & fistula between distal trachea & esophagus

Clinical
features

  • Coughing, choking, vomiting with feeding
  • Excessive oral secretions
  • Commonly part of VACTERL association

Diagnosis

  • Inability to pass enteric tube into stomach
  • X-ray: enteric tube coiled in proximal esophagus

Management

  • Surgical correction
  • VACTERL screening: echocardiography, renal ultrasound

VACTERL = Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, TracheoEsophageal, Renal, Limb defects.

"]],"other-intestinal-disorders--proctitis":[[59779,"Radiation proctitis","

Radiation proctitis

Acute radiation proctitis

Chronic radiation proctitis

Postradiation onset

  • ≤8 weeks
  • >3 months to years

Pathogenesis

  • Direct mucosal damage
  • Obliterative endarteritis & chronic mucosal ischemia
  • Submucosal fibrosis

Manifestations

  • Diarrhea, mucus discharge, tenesmus
  • Minimal bleeding
  • Severe bleeding
  • ± Strictures with constipation & rectal pain

Endoscopic appearance

  • Severe erythema
  • Edema, ulcerations
  • Multiple telangiectasias
  • Mucosal pallor & friability

Management

  • Antidiarrheals (eg, loperamide)
  • Butyrate enemas
  • Endoscopic thermal coagulation
  • Sucralfate or glucocorticoid enemas
"], [60100,"Gonococcal proctitis","

Gonococcal proctitis

Transmission

  • Receptive anal intercourse
  • Direct spread from the vagina

Manifestations

  • Mucopurulent anal discharge, occasional rectal bleeding
  • Tenesmus, constipation
  • Pruritus, rectal pain, rectal fullness

Diagnosis

  • Nucleic acid amplification test of rectal swab

Treatment

  • Ceftriaxone + doxycycline (to cover Chlamydia)
"]],"proton-pump-inhibitors":[[60954,"Proton pump inhibitors","

Proton pump inhibitors

Mechanism
of action

  • Irreversible inhibition of parietal cell hydrogen-potassium-ATPase

Common uses

  • Gastroesophageal reflux disease
  • Peptic ulcer disease

Adverse effects

  • Malabsorption of calcium, iron, magnesium & vitamin B12
    • Enhances fat absorption in patients given pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy
  • Increases risk of infection (eg, Clostridioidesdifficile, pneumonia)
  • Osteoporosis, chronic kidney disease, SIBO

SIBO = small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

"]],"hemochromatosis":[[61061,"Clinical manifestations of hereditary hemochromatosis","

Clinical manifestations of hereditary hemochromatosis

Skin

  • Hyperpigmentation

Musculoskeletal

  • Arthritis (particularly 2nd & 3rd MCP joints)
  • Chondrocalcinosis

Gastrointestinal

  • Elevated liver enzymes, hepatomegaly (early)
  • Cirrhosis & hepatocellular carcinoma (late)

Endocrine

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Hypopituitarism (eg, secondary hypogonadism, hypothyroidism)

Cardiac

  • Restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy
  • Conduction abnormalities
MCP = metacarpophalangeal.
"]],"hereditary-hyperbilirubinemias--gilbert-syndrome":[[69343,"Gilbert","

Gilbertsyndrome

Epidemiology

  • Most common inherited disorder of bilirubin metabolism

Pathogenesis

  • ↓ Hepatic UDP glucuronosyltransferase activity → ↓ conjugation of bilirubin

Clinical findings

  • Recurrent episodes of mild jaundice
  • Provoked by stress (eg, febrile illness, fasting, dehydration, vigorous exercise, menstruation, surgery)

Diagnosis

  • ↑ Unconjugated bilirubin (ie, indirect hyperbilirubinemia)
  • Normal CBC, blood smear, reticulocyte count
  • Normal AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase

Treatment

  • Benign; no treatment required

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; CBC = complete blood count.

"]],"hepatic-encephalopathy":[[80368,"Precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy","

Precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy

↑ Nitrogenous waste production

  • Upper GI bleeding
  • Hypokalemia & metabolic alkalosis
  • Muscle catabolism/wasting
  • Infections (especially SBP, urease-producing bacterial cystitis)

↓ Ammonia clearance

  • Hepatic ischemia (eg, hypovolemia, hypoxia, anemia, hypotension, PVT)
  • Hepatocyte loss (eg, toxins, replacement by HCC)
  • Constipation
  • Renal insufficiency

↑ Portosystemic shunting

  • Spontaneous
  • Iatrogenic (TIPS)

Other factors

  • CNS depressant drugs (eg, opioids, benzodiazepines)

GI = gastrointestinal; HCC = hepatocellular carcinoma; PVT = portal venous thrombosis; SBP = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; TIPS = transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt.

"]],"diverticula-of-the-gi-tract--diverticulitis":[[81364,"Clinical features of colovesical fistula","

Clinical features of colovesical fistula

Etiology

  • Diverticular disease (sigmoid most common)
  • Crohn disease
  • Malignancy (colon, bladder, pelvic organs)

Clinical presentation

  • Pneumaturia (air in urine)
  • Fecaluria (stool in urine)
  • Recurrent urinary tract infections (mixed flora)

Diagnosis

  • CT scan of the abdomen with oral or rectal (not intravenous) contrast
  • Colonoscopy to exclude colonic malignancy
"], [81413,"Clinical features of acute diverticulitis","

Clinical features of acute diverticulitis

Clinical presentation

  • Abdominal pain
  • Nausea/vomiting, altered bowel movements
  • Fever, leukocytosis
  • Possible sterile pyuria

Diagnosis

  • CT scan of the abdomen (oral & intravenous contrast)

Management

  • Bowel rest
  • Antibiotics (eg, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole)
  • Colonoscopy 6-8 weeks after resolution

Complications

  • Abscess, obstruction, fistula, perforation
"]],"ventral-wall-defects":[[86976,"Pediatric abdominal wall defects","

Pediatric abdominal wall defects

Diagnosis

Pathophysiology

Clinical features

Congenital umbilical hernia

  • Incomplete closure of umbilical ring (fascial opening)
  • Benign, reducible protrusion
  • Defect covered by skin
  • Midline (umbilical cord at apex)

Omphalocele

  • Abnormal gut rotation without physiologic reduction back into abdominal cavity
  • Sac containing bowel ± other abdominal organs
  • Defect covered by peritoneum (no skin, fascia, muscle)
  • Midline (umbilical cord at apex)

Gastroschisis

  • Full-thickness abdominal wall defect
  • Eviscerated bowel
  • Not covered by membrane
  • Located to the right of midline/umbilicus
"]],"spontaneous-bacterial-peritonitis":[[90523,"Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis","

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Clinical presentation

  • Ascites
  • Fever
  • Abdominal pain/tenderness
  • Altered mental status

Diagnosis

  • Paracentesis (ascitic fluid analysis):
    • PMNs1 ≥ 250 cells/mm3, protein < 1 g/dL
    • Positive culture: most commonly Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, streptococci

Treatment

  • 3rd-generation cephalosporin: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
  • Critically ill or risk for MDR pathogens: piperacillin/tazobactam, carbapenem (eg, meropenem)
  • Duration: 5–7 days

Prevention

  • Criteria: ≥ 1 SBP episode or ascitic fluid protein < 1.5 g/dL PLUS impaired renal or hepatic function2
  • Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim or fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin)

1. Calculated using the white blood cell count & percentage of neutrophils & bands.

2. Impaired renal function: serum creatinine ≥ 1.2 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen ≥ 25 mg/dL, or serum sodium ≤ 130 mEq/L; impaired liver function: Child-Pugh score ≥ 9 & total bilirubin ≥ 3 mg/dL.

MDR = multidrug-resistant; PMNs = polymorphonuclear leukocytes; SBP = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

"]],"barrett-esophagus":[[91971,"Barrett esophagus","

Barrett esophagus

Definition

  • Intestinal metaplasia in distal esophagus (ie, replacement of stratified squamous epithelium with metaplastic columnar epithelium)

Risk
factors

  • Chronic GERD (eg, >5 years)
  • White patient
  • Family history
  • Age >50
  • Obesity
  • Smoking

Screening &
management

  • Consider screening patients with multiple risk factors
  • Lifelong PPI (reduces cancer risk, heals esophageal damage)
  • If dysplasia is present, offer endoscopic surveillance vs eradication

Prognosis

  • <1%/year risk for malignancy development, higher if dysplasia is present

GERD = gastroesophageal reflux disease; PPI = proton pump inhibitor.

"]],"ventral-wall-defects--gastroschisis":[[94793,"Gastroschisis","

Gastroschisis

Clinical
features

  • Full-thickness abdominal wall defect lateral to umbilicus
  • Bowel herniation without covering membrane
  • Usually isolated (extraintestinal anomalies rare)

Prenatal
findings

  • ↑ Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein
  • Free-floating bowel on fetal ultrasonography

Management

  • Place lower body in plastic bag to minimize heat & fluid loss
  • Insert tube for gastric decompression
  • Start intravenous fluids & antibiotics
  • Perform surgical repair (primary or staged closure)
"]],"liver-tumors--hepatocellular-carcinoma":[[119831,"Indications for biannual hepatocellular carcinoma ultrasonographic surveillance","

Indications for biannual hepatocellular carcinoma ultrasonographic surveillance

Positive HBsAg

  • Asians: men age ≥40, women age ≥50
  • Africans and North American Black patients at diagnosis
  • Patients with HBV and cirrhosis
  • Caucasians with a high viral load
  • Family history of HCC
 

All patients with cirrhosis

HBsAg = hepatitis B surface antigen; HCC = hepatocellular carcinoma.

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["immuno"] = {"hypersensitivity-types--type-i-hypersensitivity":[[31459,"Anaphylaxis","

Anaphylaxis

Triggers

  • Food (eg, nuts, shellfish)
  • Medications (eg, β-lactam antibiotics)
  • Insect stings

Clinical
manifestations

  • Cardiovascular
    • Vasodilation → hypotension & tissue edema
    • Tachycardia
  • Respiratory
    • Upper airway edema → stridor & hoarseness
    • Bronchospasm → wheezing
  • Cutaneous
    • Urticarial rash, pruritus, flushing
  • Gastrointestinal
    • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain

Treatment

  • Intramuscular epinephrine
  • Airway management & volume resuscitation
  • Adjunct therapy (eg, antihistamines, glucocorticoids)
"], [63460,"Large local reactions","

Large local reactions

Epidemiology & pathophysiology

  • Often due to bites from Hymenoptera species (eg, bees, ants, wasps)
  • Exaggerated, IgE-mediated, local allergic response (~10% of stung individuals)
  • Associated with possible increased risk for future systemic reactions

Manifestations

  • Significant (~10 cm or more) localized swelling, erythema & warmth
  • Swelling & erythema contiguous with site of the sting
  • Develop within 24 hr, peak within 24-48 hr, resolve in 5-10 days

Treatment

  • Cold compresses
  • Oral &/or topical steroids
  • Antihistamines
  • Anti-inflammatory medications  
"], [68614,"Diagnostic challenges in anaphylaxis","

Diagnostic challenges in anaphylaxis

Nonclassic
presentation

  • No prior allergic reactions (ie, first episode)
  • Absence of hypotension, respiratory symptoms, or cutaneous signs
  • Protracted or biphasic presentation

Challenging
clinical situations

  • Preexisting conditions with similar symptoms (eg, asthma, COPD)
  • Ongoing physiologic shifts (eg, childbirth, hemodialysis)
  • Impaired communication (eg, sedation, severe psychiatric illness)

Medication
effects

  • Directly activate mast cells (eg, opiates, NSAIDs)
  • Interfere with epinephrine effect (eg, β-blockers,
    α-adrenergic blockers)

COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

"], [68825,"Clinical features of anaphylaxis","

Clinical features of anaphylaxis

Cutaneous/
mucosal

  • Ocular: periorbital swelling, injected conjunctiva, tearing
  • Oral mucosa: swelling, tingling, or itching of tongue & lips; metallic taste
  • Skin: urticaria, flushing, pruritus

Respiratory

  • Nose: congestion, rhinorrhea
  • Upper airway: edema → hoarseness & stridor
  • Lower airway: bronchospasm → wheezing, dyspnea, tachypnea

Cardiovascular

  • Vasodilation → hypotension, light-headedness/syncope, tachycardia
  • Cardiac dysfunction, cardiac arrest

Gastrointestinal

  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea

Neurologic

  • Headache, confusion, anxiety, feeling of impending doom
"], [68829,"Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis","

Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis is likely if there is rapid symptom onset & any 1 of the following criteria:

1

Skin/mucosa involvement (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling) & either hypotension or respiratory distress

2

Involvement of ≥2 organ systems after exposure to a likely allergen

  • Skin/mucosa (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling)
  • Respiratory (eg, wheezing, stridor, dyspnea)
  • Cardiovascular (eg, hypotension, tachycardia, syncope)
  • Gastrointestinal (eg, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea)

3

Hypotension after exposure to a known allergen

Immunologic and nonimmunologic anaphylaxis

Immunologic
(IgE-mediated)

Nonimmunologic
(Non-IgE-mediated)

Mechanism

Initial sensitization (priming) followed by mast cell degranulation upon reexposure (surface IgE crosslinking)

Non-IgE-mediated: Direct mast degranulation

Triggers

  • Foods (eg, peanut, shellfish)
  • Insect venom (eg, wasps)

"], [128856,"Anaphylaxis","

Anaphylaxis

Triggers

  • Food (most common): nuts, shellfish, eggs
  • Medications (β-lactam antibiotics)
  • Insect stings

Diagnostic criteria

Acute onset (minutes to hours) of one of the following:

  • Criterion 1: skin/mucosal involvement (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling) PLUS hypotension OR respiratory distress
  • Criterion 2: involvement of ≥2 organ systems (skin/mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal)
  • Criterion 3: hypotension after exposure to known allergen

Treatment

  • Intramuscular epinephrine
  • Airway management & volume resuscitation (if needed)
  • Adjunctive therapy for severe or prolonged cases (steroids, H1 & H2 blockers)

Follow-up

  • Allergy testing & avoidance
  • Epinephrine autoinjector
"]],"immunodeficiencies-continued--chronic-granulomatous-disease":[[31667,"Chronic granulomatous disease","

Chronic granulomatous disease

Pathogenesis

  • X-linked recessive mutation of NADPH oxidase
  • Impaired respiratory burst & ↓ reactive oxygen species → inhibition of phagocytic intracellular killing

Clinical features

  • Recurrent infections with catalase-positive* bacteria & fungi
  • Lungs, skin, liver, lymph node involvement
  • Diffuse granulomas (eg, gastrointestinal, genitourinary)

Diagnosis

  • Measurement of neutrophil superoxide production:
    • DHR flow cytometry (preferred)
    • NBT testing

Treatment

  • Prophylaxis: TMP-SMX, itraconazole, interferon gamma
  • Active infection: culture-based, antimicrobial therapy
  • Hematopoietic cell transplant is curative

*Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia (Pseudomonas) cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus.

DHR = dihydrorhodamine; NBT = nitroblue tetrazolium test; TMP-SMX = trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

"], [54946,"Chronic granulomatous disease","

Chronic granulomatous disease

Pathogenesis

  • X-linked recessive mutation of NADPH oxidase
  • Impaired respiratory burst & ↓ reactive oxygen species → inhibition of phagocytic intracellular killing

Microbiology

  • Catalase-positive organisms
    • Bacteria: Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia, Serratia, Nocardia
    • Fungi: Aspergillus

Clinical features

  • Recurrent infections of lungs, skin, liver, lymph nodes
  • Diffuse granuloma formation

Diagnosis

  • Measurement of neutrophil superoxide production
    • DHR flow cytometry (preferred)
    • NBT testing

DHR = dihydrorhodamine; NBT = nitroblue tetrazolium.

"]],"immunodeficiencies--common-variable-immunodeficiency":[[33026,"Common variable immunodeficiency","

Common variable immunodeficiency

Pathophysiology

  • Abnormal differentiation of B cells into plasma cells → decreased immunoglobulin production

Clinical manifestations

  • Symptom onset classically age 20-40, as early as puberty
  • Recurrent respiratory infections (eg, pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis)
  • Recurrent GI infections (eg, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Giardia)
  • Chronic disease:
    • Autoimmune (eg, RA, thyroid disease)
    • Pulmonary (eg, bronchiectasis, fibrosis)
    • GI (eg, chronic diarrhea, IBD-like conditions)

Diagnosis

  • ↓↓ IgG, ↓ IgA/IgM
  • No response to vaccination

Management

  • Immunoglobulin replacement therapy

GI = gastrointestinal; IBD = inflammatory bowel disease; RA = rheumatoid arthritis.

"], [89988,"22q11.2 deletion syndromes","

22q11.2 deletion syndromes

Phenotypes

  • DiGeorge syndrome, velocardiofacial syndrome*

Pathogenesis

  • Loss of genes that control embryonic tissue template transformation (eg, pharyngeal apparatus, secondary heart field) and migration of neural crest cells

Clinical features (CATCH)

  • Cardiac outflow tract anomalies (eg, tetralogy of Fallot, persistent truncus arteriosus)
  • Anomalous face (eg, prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears, micrognathia/retrognathia)
  • Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia → decreased T-cell immunity
  • Cleft palate
  • Hypoparathyroidism (hypoplastic/aplastic parathyroids) → hypocalcemia

*DiGeorge requires thymic involvement (CD3+ T-cell count <500/mm3); velocardiofacial syndrome requires facial abnormalities.

"]],"vaccination":[[41129,"Indications & contraindications for influenza vaccination","

Indications & contraindications for influenza vaccination

Live attenuated intranasal vaccine

Indications

  • Healthy individuals age 2-49 

Contraindications

  • Age <2 or ≥50
  • Immunosuppressed patients (eg, HIV with CD4+ cell count <200/mm3) & close contacts
  • Chronic cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, neuromuscular, or metabolic (eg, diabetes, renal insufficiency) diseases
  • History of Guillain-Barré syndrome following previous influenza immunization
  • Pregnant women
  • Children/adolescents receiving long-term aspirin therapy
  • Severe allergy to vaccine or its components 

Inactivated vaccine

Indications

  • Individuals age ≥6 months

Contraindications

  • Severe allergy to vaccine or its components

"]],"transplant-rejection":[[52544,"Transplant rejection reactions","

Transplant rejection reactions

Type of rejection

Onset time

Etiology

Morphology

Hyperacute

Minutes to hours

  • Preformed recipient antibodies against graft antigens
  • Gross mottling & cyanosis
  • Arterial fibrinoid necrosis & capillary thrombotic occlusion

Acute

Usually <6 months

  • Exposure to donor antigens induces activation of naive immune cells 
  • Predominantly cell-mediated
  • Cellular: lymphocytic interstitial infiltrate & endotheliitis
  • Humoral: C4d deposition, neutrophilic infiltrate, necrotizing vasculitis

Chronic

Months to years

  • Chronic low-grade immune response refractory to immunosuppression
  • Mixed cell-mediated and humoral
  • Vascular wall thickening & luminal narrowing
  • Interstitial fibrosis & parenchymal atrophy
"], [69324,"Complications of solid organ transplantation","

Complications of solid organ transplantation

Acute

<1 month

Postacute

Infectious

Nosocomial bacteria: blood stream infections, HAP, Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile

<12 months: opportunistic pathogens

  • Bacteria: mycobacteria
  • Viruses: CMV, HSV
  • Fungi: PCP, Candida, Aspergillus, Mucor spp.
 

≥12 months: community-acquired respiratory viruses & bacteria

Noninfectious

  • Surgical site: anastomotic dehiscence
  • Primary graft dysfunction: ARDS, ATN
  • Drug toxicity: nephrotoxicity (eg, calcineurin inhibitors), osteoporosis (eg, corticosteroids)
  • Malignancy: posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder (EBV)

Immunologic

  • Hyperacute rejection: ABO mismatch
  • Acute* rejection: cell or antibody mediated
  • Chronic rejection (>12 months): fibrosis of graft structures (eg, bronchiolitis obliterans of airways, sclerosis of glomeruli)

*Acute cellular rejection most common in first 90 days but can occur at any time after transplant.

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; ATN = acute tubular necrosis; CMV = cytomegalovirus; EBV = Epstein-Barr virus; HAP = hospital-acquired pneumonia; HSV = herpes simplex virus.

Hyper-IgE syndrome

"]],"immunodeficiencies-continued--hyper-igm-syndrome":[[72291,"Hyper-IgM syndrome","

Genetics

  • Sinopulmonary, gastrointestinal & opportunistic infections
  • Failure to thrive
  • Small lymphoid tissue

Diagnosis

  • ↑ IgM
  • ↓ IgG, IgA, IgE
  • Absent CD40L on CD4+ lymphocytes

APCs = antigen-presenting cells; CD40L = CD40 ligand.

"]],"immunodeficiencies-continued--ataxia-telangiectasia":[[73657,"Ataxia-telangiectasia","

Ataxia-telangiectasia

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal recessive
  • Defective DNA break repair

Clinical features

  • Presents in early childhood
  • Neurologic dysfunction
    • Progressive cerebellar ataxia
    • Uncoordinated head/eye movements
  • Telangiectasias: face & conjunctivae
  • Immune deficiency: recurrent sinopulmonary infections
  • ↑ Malignancy risk

Diagnosis

  • Mutation analysis
"]],"immunodeficiencies-continued--severe-combined-immunodeficiency":[[74855,"Severe combined immunodeficiency","

Severe combined immunodeficiency

Etiology

  • Gene defect leading to failure of T-cell development
  • B-cell dysfunction due to absent T cells

Inheritance

  • X-linked recessive
  • Autosomal recessive

Clinical features

  • Recurrent, severe viral, fungal, or opportunistic (ie, Pneumocystis) infections
  • Failure to thrive
  • Chronic diarrhea

Treatment

  • Stem cell transplant
"]],"complement-disorders--c1-inhibitor-deficiency":[[81066,"Causes of angioedema","

Causes of angioedema

Mast cell activation

  • Type 1 hypersensitivity reactions (IgE-mediated)
  • Direct mast cell activation (eg, opioids)

Associated pruritus & urticaria

Excess bradykinin

  • ACE inhibitors
  • C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary/acquired)

No pruritus or urticaria

"]],"immunodeficiencies--selective-iga-deficiency":[[81535,"Selective IgA deficiency","

Selective IgA deficiency

Epidemiology

  • Most common primary immune deficiency

Clinical features

  • Usually asymptomatic
  • Recurrent sinopulmonary & gastrointestinal infections
  • Associated with autoimmune disease (eg, celiac) & atopy (eg, asthma, eczema)
  • Anaphylaxis during transfusions

Diagnosis

  • Low or absent IgA
  • Normal IgG, IgM levels, B cells

Treatment

  • Supportive care
  • Medical alert bracelet for transfusion reactions (for severe deficiency)
"]],"complement-disorders--paroxysmal-nocturnal-hemoglobinuria":[[81696,"Clinical features of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria","

Clinical features of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

Clinical manifestations

  • Hemolysis → fatigue
  • Cytopenias (impaired hematopoiesis)
  • Venous thrombosis (intraabdominal, cerebral veins)

Work-up

  • Complete blood count (hypoplastic/aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia)
  • Elevated lactate dehydrogenase and low haptoglobin (hemolysis)
  • Indirect hyperbilirubinemia
  • Urinalysis (hemoglobinuria)
  • Flow cytometry (absence of CD55 & CD59)

Treatment

  • Iron & folate supplementation
  • Eculizumab (monoclonal antibody that inhibits complement activation)
"]],"innate-vs-adaptive-immunity":[[98951,"Danger signals (alarmins)","

Danger signals (alarmins)

 

PAMPs

Septic inflammation

Foreign molecular motifs found on invading organisms

  • Bacteria: lipopolysaccharide, lipoteichoic acid
  • Fungi: β-glucan
  • Protozoa: profilin
  • Viruses: double-stranded RNA

DAMPs

Sterile inflammation (eg, pancreatitis)

Self motifs released from damaged host cells and tissues

  • Exposed intracellular contents: mitochondrial DNA, histones, uric acid
  • Fragmented extracellular matrix: fibrinogen, hyaluronic acid

DAMPs & PAMPs drive systemic inflammation by engaging immune cell pattern recognition receptors (eg, toll-like receptors)

DAMP = damage-associated molecular pattern; PAMP = pathogen-associated molecular pattern.

"], [120171,"Innate & adaptive immunity","

Innate & adaptive immunity

Innate
(eg, response to a dirty cut)

Adaptive
(eg, response to vaccination)

Function

  • Immediate general response to a broad range of pathogens
  • Same response with repeated exposures
  • Memory-based response to specific pathogens
  • Greater response with repeated exposures

Components

  • Natural barriers (eg, cilia)
  • Contact activation system (eg, local coagulation)
  • Neutrophils, NK cells, macrophages, dendritic cells
  • Inflammasome
  • Alternative complement pathway
  • Cell-mediated immunity: cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) & helper T cell (CD4+) response
  • Antibody-mediated (humoral) immunity: B cells, plasma cells, antibodies
  • Classical complement pathway

Activation

At site of invasion (eg, skin):

  • PAMPs & DAMPs activate innate immune receptors (eg, TLR)

In germinal centers of secondary lymphoid organs (eg, nodes, spleen):

  • APCs (eg, dendritic cells) process & display antigens on MHC, engaging TCRs
  • Affinity maturation (somatic hypermutation) of B cells to produce specific antibodies

APC = antigen-presenting cell; DAMP = damage-associated molecular pattern (eg, mitochondrial DNA); MHC = major histocompatibility complex; NK = natural killer; PAMP = pathogen-associated molecular pattern (eg, lipopolysaccharide); TCR = T-cell receptor; TLR = toll-like receptor.

"]],"major-histocompatibility-complex-i-and-ii":[[126402,"Antigen processing pathways","

Antigen processing pathways

MHC class I

MHC class II

Cell types

All nucleated cells

Professional APCs (B cells, DCs, macrophages)

Peptide origin

Cytoplasmic

Extracellular

Transport mechanism

Proteasome degradation → TAP

Endocytosis → lysosomal degradation

T-cell response

CD8+ cytotoxic T cells

CD4+ T-helper cells

APC = antigen-presenting cell; DC = dendritic cell; MHC = major histocompatibility complex; TAP = transporter associated with antigen processing.

"]]};

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["micro"] = {"legionella-pneumophila":[[31142,"Epidemiology","

Legionella pneumonia

Epidemiology

  • Contaminated water
    • Hospital
    • Travel (cruise, hotel)

Clinical features

  • Fever >38.8 C (101.8 F)
  • Relative bradycardia
  • Gastrointestinal: diarrhea, vomiting, cramps
  • Pulmonary: delayed symptoms

Diagnosis

  • Hyponatremia
  • Chest x-ray: lobar infiltrate
  • Sputum Gram stain: PMNs, few/no organisms
  • Urine Legionella antigen

Treatment

  • Respiratory fluoroquinolone or newer macrolide

PMNs = polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

"], [131542,"infection","

Legionella infection

Epidemiology

  • Species: Legionella pneumophilia (most common), Legionella longbeachae
  • Environmental reservoir: human-made water systems, soil
  • Transmission: inhalation of aerosolized particles

Clinical
manifestations

  • Legionnaires' disease (atypical CAP)
    • Fever, dyspnea, cough
    • GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting, diarrhea)
    • Hyponatremia
    • Relative bradycardia
    • Chest x-ray: lobar/multilobar patchy infiltrate
  • Pontiac fever (nonspecific, febrile illness)
    • Rapid onset (hours after transmission)
    • Fever, headache, chills, myalgia, GI symptoms
    • No lower respiratory manifestations

Diagnosis

  • PCR (sputum, BAL)
  • Urine Legionella antigen
  • Culture

Treatment

  • Respiratory fluoroquinolone
    OR
  • Azithromycin

BAL = bronchoalveolar lavage; CAP = community-acquired pneumonia; GI = gastrointestinal.

"]],"mycoplasma-pneumoniae":[[31143,"pneumonia","

Mycoplasma pneumonia

Epidemiology

  • Respiratory droplets
  • Close quarters/young (eg, school, military)
  • Fall or winter

Clinical

  • Indolent headache, malaise, fever, persistent dry cough
  • Pharyngitis(nonexudative)
  • Macular/vesicular rash

Diagnostic

  • Normal leukocyte count
  • Subclinical hemolytic anemia (cold agglutinins)
  • Interstitial infiltrate (chest x-ray)

Treatment

  • Usually empiric
  • Macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone
"]],"urinary-tract-infections":[[31219,"Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy","

Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

Definition

  • ≥100,000 CFU/mL bacteria

Risk
factors

  • Pregestational diabetes mellitus
  • History of urinary tract infection
  • Multiparity

Common
pathogens

  • Escherichia coli (most common)
  • Klebsiella
  • Enterobacter
  • Group B Streptococcus

Potential complications

  • Acute pyelonephritis
  • Preterm labor & delivery

Treatment

  • Cefpodoxime
  • Fosfomycin
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Nitrofurantoin*

*Avoided in first & third trimesters.

CFU = colony-forming units.

"], [33047,"Urinary tract infection antibiotics in pregnancy","

Urinary tract infection antibiotics in pregnancy

Recommended

Contraindicated

  • Nitrofurantoin*
  • Amoxicillin
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Cephalexin
  • Fosfomycin
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole*
  • Tetracyclines
  • Fluoroquinolones

*Avoid in 1st trimester & near term.

"], [33193,"Recurrent urinary tract infection","

Recurrent urinary tract infection

Definition

  • ≥2 infections in 6 months
  • ≥3 infections in 1 year

Risk factors

  • History of cystitis at age ≤15
  • Spermicide use
  • New sexual partner
  • Postmenopausal status

Evaluation

  • Urinalysis
  • Urine culture

Prevention

  • Behavior modification
  • Postcoital or daily antibiotic prophylaxis
  • Topical vaginal estrogen for postmenopausal patients   
"], [36512,"Urinary tract infection (UTI) in children","

Urinary tract infection (UTI) in children

Risk factors

  • Female sex
  • Uncircumcised male infants
  • Urologic abnormalities (eg, vesicoureteral reflux)
  • Bowel/bladder dysfunction (eg, constipation)

Clinical features

  • Infants: fever, fussiness, poor feeding
  • Older children: dysuria, suprapubic/flank pain

Laboratory findings

  • Urinalysis: leukocyte esterase, nitrites, WBCs
  • Urine culture: bacteriuria

Management

  • Antibiotics (eg, cephalosporin)
  • First febrile UTI:
    • Age <2 years: RBUS, followed by VCUG if abnormal
    • Age ≥2 years: observation alone
  • Recurrent febrile UTIs: RBUS & VCUG

RBUS = renal & bladder ultrasonography; VCUG = voiding cystourethrogram; WBCs = white blood cells.

"], [74924,"Catheter-associated urinary tract infection","

Catheter-associated urinary tract infection

Clinical features

  • Fever, flank pain, suprapubic pain
  • ≥103 cfu/mL of uropathogenic organism (eg, Escherichia coli, Enterococcus, Klebsiella)
  • Current (or within 48 hr) use of urethral, suprapubic, or condom catheter

Risk factors

  • Duration of catheter use, especially >48 hr (most important)
  • Female sex
  • Advanced age
  • Diabetes mellitus

Prevention

  • Avoid unnecessary catheterization (eg, not indicated for incontinence)
  • Use sterile technique when placing catheter
  • Remove catheter promptly when no longer needed

cfu = colony-forming units.

"], [91032,"Candiduria","

Candiduria

Risk factors

  • Chronic colonization
  • Urinary tract drainage device (eg, Foley catheter)
  • Prior antibiotic use
  • Diabetes mellitus

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic UTI (most common)
  • Cystitis: suprapubic pain
  • Pyelonephritis: flank pain, CVA tenderness
  • Disseminated candidemia

Treatment

  • Asymptomatic: none indicated
  • Symptomatic UTI & disseminated infection: antifungal therapy*

Complications

  • Perinephric abscess
  • Fungus ball

*Fluconazole (amphotericin B if fluconazole resistant).

CVA = costovertebral angle; UTI = urinary tract infection.

"], [91456,"Urinalysis interpretation in urinary tract infections","

Urinalysis interpretation in urinary tract infections

Result

Pathophysiology

Clinical significance

White blood cells

  • Congregate in response to infection
  • Pyuria (WBC > 10 cells/mm3) indicates UTI

Red blood cells

  • Structural disruption caused by inflammation or infection
  • Not specific to infection, but often positive in UTIs

Bacteria

  • Bacteria ascend urinary tract to colonize and/or cause infection
  • Contamination (eg, improper sampling), colonization (eg, asymptomatic bacteriuria), or infection

Leukocyte esterase

  • Released by lysed neutrophils/macrophages
  • Marker of WBC & pyuria

Nitrites*

  • Urinary nitrate is converted to nitrite by nitrate reductase
  • Marker of nitrate reductase–producing bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus mirabilis)

pH

  • Alkaline urine (pH > 8) due to ammonia produced from hydrolysis of urea by urease
  • Marker of urease-producing bacteria (eg, Proteus mirabilis)
*The absence of nitrites does not exclude these bacteria.

UTI = urinary tract infection; WBC = white blood cells.

"]],"ectoparasites--sarcoptes-scabiei":[[31413,"Scabies","

Scabies

Pathogenesis

  • Sarcoptes scabiei mite infestation
  • Spread by direct person-to-person contact

Clinical features

  • Extremely pruritic, small, erythematous papules
  • Distribution: interdigital web spaces, flexor wrists, extensor elbows, axillae, feet, umbilicus & genitalia
  • Burrows (thin serpiginous lines) may not be visible but pathognomonic if present

Diagnosis

  • Clinical
  • Skin scraping with microscopy is confirmatory

Treatment

  • Topical 5% permethrin OR oral ivermectin
  • Treat household members & close personal contacts
  • Environmental measures (eg, launder clothing/bedding)
"]],"salmonella-vs-shigella--shigella":[[31425,"gastroenteritis","

Shigella gastroenteritis

Pathogenesis

  • Fecal-oral transmission, ingestion of contaminated food or water
  • Invasion of colonic mucosal cells → inflammation & ulceration
  • Often in outbreaks (eg, day care)

Clinical presentation

  • High fever, abdominal pain, tenesmus
  • Bloody/mucoid diarrhea (often watery initially)
  • Extraintestinal complications: seizure, bacteremia, HUS*

Evaluation

  • Stool microscopy: positive for WBCs & RBCs
  • Stool PCR testing
  • Stool & blood cultures with susceptibilities (due to antibiotic resistance)

Management

  • Fluid & electrolyte replacement
  • Antibiotics

*S dysenteriae infection only.

HUS = hemolytic uremic syndrome; RBC = red blood cell; WBC = white blood cell.

"]],"_more":[[31441,"Airborne precautions","

Airborne precautions

Indications

  • Tuberculosis
  • Varicella* (chickenpox)
  • Herpes zoster** (shingles)
  • Rubeola (measles)

Components

  • N95 respirator or powered air-purifying respirator
  • Negative pressure isolation room with
    high-efficiency particulate air filter
  • As needed if contact with body fluid is anticipated:
    clean gloves, disposable gown, goggles/face shield

*Only when uncrusted lesions are present; contact precautions also required.
**Only in disseminated disease or immunocompromised clients; contact
precautions also required.

"], [32198,"Neonatal sepsis","

Neonatal sepsis

Etiology

  • Group B Streptococcus
  • Escherichia coli
  • Listeria monocytogenes (age <7 days)

Clinical features

  • Temperature instability (eg, fever, hypothermia)
  • CNS signs (eg, lethargy, irritability, apnea)
  • Poor feeding
  • Respiratory distress (eg, tachypnea, grunting)
  • Jaundice

Evaluation

  • Inflammatory markers (ie, CRP, ANC, procalcitonin)
  • Blood, urine, CSF cultures*

Treatment

  • Parenteral antibiotics (ampicillin & gentamicin)

* Limited evaluation (without CSF studies) & outpatient management may be considered in well-appearing, febrile neonates age >21 days.

ANC = absolute neutrophil count; CRP = c-reactive protein, CSF = cerebrospinal fluid.

"], [34084,"Surgical mask","

Common applications
of droplet precautions

Personal protective
equipment

  • Neisseria meningitidis
  • Haemophilus influenzae type B
  • Diphtheria
  • Mumps
  • Rubella
  • Pertussis
  • Group A Streptococcus (streptococcal pharyngitis)
  • Influenza
  • Surgical mask when providing care
  • Place client in private room if possible
  • As needed for procedures with risk for splash or body fluid contact: gloves, gown, goggles/face shield
"], [34608,"Diphtheria–tetanus–acellular pertussis immunization","

Diphtheria–tetanus–acellular pertussis immunization

Components

  • Diphtheria toxoid
  • Tetanus toxoid
  • Conjugated pertussis antigen (pertactin)

Schedule

  • 5 doses given at ages:
    • 2, 4 & 6 months
    • 15-18 months
    • 4-6 years

Contraindications

  • Encephalopathy after previous dose
  • Anaphylaxis to vaccine component
"], [35908,"Bite wounds with a high risk of infection","

Bite wounds with a high risk of infection

  • Crush injuries
  • Bites on hands or feet
  • Wounds on body >12 hr or on face >24 hr
  • Cat bites (except on face)
  • Human bites (except on face)
  • Bite wounds in immunocompromised hosts
"], [81282,"Medically important fungi","

Medically important fungi

Cutaneous

  • Dermatophytosis (eg, tinea, onychomycosis)
  • Pityriasis versicolor

Subcutaneous

  • Sporotrichosis

Systemic

  • Histoplasmosis
  • Coccidioidomycosis
  • Blastomycosis

Opportunistic

  • Candida
  • Aspergillus
  • Mucor
  • Rhizopus
"], [81907,"Infection control: isolation precautions","

Infection control: isolation precautions

Type

Pathogen*

Key requirements

Airborne

  • Bacterial: tuberculosis
  • Viral: primary VZV (chickenpox), disseminated VZV reactivation (shingles/zoster), dermatomal VZV reactivation (shingles/zoster) in immunocompromised patients, SARS-CoV-2, measles
  • Negative pressure room
  • N95 respirator

Contact

  • Multidrug-resistant organism (eg, MRSA, VRE, ESBL producing)
  • Bacterial: Clostridioides difficile, Escherichia coli O157:H7
  • Viral: RSV, primary VZV (chickenpox), disseminated VZV reactivation (shingles/zoster), dermatomal VZV reactivation (shingles/zoster) in immunocompromised patients
  • Gloves & gowns
  • Single-use equipment (eg, stethoscope)

Droplet

  • Bacterial: Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type B, Mycoplasma pneumoniae
  • Viral: influenza virus, adenovirus
  • Mask within 1-2 m (3-6 ft) of patient

Standard

  • Followed for all patients even when no infection is apparent
  • Hand hygiene
  • Gowns/gloves/masks when appropriate (eg, during procedures)

*Precaution is started immediately when infection with pathogen is suspected.

ESBL = extended-spectrum beta-lactamase; MRSA = methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; RSV = respiratory syncytial virus; SARS-CoV-2 = severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2; VRE = vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus; VZV = varicella-zoster virus.

"], [118461,"Epidemiology","

Epidemiology

Pathogen

Freshwater

Aeromonas hydrophila, Plesiomonas shigelloides

Saltwater, shellfish (oysters)

Vibrio vulnificus, Vibrio parahaemolyticus

Bites

Human: Eikenella corrodens

Animal: Pasteurella multocida, Capnocytophaga canimorsus

Nail puncture

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Soil

Clostridium, Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Neutropenia

Pseudomonas aeruginosa, gram-negative, fungal

"], [120100,"Some antibiotics commonly used for invasive","

Some antibiotics commonly used for invasive methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infections

Mechanism of action

Adverse effects

Vancomycin

Blocks glycopeptide polymerization by binding tightly to D-alanyl-D-alanine

  • Red man syndrome
  • Nephrotoxicity

Daptomycin

Depolarizes cellular membrane by creating transmembrane channels

  • Myopathy & CPK elevation
  • Note: Inactivated by pulmonary surfactant

Linezolid

Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to 50S subunit

  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Optic neuritis
  • High risk for serotonin syndrome

CPK = creatine phosphokinase.

"], [126227,"Protozoa structure","

Induration size

≥5 mm

"]],"hiv-therapy":[[35548,"HIV management during pregnancy","

HIV management during pregnancy

Antepartum

  • Testing of HIV-1 viral load monthly until undetectable, then every 3 months
  • CD4 cell count every 3 months

  • Initiation or continuation of HAART
  • Avoidance of amniocentesis if viral load is detectable

Intrapartum

  • Avoidance of artificial ROM, fetal scalp electrode, operative vaginal delivery
  • Viral load ≤50 copies/mL: ART + vaginal delivery
  • Viral load >50 copies/mL to ≤1,000 copies/mL: ART ± zidovudine + vaginal delivery
  • Viral load >1,000 copies/mL: ART + zidovudine + cesarean delivery

"]],"clostridia--clostridium-botulinum":[[35766,"Infant botulism","

"]],"bacteria-with-exotoxins":[[42013,"Mechanism of action of selected bacterial exotoxins","

Mechanism of action of selected bacterial exotoxins

Organism

Toxin

Mechanism & effects

Bacillus anthracis

Anthrax exotoxin

Edema factor: Increases cyclic AMP concentration by acting as an adenylate cyclase, causing edema & phagocyte dysfunction

Lethal factor: Zinc-dependent protease that inhibits mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, causing apoptosis & multisystem physiologic disruption

Bordetella pertussis

Pertussis toxin

Disinhibits adenylate cyclase through Gi ADP-ribosylation, increasing cAMP levels; causes edema & phagocyte dysfunction

Adenylate cyclase toxin

Functions as an adenylate cyclase, increasing cAMP levels; causes edema & phagocyte dysfunction

Clostridium botulinum

Botulinum toxin

Blocks presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, resulting in flaccid paralysis

Clostridium difficile

Toxin A

Recruits & activates neutrophils, leading to release of cytokines that cause mucosal inflammation, fluid loss & diarrhea

Toxin B

Induces actin depolymerization, leading to mucosal cell death, bowel wall necrosis & pseudomembrane formation

Shigella dysenteriae

Shiga toxin

Halts protein synthesis by disabling the 60S ribosomal subunit, leading to intestinal epithelial cell death & diarrhea

Streptococcus pyogenes

Pyrogenic exotoxin

Acts as a superantigen, inducing fever & shock; associated with scarlet fever & streptococcal toxic shock syndrome

Streptolysin O&S

Damages erythrocyte membranes, causing beta hemolysis

"]],"arboviruses-transmitted-by-aedes-mosquitoes--dengue-virus":[[52941,"Clinical features of dengue","

Clinical features of dengue

Dengue without
warning signs

Following travel to a dengue-endemic area, fever with:

  • Flu-like febrile illness with marked myalgia &/or arthralgia
  • Diffuse maculopapular rash
  • Leukopenia
  • Positive tourniquet test (petechiae after sphygmomanometer cuff inflation for 5 min)

Dengue with
warning signs

Addition of any of the following:

  • Abdominal pain &/or persistent vomiting
  • Fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion)
  • Mucosal bleeding
  • Lethargy or restlessness
  • Hepatomegaly >2 cm
  • Increased hematocrit with rapidly decreasing platelet count

Severe dengue

Progression to:

  • Severe plasma leakage causing shock or respiratory distress
  • Severe bleeding
  • Severe organ involvement (AST or ALT ≥1,000 U/L, impaired conciousness, organ failure)

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase.

  • Positive anti-HCV
  • Positive HCV RNA
  • ↑ Aminotransferases
  • ↑ Bilirubin
  • Hypoalbuminemia
  • Prolonged PT
  • Thrombocytopenia

Pathology
findings

  • Panlobular lymphocytic inflammation
  • Hepatocyte injury (eg, ballooning degeneration)

  • Extensive fibrosis & bridging fibrous septa
  • Regenerative parenchymal nodules

AP = alkaline phosphatase; HCV = hepatitis C virus.

"]],"opportunistic-fungal-infections--mucor-and-rhizopus-spp":[[81606,"Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis*","

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis*

Risk factors

  • Diabetes mellitus (ketoacidosis)
  • Hematologic malignancy
  • Solid organ or stem cell transplant

Manifestations

  • Acute/aggressive
  • Fever, nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, headache, sinus pain
  • Necrotic invasion of palate, orbit, brain

Diagnosis

  • Sinus endoscopy with biopsy & culture

Treatment

  • Surgical debridement
  • Liposomal amphotericin B
  • Elimination of risk factors (eg, ↑ glucose, acidosis)

*Largely due to Rhizopus species.

"]],"systemic-mycoses--blastomycosis":[[81612,"Blastomycosis","

Blastomycosis

Epidemiology

  • South/South Central states, Mississippi & Ohio River valleys, Upper Midwest states, Great Lakes states & Canadian provinces
  • Disseminated disease may occur even in immunocompetent patients
  • Generally more severe in immunocompromised patients

Clinical features

  • Lung: acute & chronic pneumonia (usually mild to moderate but may be severe)
  • Skin: wart-like lesions, violaceous nodules, skin ulcers
  • Bone: osteomyelitis
  • Genitourinary: prostatitis, epididymo-orchitis
  • CNS: meningitis, epidural or brain abscesses

Diagnosis

  • Culture (blood, sputum, tissue specimens)
  • Microscopy (body fluids, sputum, tissue specimens)
  • Antigen testing (urine, blood)

Treatment

  • Mild pulmonary disease in immunocompetent patients: may consider not treating
  • Mild-to-moderate pulmonary disease, mild disseminated disease: oral itraconazole
  • Severe pulmonary disease, moderately severe to severe disseminated disease, immunocompromised patients: intravenous amphotericin B
"]],"cestodes-tapeworms--taenia-solium":[[81751,"Neurocysticercosis","

Neurocysticercosis

Epidemiology

  • Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) eggs
  • Fecal-oral human transmission
  • Central & South America, sub-Saharan Africa, Asia

Manifestations

  • Prolonged incubation (months to years)
  • Seizures
  • ICH (headache, vomiting, AMS)

Diagnosis

  • CT/MRI scans: cysts (hypodense, enhancement/edema, or calcified)
  • T solium serology

Treatment

  • Seizure/ICH management
  • Antiparasitic therapy (albendazole)
  • Corticosteroids

AMS = altered mental status; ICH = intracranial hypertension.

"]],"nematodes-roundworms--ancylostoma-spp-necator-americanus":[[81754,"Cutaneous larva migrans","

Cutaneous larva migrans

Epidemiology

  • Hookworm larvae
    • Dog (Ancylostoma caninum) or cat (Abraziliense)
  • Humans are incidental hosts
  • Barefoot contact with contaminated sand or soil

Clinical

  • Primarily lower extremity
  • Cutaneous (deeper infection rare)
  • Erythematous, pruritic papule at site of entry
  • Intensely pruritic, migrating, serpiginous, reddish-brown tracks

Diagnosis

  • History & clinical findings
  • Eosinophils usually normal

Treatment

  • Antihelmintic (eg, ivermectin)

"]],"opportunistic-fungal-infections--candida-albicans":[[84513,"endophthalmitis","

Candida endophthalmitis

Epidemiology

  • Transient/persistent fungemia → hematogenous dissemination to the choroid → invasion of the retina & fluid chambers
  • Risk factors: indwelling central catheter, TPN, broad-spectrum antibiotic use, gastrointestinal surgery & immunocompromise
  • Most cases arise in hospitalized patients or in those with recent eye surgery/trauma

Manifestations

  • Usually unilateral floaters & progressive vision loss
  • Pain rare until late in disease process
  • Fever may be absent & patient may otherwise feel well

Diagnosis

  • Blood cultures (often negative)
  • Vitreous fluid sampling & culture

Treatment

  • Systemic antifungal therapy
  • Vitrectomy + vitreous injection (when fluid chamber involved)

TPN = total parenteral nutrition.

"]],"hiv-diagnosis":[[87464,"HIV infection–coinfection screening","

HIV infection–coinfection screening

Sexually transmitted infections

  • Syphilis (eg, RPR followed by FTA-ABS)
  • Gonorrhea & chlamydia (eg, NAAT)

Hepatitis A

  • Hepatitis A antibody (IgG)

Hepatitis B

  • Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) & antibody (anti-HBs)
  • Antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc)

Hepatitis C

  • Hepatitis C antibody (consider hepatitis C RNA)

Latent tuberculosis

  • Tuberculin skin test OR
  • Interferon-gamma release assay

FTA-ABS = fluorescent treponemal antibody-absorption; NAAT = nucleic acid amplification test; RPR = rapid plasma reagin.

"]],"antiprotozoal-therapy":[[88916,"Malaria prevention","

Malaria prevention

High-risk groups

  • Travelers new to endemic regions
  • Travelers returning to endemic region after long absence
  • Pregnant women

Mosquito bite
avoidance

  • Avoid being outside from dusk → dawn
  • Cover skin with clothing
  • Wear insect repellant
  • Use insecticide-treated bed nets
  • Sleep in screened/air-conditioned rooms

Chemoprophylaxis

  • Atovaquone-proguanil
  • Mefloquine
  • Doxycycline
  • Tafenoquine

"]],"protozoa-hematologic-infections--plasmodium":[[89456,"Malaria","

Malaria

Epidemiology

  • Vector: female Anopheles mosquito
  • 4 major species of Plasmodium: P falciparum, P vivax, P ovale, P malariae
  • Highest burden of disease is in Africa but is found in most tropical/subtropical areas worldwide

Manifestations

  • Periodic febrile paroxysms
  • Nonspecific malaise, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, myalgia

Complications

  • Cerebral (eg, delirium, seizure), hypoglycemia, ARDS, acidosis, renal/hepatic failure, coagulopathy

Diagnosis

  • Thin & thick peripheral blood smears
  • Rapid testing

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome.

"]],"common-causes-of-meningitis":[[91289,"Common causes of bacterial meningitis by age","

"]],"helicobacter-pylori":[[91531,"Test","

Diagnosis of Helicobacter pylori

Test

Uses & limitations

Urea breath test

  • Confirms new infection or eradication
  • False-negative results with recent* use of PPI, antibiotics, bismuth

Stool antigen test

  • Confirms new infection or eradication
  • False-negative results with recent* use of PPI, antibiotics, bismuth

Serologic test (IgG)

  • Limited use
  • Cannot distinguish between past & current infection

Endoscopic biopsy urease test

  • Confirms new infection or eradication
  • False-negative results with recent* use of PPI, antibiotics, bismuth

*False-negative results possible with <2 weeks of PPI use or <4 weeks of bismuth or antibiotics.

PPI = proton pump inhibitor.

"], [121900,"Preferred initial therapy","

Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection

Preferred initial therapy

Quadruple therapy: PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline for 10-14 days

Alternate therapy

Avoid if high risk of macrolide resistance*

Triple therapy: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole**) for 10-14 days

*In areas of endemic resistance (eg, United States), previous macrolide use.

**For patients with penicillin allergy.

PPI = proton pump inhibitor.

"], [131220,"Regimen","

Empiric Helicobacter pylori treatment regimens

Regimen

Medications included

Prescribing notes

Bismuth quadruple therapy (BQT)

  • Bismuth subsalicylate
  • Metronidazole
  • Tetracycline
  • PPI
  • Available also in fixed-dose capsule (with bismuth subcitrate)
  • Appropriate for patients with penicillin allergy
  • Avoid in pregnancy & small children

Rifabutin triple therapy

  • Rifabutin
  • Amoxicillin
  • PPI
  • More expensive, potential for drug-drug interactions
  • Alternative to BQT for patients without penicillin allergy

PCAB dual therapy

  • Amoxicillin
  • Vonoprazan
  • Simplest regimen, but more costly
  • May have less adverse effects than other regimens

PCAB = potassium-competitive acid blocker; PPI = proton pump inhibitor (eg, esomeprazole, rabeprazole).

"]],"protozoa-hematologic-infections--babesia":[[94205,"Babesiosis","

Babesiosis

Epidemiology

  • Vector: Tick (Ixodes scapularis), blood transfusion
  • Location: Northeastern/Upper Midwestern United States
  • Risk factors for severe disease: splenectomy, HIV, immunosuppression

Manifestations

  • Mild: fevers, fatigue, myalgias, headache
  • Severe:  ARDS, CHF, DIC, AKI, liver failure, splenic rupture
  • Anemia & thrombocytopenia

Diagnosis

  • Thin blood smear: intraerythrocytic pleomorphic ring forms ("Maltese cross")
  • PCR: detection of Babesia DNA in the blood
  • Serology: may be negative in acute infection

AKI = acute kidney injury; ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; CHF = congestive heart failure; DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation

"]],"terbinafine":[[94399,"Treatment of onychomycosis","

Treatment of onychomycosis

Indications

  • Pain or functional limitation
  • Secondary cellulitis or risk factors for cellulitis
    (eg, diabetes mellitus, peripheral artery disease)
  • Cosmetic preference

Mild to moderate disease

  • Oral terbinafine
  • Topical efinaconazole, ciclopirox, tavaborole, amorolfine

Moderate to severe disease

  • Oral terbinafine
  • Oral itraconazole
"]],"hepatitis-viruses--hav":[[117138,"Acute hepatitis A virus infection","

Acute hepatitis A virus infection

Transmission

Diagnostic

  • Anti–hepatitis A serology (IgG, IgM)

Management

IgG = immunoglobulin G; IgM = immunoglobulin M.
