"]],"protozoa-others--leishmania-spp":[[128219,"Leishmaniasis","

Leishmaniasis

Localized cutaneous

  • Painless, shallow, pink ulcer with indurated borders (± soft center) at sand fly bite site
  • Overlying eschar (Old World leishmaniasis) or fibrinous material (New World leishmaniasis)*
  • Spontaneous healing over months/years → atrophic scar/keloid

Mucocutaneous

  • Primarily in New World leishmaniasis, with or after cutaneous lesions
  • Mucosal erosions
    • Nasal: stuffiness, bleeding, facial disfigurement (cartilage destruction)
    • Larynx: hoarseness, brassy cough
    • Epiglottis/pharynx/palate: odynophagia

Visceral

(kala azar)

  • Often asymptomatic/subclinical (lifelong viable parasites, reactivation with immunosuppression)
  • Insidious clinical illness (2-6 months after transmission) from reticuloendothelial spread:
    • Constitutional (malaise, fever, weight loss)
    • Splenomegaly, left upper quadrant fullness
    • Skin darkening classic but uncommon (kala azar = "black fever")
  • Diagnosis: histopathology (amastigotes with kinetoplast)/culture, serology (resource-limited area)
  • >90% mortality without treatment

*Old World (Africa, Middle East, South Asia) vs New World (Central/South America) leishmaniasis reflects geographic & clinical differences.

"]],"nematodes-roundworms--onchocerca-volvulus":[[129198,"Onchocerciasis (river blindness)","

Onchocerciasis (river blindness)

Epidemiology

  • Leading cause of blindness in endemic areas (>99% of cases occur in Africa)
  • Black fly bite transmits filarial nematodes (Onchocerca volvulus) to skin → matures in subcutaneous nodules → microfilariae travel through lymph, skin, eyes

Manifestations

  • Subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas): over bony prominences: usually deep and asymptomatic
  • Cutaneous: intense pruritus, papular dermatitis, depigmentation
  • Ocular: keratitis, chorioretinitis, blindness

Diagnosis

  • Skin snip biopsy (gold standard)
  • Slit-lamp examination (visualize microfilariae)
  • Serologic testing (limited utility)

Treatment

  • Ivermectin
  • Doxycycline (kills endosymbiotic bacteria)
  • Vector control/mass treatment
"]],"nematodes-roundworms--strongyloides-stercoralis":[[129282,"Strongyloidiasis","

Strongyloidiasis

Epidemiology

  • Tropical/subtropical climates worldwide
  • Poor sanitary practices
  • Warm, moist soil exposure (eg, barefoot)

Manifestations

  • Largely asymptomatic (immunocompetent)
  • Skin:
    • Acute: maculopapular rash
    • Chronic: pruritic urticaria or larva currens*
  • Respiratory:
    • Dry cough, dyspnea, hoarseness, wheezing
  • Gastrointestinal:
    • Nonspecific (eg, bloating, crampy pain, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, anorexia)
    • Severe cases: bleeding, ulceration, obstruction, enteropathy, or perforation
  • Hyperinfection/dissemination (immunocompromised)

Diagnosis

  • Serology
  • Stool microscopy (rhabditiform larvae) or PCR

Treatment

  • Ivermectin
  • Follow-up (symptom resolution, test improvement)

*Larva currens is a quickly-moving, pruritic, serpiginous rash.

"]],"nematodes-roundworms--wuchereria-bancrofti-brugia-malayi":[[129991,"Lymphatic filariasis","

Lymphatic filariasis

Microbiology & risk factors

  • Parasitic nematode infection: Wuchereria bancrofti (~90%), Brugia malayi, Brugia timori
  • Mosquito vector
  • Endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, Pacific Islands, parts of Latin America & Caribbean

Pathogenesis

  • Third-stage larvae in mosquitoes infect host → mature to adult worms in lymphatics & reside in lymph nodes → adults release microfilariae into bloodstream → microfilariae ingested by mosquitoes  → third-stage larvae develop in mosquito GI tract

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic: most common
  • Acute: acute filarial lymphangitis, acute dermatolymphangioadenitis, filarial fever, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia
  • Chronic: severe lymphedema, hydrocele, elephantiasis

Diagnosis

  • Significant eosinophilia
  • Blood smear with Giemsa stain: circulating microfilariae
  • Circulating antigen detection (W bancrofti)

Treatment & prevention

  • Monoinfection: diethylcarbamazine
  • Coinfection*: combination regimen (eg, doxycycline, ivermectin, albendazole)
  • Prevention: mass drug administration

Prognosis

  • Chronic lymphedema, elephantiasis

*Coinfection with loiasis and/or onchocerciasis. Regimen dependent on type of coinfection and disease burden.

"]],"leptospira-interrogans":[[131338,"Leptospirosis","

Leptospirosis

Epidemiology

  • Spirochete from genus Leptospira
  • Endemic in tropical regions with poor sanitation
  • Reservoir is renal tubules of domestic/wild animals (eg, rodents)
  • Transmission occurs when contaminated soil/water contacts abraded skin, mucous membranes, conjunctiva

Manifestations

  • Mostly asymptomatic or mild/self-limited
  • Anicteric leptospirosis: acute febrile illness (fever, rigor, myalgia, headache), immune complications (uveitis, aseptic meningitis)
  • Icteric leptospirosis (Weil disease): fever, jaundice, end-organ complications (eg, renal failure, pulmonary hemorrhage)
  • Notable feature: conjunctival hyperemia with no purulence

Diagnosis

  • PCR
  • Serology

Treatment

  • Mild: oral doxycycline or azithromycin
  • Severe: intravenous penicillin, doxycycline, 3rd generation cephalosporin
"]],"nematodes-roundworms--toxocara-canis":[[131533,"Toxocariasis","

Toxocariasis

Epidemiology

  • Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati eggs ingested in contaminated soil or food
  • Humans are dead-end hosts (larvae do not mature)
  • Young children at greatest risk

Manifestations

  • Often asymptomatic or mild/self-limited
  • VLM
    • Liver: hepatomegaly or nodules
    • Lung: dyspnea, wheezing, nonproductive cough
    • Gastrointestinal: abdominal pain
  • OLM
    • Unilateral vision loss, photophobia, floaters, leukocoria, strabismus
    • Lesions (white granuloma) in posterior pole/periphery

Diagnosis

  • Serology (excretory-secretory antigen ELISA)
  • Eosinophilia
  • Elevated IgE
  • Ophthalmologic consultation (for OLM)

Treatment

  • Albendazole
  • Corticosteroids added for OLM/severe symptoms

ELISA = enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; OLM = ocular larva migrans; VLM = visceral larva migrans.

"]],"nematodes-roundworms--loa-loa":[[131940,"Loiasis","

Loiasis

Epidemiology

  • Caused by Loa loa (filarial nematode)
  • Transmitted by bite of Chrysops fly
  • Endemic to rainforests of Central/West Africa
  • Larvae, adult worms migrate through subcutaneous tissue/subconjunctiva, producing microfilariae

Manifestations

  • Calabar swellings: transient, focal areas of angioedema usually with localized pain/pruritic
  • Eye symptoms: transient tearing, foreign body sensation, conjunctival hyperemia (while worm passes through subconjunctiva)
  • Arterial thickening, nephropathy (chronic microfilaremia)
  • Encephalopathy (usually following treatment)

Diagnosis

  • Direct visualization of worms in eye or skin
  • Blood smear showing microfilaremia

Treatment

  • Must quantify microfilaremia and evaluate for onchocerciasis coinfection prior to starting treatment:
    • >20,000/mL: hospitalize + albendazole + recheck
    • 2,500-20,000/mL: ivermectin + recheck
    • <2,500/mL and no onchocerciasis: DEC
  • DEC is the definitive treatment

DEC = diethylcarbamazine.

"]],"rickettsial-diseases-and-vector-borne-illnesses--q-fever":[[132419,"Q fever","

Q fever

Epidemiology

  • Coxiella burnetii (obligate intracellular, gram-negative) is transmitted via aerosols from domestic animal products
  • Risk increased with certain occupations (farmer, abattoir/lab worker) or living near livestock
  • Low infectious dose; potential bioterrorism agent

Manifestations

  • Acute Q fever (self-limited): ~50% asymptomatic
    • Influenza-like febrile illness
    • Community-acquired pneumonia
    • Acute hepatitis
  • Chronic Q fever
    • Culture-negative endocarditis (prior valve disease)
    • Vascular infection (prior arterial disease/graft)
    • Bone/joint infection

Diagnosis

  • Serology (Coxiella LPS IgG)*
  • PCR (highest sensitivity in acute infection)

Treatment

  • Acute Q fever: oral doxycycline
  • Chronic Q fever: oral doxycycline + hydroxychloroquine × 18-24 months
  • Serial serology + clinical visits required to ensure resolution

*Phase I IgG (in vivo; weakly immunogenic) is elevated in chronic infection; phase II IgG (in vitro; strongly immunogenic) is elevated in acute infection.

LPS = lipopolysaccharide.

"]],"dna-viruses--poxvirus":[[132990,"Mpox","

Mpox

Epidemiology

  • dsDNA orthopoxvirus similar to smallpox
  • Zoonotic spread in endemic areas (Central/West Africa)
  • Person-to-person spread in nonendemic areas during outbreaks (primarily MSM) 

Manifestations

  • Systemic symptoms: fever, headache, myalgia, LAD
  • Rash: macule → papule →  vesicle → pseudopustule → crusted lesion → scab → resolution
  • More rarely, pneumonitis, encephalitis, tonsillitis/pharyngitis, proctitis

Diagnosis

  • Clinical + PCR testing or serology

Management

  • Self-limited in most cases
  • Supportive care (eg, analgesics)
  • Antivirals if immunocompromised, severely ill, or young/pregnant
    • Techovirimat + brincidofovir
  • Vaccine available for preexposure or postexposure prophylaxis

dsDNA = double-stranded DNA; LAD = lymphadenopathy; MSM = men who have sex with men.

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["neuro"] = {"headaches--migraine":[[31097,"Migraine therapies","

Migraine therapies

Abortives

  • Simple analgesics (eg, NSAIDs, acetaminophen)
  • Antiemetics (eg, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)
  • Triptans (eg, sumatriptan)
  • Ergotamine, dihydroergotamine
  • CGRP receptor antagonists (eg, rimegepant)

Preventives

  • Antiepileptics (eg, topiramate, divalproex sodium)
  • Tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline)
  • β Blockers (eg, propranolol)
  • CGRP monoclonal antibodies (eg, erenumab)

CGRP = calcitonin gene-related peptide; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

"]],"otitis-externa":[[31222,"Otitis externa","

Otitis externa

Risk factors

  • Water exposure
  • Trauma (eg, cotton swabs, ear candling)
  • Foreign material (eg, hearing aid, headphones)
  • Dermatologic conditions (eg, eczema, contact dermatitis)

Microbiology

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Staphylococcus aureus

Clinical
manifestations

  • Otalgia, pruritus, discharge, hearing loss
  • Pain with auricle manipulation
  • Ear canal erythema, edema, debris
  • Tympanic membrane spared (clear, not inflamed, no middle ear fluid)

Treatment

  • Remove debris
  • Topical antibiotic (eg, fluoroquinolone)
  • ± Topical glucocorticoid
  • Consider wick placement to facilitate medication delivery
"], [36890,"Acute otitis externa","

Acute otitis externa

Severity

Clinical features

Treatment

Mild*

  • Minor discomfort & pruritus
  • Minimal canal edema
  • Topical acidifying solution (eg, acetic acid)
 

Moderate/severe*

  
  • Moderate pain & pruritus
  • Partial or complete occlusion from edema
  • Clean the ear canal with wire loop
  • Topical antibiotics
    • Polymyxin B/neomycin
    • Colistin/neomycin
    • Fluoroquinolones (eg, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin)
  • Wick placement if canal is completely occluded
 

Invasive otitis (malignant otitis externa)

  • Risk factors: Diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression
  • Intense pain
  • Complete canal occlusion from edema
  • Periauricular erythema, lymphadenopathy & fever
  
  • Broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics (eg, ciprofloxacin)
  • ± Debridement

*Consider adding topical glucocorticoid (eg, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone) if significant pain or itching is present.

"], [47377,"Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa","

Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa

Pathophysiology

  • Life-threatening infectious complication of acute otitis externa
  • Aggressive spread beyond external ear canal into skull base & adjacent tissues

Risk factors

  • Older age (>60)
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Ear irrigation (cerumen removal)

Microbiology

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Clinical features

  • Severe, unremitting ear pain (worse at night & with chewing)
  • Purulent otorrhea
  • Granulation tissue along floor of ear canal
  • ± Cranial nerve palsy (eg, facial droop from CN VII involvement)
  • Elevated ESR

Treatment

  • IV antipseudomonal antibiotic (eg, ciprofloxacin)

CN VII = facial nerve; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; IV = intravenous.

"]],"neural-tube-defects":[[31236,"Neural tube defects","

Neural tube defects

Types

  • Anencephaly
  • Encephalocele
  • Spina bifida, myelomeningocele

Risk

factors

  • Low folic acid intake
  • Methotrexate, antiepileptics
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Prior pregnancy with neural tube defect

Prenatal
screening

  • 2nd-trimester ultrasonography
  • Maternal serum α-fetoprotein

Prevention

  • Average risk: 0.4 mg folic acid daily
  • High risk: 4 mg folic acid daily
"], [35767,"Spina bifida","

Spina bifida

Pathogenesis

  • Failure of neural tube to close

Risk factors

  • Prenatal maternal folate deficiency (eg,
    inadequate supplementation, antifolate drugs)

Clinical features
& comorbidities

  • Motor/sensory dysfunction
  • Neurogenic bladder/bowel
  • Hydrocephalus
  • Scoliosis

Treatment

  • Surgical closure
  • Clean intermittent catheterization
  • Scheduled laxatives/enemas
  • Bracing; correction of deformities
"], [72832,"Closed spinal dysraphism","

Closed spinal dysraphism

Pathophysiology

  • Failure of posterior vertebral arch fusion
  • ± Spinal cord anomalies (eg, lipoma, cyst)
  • Stretch-induced distal spinal cord dysfunction (tethered cord)

Clinical features

  • May be asymptomatic
  • Cutaneous, lumbosacral anomalies (eg, hair tuft, mass)
  • Tethered cord syndrome*:
    • Neurologic: LMN signs (weakness, hyporeflexia)
    • Urologic: incontinence/retention; recurrent UTI
    • Orthopedic: back pain, scoliosis, foot deformities

Management

  • MRI of the spine
  • Surgical detethering of cord if symptomatic

*Age of onset & organ system involvement are variable.

LMN = lower motor neuron; UTI = urinary tract infection.

"]],"cranial-nerve-iii-iv-vi-palsies":[[31598,"Nerve","

Nerve

Eye muscle(s) innervated

Oculomotor functions

Lesion findings

Oculomotor
(CN III)

  • Superior rectus
  • Medial rectus
  • Inferior rectus
  • Inferior oblique
  • Levator palpebrae superioris
  • Abduction
  • Depression
  • Elevation
  • External rotation
  • Eye deviated downward & laterally
  • Diagonal diplopia
  • Dilation of pupil & loss of accommodation
  • Ptosis

Trochlear
(CN IV)

  • Superior oblique
  • Abduction
  • Internal rotation
  • Depression while adducted
  • Eye deviated upward
  • Vertical & torsional diplopia

Abducens
(CN VI)

  • Lateral rectus
  • Abduction
  • Eye deviated medially
  • Horizontal diplopia
"]],"dementia-continued":[[32369,"Differential diagnosis of dementia subtypes","

Differential diagnosis of dementia subtypes

Alzheimer disease

  • Early, insidious short-term memory loss
  • Language deficits & spatial disorientation
  • Later personality changes

Vascular dementia

  • Stepwise decline
  • Early executive dysfunction
  • Cerebral infarction &/or deep white matter changes on neuroimaging

Frontotemporal dementia

  • Early personality changes
  • Apathy, disinhibition & compulsive behavior
  • Frontotemporal atrophy on neuroimaging

Dementia with Lewy bodies

  • Visual hallucinations
  • Spontaneous parkinsonism
  • Fluctuating cognition
  • Rapid eye movement behavior disorder

Normal pressure hydrocephalus

  • Ataxia early in disease
  • Urinary incontinence
  • Dilated ventricles on neuroimaging

Prion disease

  • Behavioral changes
  • Rapid progression
  • Myoclonus &/or seizures
"]],"headaches":[[32372,"Headache red flags","

Headache red flags

Red flag feature

Common diagnoses

  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage

  • Giant cell (temporal) arteritis

  • Mass lesion
  • Subdural hematoma

Worsened by physical activity

  • Mass lesion
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Focal neurologic signs, papilledema

  • Mass lesion
  • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
  • Arteriovenous malformation

Personality changes

  • CNS infection
  • Mass lesion
  • Intracerebral hemorrhage

Systemic symptoms (eg, fever, rash)

  • Encephalitis
  • Meningitis

"], [81846,"Thunderclap headache","

Thunderclap headache

Clinical features

  • Sudden (maximum intensity <1 hr), severe headache
  • ± Seizure, neurologic deficits, mental status abnormality
  • ± Nausea/vomiting

Etiology

Most common:

  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage: hypertension, neck stiffness
  • RCVS: recurrent episodes over days to weeks

Less common:

  • Pituitary apoplexy: ophthalmoplegia, visual field defects, adrenal insufficiency
  • Cervical artery dissection: posterior headache, neck pain
  • Cavernous sinus thrombosis: slower onset, proptosis, fever (if septic)
  • Meningitis: slower onset, fever, neck pain & stiffness
  • PRES: subacute headache, hypertensive crisis

Evaluation

  • Immediate noncontrast CT scan of the head
  • Lumbar puncture
  • Expedited MRI of the head

PRES = posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome; RCVS = reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome.

"]],"vertigo":[[32398,"Peripheral vertigo","

Peripheral vertigo

Central vertigo

Etiologies

  • BPPV
  • Ménière disease
  • Vestibular neuritis
  • Stroke (eg, cerebellar)
  • Multiple sclerosis
  • Migraine

Nystagmus
characteristics

  • Never purely vertical
  • Inhibited by fixation of gaze
  • Fatigable (<1-min duration)
  • Latency period (2-40 sec)
  • May have any trajectory
  • Not inhibited by fixation of gaze
  • Not fatigable (>1-min duration)
  • No latency period

Other possible
neurologic signs

  • Hearing loss/tinnitus may be present
  • Walking usually preserved
  • No other CNS symptoms
  • Hearing loss/tinnitus absent
  • Severe postural instability
  • Other CNS symptoms (eg, headache, diplopia, weakness/numbness of face or limbs, dysarthria) often present

BPPV = benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

"], [35451,"Common causes of vertigo","

Common causes of vertigo

Ménière disease

  • Recurrent episodes lasting 20 minutes to several hours
  • Sensorineural hearing loss
  • Tinnitus &/or feeling of fullness in the ear

BPPV

  • Brief episodes triggered by head movement
  • Dix-Hallpike maneuver causes nystagmus

Vestibular neuritis

  • Acute, single episode that can last days
  • Often follows viral syndrome
  • Abnormal head thrust test

Migraine

  • Vertigo associated with headache or other migrainous phenomenon (eg, visual aura)
  • Symptoms resolve completely between episodes

Brainstem/
cerebellar stroke

  • Sudden-onset, persistent vertigo
  • Usually other neurologic symptoms

BPPV = benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

Common causes of vertigo

BPPV

  • Often follows viral syndrome

cerebellar stroke

  • Sudden-onset, persistent vertigo

"], [91045,"Dizziness type by symptoms","

Dizziness type by symptoms

Category

Description

Potential causes

Vertigo

● Sense of motion (eg, "spinning," "whirling," "tilting")
● Worse with head movement
● Associated nausea & vomiting

● Peripheral (eg, BPPV, Ménière disease, vestibular neuritis)
● Central (eg, posterior circulation stroke or hemorrhage, migraine, MS)

Presyncope

● Lightheadedness (eg, "almost fainted," "nearly blacked out")
● Triggered by standing or exertion
● Associated diaphoresis, warmth

● Orthostatic (eg, hypovolemia, autonomic dysfunction)
● Cardiac (eg, dysrhythmia, valvular disease)
● Reflex (eg, vasovagal, situational)

Disequilibrium

● Imbalance (eg, "unsteady")
● Worse with walking or standing
● Associated falls without vertigo or presyncope

● Sensory input (eg, visual impairment, polyneuropathy, cervical spondylosis)
● Motor output (eg, Parkinson disease, MS, cerebellar disorder)

Nonspecific

● Vague symptom (eg, "giddiness," "floating") not fitting another description
● Associated psychiatric condition, polypharmacy, recreational drugs

● Psychiatric (eg, anxiety, depression, panic disorder)
● Other (eg, hyperventilation, medications, substance use disorder)

BPPV = benign paroxysmal positional vertigo; MS = multiple sclerosis.

"], [91046,"Peripheral vs central vertigo","

Peripheral vs central vertigo

Peripheral (labyrinth or CN VIII)

Central (cerebellum or brainstem)

CNS deficits

● Absent

● Common (eg, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia)

Auditory signs

● Common (↓ hearing &/or tinnitus)

● Absent

Imbalance

● One direction (sways toward lesion)

● Severe instability (often unable to walk)

Nystagmus

● One direction (never pure vertical)
● Same direction in all gazes
● Suppressed by visual fixation

● Any direction (pure vertical = central)
● May change direction with gaze
● Unsuppressed by visual fixation

Causes

● BPPV
● Ménière disease
● Vestibular neuritis (labyrinthitis)

● Vestibular migraine
● Multiple sclerosis
● Stroke or hemorrhage (eg, cerebellar)

BPPV = benign paroxysmal positional vertigo; CN = cranial nerve.

"], [91670,"HINTS examination to distinguish peripheral from central vertigo*","

HINTS examination to distinguish peripheral from central vertigo*

Peripheral
(vestibular nerve or labyrinth)

Central
(cerebellum or brainstem)

Head Impulse test
(rapid head movement
to each side)

●  Abnormal VOR: eyes dragged off
      target, followed by a corrective saccade
●  Peripheral structures trigger the VOR

●  Normal VOR:  eyes stay on target
●  Cerebellum is not involved in the
      VOR

Nystagmus
(observe in all gazes)

●  Unidirectional
●  Peripheral lesions cause unilateral
      imbalance of tonic vestibular inputs

●  Changes direction with gaze
●  Cerebellar and brainstem lesions
      can affect gaze-holding pathways

Test of Skew
(cover and uncover
each eye)

●  No vertical shift when eye uncovered
●  Peripheral lesions do not typically affect
      vertical eye alignment

●  Vertical shift when eye uncovered
●  Brainstem lesions can affect
      vertical eye alignment pathways

*Sustained vertigo with nystagmus must be present (ie, not useful for episodic vertigo).
 VOR = vestibulo-ocular reflex.

"]],"dyskinesias--essential-tremor":[[32501,"Essential tremor","

Essential tremor

Epidemiology

  • Family history often present
  • Up to 5% of population affected

Clinical
features

  • Action tremor (eg, hands outstretched)
  • Usually bilateral
  • Hands > arms > head >> legs
  • Worsens with stress, improves with alcohol

Treatment

  • Beta blockers: propranolol
  • Anticonvulsants: primidone
"]],"conjunctivitis":[[32563,"Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis","

Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis

Transmission

  • Contact with infected genital secretions during delivery

Clinical presentation

  • Copious exudate & eyelid swelling (typically age 2-5 days)

Complications

  • Corneal ulceration & scarring → vision loss

Diagnosis

  • Nucleic acid amplification testing
  • Gram stain (gram-negative intracellular diplococci) & culture (Thayer-Martin medium)

Treatment

  • IM third-generation cephalosporin (eg, cefotaxime)

Prevention

  • Maternal screening (age <25 or with risk factors) & treatment
  • Ophthalmic erythromycin ointment at birth
IM = intramuscular.
"], [32576,"Neonatal conjunctivitis","

Neonatal conjunctivitis

Type

Onset age

Findings

Treatment

Chemical

<24 hr

  • Mild conjunctival irritation & tearing
  • Uncommon adverse effect of topical medication (eg, erythromycin)
 Artificial tears

Gonococcal

2-5 days

  • Profuse purulent discharge
  • Marked conjunctival injection & eyelid edema
 IM/IV cefotaxime (single dose)

Chlamydial

5-14 days       

  • Watery, serosanguineous, or mucopurulent eye discharge
  • Mild eyelid swelling

Oral erythromycin

IM/IV = intramuscular/intravenous.

"], [33447,"Acute conjunctivitis causes & treatment","

Acute conjunctivitis causes & treatment

Diagnosis

Common etiologies

Treatment

Bacterial
conjunctivitis

  • Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Pseudomonas (contact lens)
  • Erythromycin ointment or polymyxin-trimethoprim drops
  • Fluoroquinolone drops (contact lens wearers)

Viral
conjunctivitis

  • Adenovirus
  • Supportive care (eg, warm or cold compress, lubricating drops)

Allergic
conjunctivitis

  • Airborne allergens (eg, pollen, dust mites, pet dander)
  • Antihistamine plus decongestant or mast cell stabilizer drops (eg, olopatadine, ketotifen)
"], [34585,"Chlamydial conjunctivitis","

Chlamydial conjunctivitis

Mode of transmission

  • Direct contact with maternal genital secretions during delivery

Age at onset

  • 5-14 days

Clinical manifestations

  • Thickened, injected conjunctivae (chemosis)
  • Watery or mucopurulent discharge
  • Eyelid swelling

Treatment

  • Oral macrolide

Prevention

  • Identification & treatment of maternal infection during pregnancy*

*Standard ophthalmic prophylaxis (ie, erythromycin) at birth prevents only gonococcal, not chlamydial, conjunctivitis.

"], [38223,"Acute conjunctivitis*","

Acute conjunctivitis*

Viral

Bacterial

Allergic

Distribution

Unilateral or bilateral

Unilateral or bilateral

Bilateral

Discharge

Watery/mucoid

Purulent

Watery

Conjunctival appearance

Diffuse injection; follicular (bumpy)

Diffuse injection; nonfollicular

Diffuse injection; follicular (bumpy)

Associated findings

Viral prodrome

Unremitting discharge (reaccumulates within minutes)

Ocular pruritus, history of atopy (eg, allergic rhinitis, asthma)

1-2 weeks

1-2 weeks

<30 minutes (often sudden onset) to perennial

*Red flags suggestive of alternate etiology: decreased visual acuity, photophobia, pain with extraocular movement & fixed/distorted pupil.

"], [126747,"Trachoma grading system","

Trachoma grading system

Stage

Name

Definition

TF

Trachomatous inflammation – Follicular

  • ≥5 lymphoid follicles on the upper tarsal conjunctiva

TI

Trachomatous inflammation – Intense

  • Inflammatory thickening obscuring >50% of the deep tarsal vessels

TS

Trachomatous scarring

  • Scarring on the tarsal conjunctiva

  • ≥1 eyelash touching the globe or evidence of eyelash removal

"]],"otitis-media":[[32754,"Acute otitis media","

Acute otitis media

Microbiology

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae
  • Moraxellacatarrhalis

Clinical features

  • Ear pain ± fever
  • Otoscopy:
    • Bulging TM
      AND/OR
    • Middle ear effusion (eg, air-fluid level, impaired mobility) plus TM erythema

Treatment*

  • 1st-line: amoxicillin
  • 2nd-line: amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Penicillin-allergic: azithromycin or clindamycin

Complications

  • TM perforation
  • Conductive hearing loss
  • Local extension (eg, mastoiditis, meningitis, brain abscess)

*Observation can be considered for children age >6 months with unilateral disease, no/mild pain, and low-grade fever (<39 C [102.2 F]).

TM = tympanic membrane.

"], [35416,"Mastoiditis","

Mastoiditis

Pathophysiology

  • Infection of the mastoid air cells
  • Complication of acute otitis media
  • Most commonly due to Streptococcus pneumoniae

Clinical findings

  • Fever & otalgia
  • Inflammation of mastoid
  • Protrusion of the auricle
  • Opacification of mastoid air cells on CT scan or MRI

Management

  • Intravenous antibiotics
  • Drainage of purulent material (eg, tympanostomy, mastoidectomy)

Complications

  • Extracranial extension (subperiosteal abscess, facial nerve palsy, hearing loss, labyrinthitis)
  • Intracranial extension (brain abscess, meningitis)
"], [64199,"Chronic suppurative otitis media","

Chronic suppurative otitis media

Microbiology

  • Often polymicrobial
  • Staphylococcus aureus & Pseudomonas aeruginosa most common

Clinical features

  • Chronic (>6 weeks) otorrhea
  • ± Hearing loss

Examination

  • TM perforation with purulent middle ear drainage
  • Normal-appearing external auditory canal

Management

  • Otic fluoroquinolone drops (eg, ofloxacin)

Complications

  • Infectious spread (eg, mastoiditis, brain abscess)
  • Permanent hearing loss

TM = tympanic membrane.

"]],"neurocutaneous-disorders--neurofibromatosis-type-i":[[33087,"Neurofibromatosis type I","

Neurofibromatosis type I

Epidemiology

  • Autosomal dominantNF1 mutation
 

Manifestations

  • Café-au-lait spots
  • Clustered freckles - axilla, inguinal
  • Lisch nodules
  • Neurofibromas
  • Optic glioma
"]],"_more":[[33404,"Glasgow Coma Scale","

Glasgow Coma Scale

(E)ye opening
(Maximum = 4)

4 - Spontaneous (open with blinking at baseline)

3 - To speech

2 - To pain only

1 - None

(V)erbal response
(Maximum = 5)

5 - Oriented

4 - Confused (converses but confused, disoriented)

3 - Inappropriate (inappropriate words)

2 - Incomprehensible (sounds, no words)

1 - None

(M)otor response
(Maximum = 6)

6 - Obeys commands for movement

5 - Localizes to pain

4 - Withdraws from pain

3 - Flexion in response to pain (decorticate posturing)

2 - Extension in response to pain (decerebrate posturing)

1 - None

  • Use best response for each category (range = 3-15).
  • Coma: Does not open eyes, does not follow commands & does not utter understandable words; Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score 3-8.
  • Head injury classification: Mild, GCS score 13-15; moderate, GCS score 9-12; severe, GCS score ≤8.
"], [37341,"Auricular hematoma","

Auricular hematoma

Risk

factors

  • Contact sports injury (eg, wrestling, martial arts)

Clinical features

  • Tender, fluctuant blood collection on anterior pinna

Treatment

  • Immediate incision & drainage
  • Pressure dressing

Complications

  • Cauliflower ear (fibrocartilage overgrowth)
  • Bacterial superinfection
  • Reaccumulation of hematoma
"], [38808,"Carotid artery dissection","

Carotid artery dissection

Etiology

  • Trauma; spontaneous occurrence
  • Underlying contributors: HTN, smoking, CTD

Clinical presentation

  • Unilateral head & neck pain, transient vision loss
  • Ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome
    • Ptosis & miosis without anhidrosis
  • Signs of cerebral ischemia (eg, focal weakness)

Diagnosis

  • Neurovascular imaging (eg, CT angiography)

Treatment

  • Thrombolysis (if ≤4.5 hr after symptom onset)
  • Antiplatelet therapy (eg, aspirin) ± anticoagulation

CTD = connective tissue disease; HTN = hypertension.

"], [45199,"Cerumen impaction","

Cerumen impaction

Risk factors

  • Institutional residence (eg, nursing home)
  • Intellectual disability
  • Hearing aids

Symptoms

  • Mild pain, fullness, itching
  • Reduced hearing
  • Tinnitus, vertigo
  • Reflexive cough

Management

  • Cerumenolytics: carbamide peroxide,
    mineral oil, hydrogen peroxide, docusate
  • Irrigation
  • Curette disimpaction

Prevention

  • Emollients or mineral oil
  • Intermittent irrigation
  • Avoidance of cotton swabs in the ear
"], [47832,"Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy","

Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy

Pathophysiology & causes

Repetitive bone & joint trauma due to impaired sensation/ proprioception

  • Diabetes mellitus (most common)
  • Posterior column disease (eg, B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis)

Clinical manifestations

Acute

  • Inflammatory erythema, warmth & edema of the foot
  • Minimal bone involvement (x-rays often normal)

Chronic

  • Bone deformities (eg, subluxation, collapsed arch, stress fracture)

"], [66772,"Diagnosis of brain death","

Diagnosis of brain death

Clinical criteria

  • Known cause (eg, TBI, stroke)
  • Evidence (eg, clinical, neuroimaging) of devastating CNS event
  • Exclusion of confounding conditions (eg, electrolyte abnormality, intoxication, paralytics)
  • Core temperature >36 C (96.8 F), SBP >100 mm Hg

Clinical examination

  • Coma
  • Absent brainstem reflexes:
    • Pupillary
    • Corneal
    • Oculocephalic, oculovestibular
    • Jaw jerk
    • Cough
    • Gag
  • Absent brain-originating* motor responses (including decerebrate & decorticate posturing)

*Movements originating from the spinal cord (eg, deep tendon reflexes) may still be present.

SBP = systolic blood pressure; TBI = traumatic brain injury.

"]],"other-demyelinating-and-dysmyelinating-disorders--acute-inflammatory-demyelinating-polyneuropathy":[[34551,"Guillain-Barré syndrome","

"]],"fever-vs-heat-stroke":[[36213,"Heat stroke","

Heat stroke

Risk factors

  • Exertional heat stroke: strenuous activity in hot & humid weather
  • Nonexertional heat stroke: advanced age, impaired mobility, obesity, neuropsychiatric disease, recreational drugs (eg, cocaine, amphetamines), certain medications (eg, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, β blockers, diuretics)

Clinical manifestations

  • Core temperature >40 C (104 F), tachycardia, hypotension
  • Central nervous system dysfunction: confusion, weakness, dizziness, lethargy, ataxia, seizures
  • Rhabdomyolysis & acute kidney injury
  • Acute liver injury
  • Pulmonary edema & acute respiratory distress syndrome
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation

Management

  • Rapid cooling: misting systems, ice water immersion, ice packs
  • Fluid resuscitation
  • Electrolyte correction
"], [60289,"Exertional heat stroke","

Exertional heat stroke

Risk factors

  • Strenuous activity during hot & humid weather
  • Dehydration, poor acclimatization
  • Lack of physical fitness, obesity
  • Medications: anticholinergics, antihistamines, phenothiazines, tricyclics, antipsychotics

Clinical manifestations

  • Core temperature >40 C (104 F) with CNS dysfunction (eg, AMS, seizure)
  • Organ or tissue damage: renal or hepatic failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome

Management

  • Rapid cooling: ice water immersion preferred; can consider high-flow cold water dousing, ice-wet towel rotation, evaporative cooling
  • Fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction
  • Management of end-organ complications
  • No role for antipyretic therapy

AMS = altered mental status.

"], [60389,"Heat exhaustion","

Heat exhaustion

Risk factors

  • Strenuous activity during hot & humid weather
  • Dehydration, poor acclimatization
  • Lack of physical fitness, obesity
  • Acute illness
  • Medications: anticholinergics, antihistamines, phenothiazines, tricyclics, antipsychotics

Manifestations

  • Hyperthermia ≤40 C (104 F) with normal mental status
  • Profuse sweating
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Headache, dizziness
  • Tachycardia, hypotension

Management

  • Cool patient (eg, air conditioning, cool water shower)
  • Salt-containing oral fluids
"], [60961,"Nonexertional (classic) heat stroke","

Nonexertional (classic) heat stroke

Risk factors

  • Elderly, obesity, poor physical fitness
  • Alcohol, medications (eg, diuretics, β blockers, anticholinergics, stimulants)
  • High temperatures, high humidity, lack of air conditioning

Manifestations

  • Temperature ≥40 C (104 F) with CNS dysfunction (eg, encephalopathy, seizure)
  • Tachycardia, tachypnea ± hypotension
  • Flushing ± diaphoresis
  • End-organ dysfunction (eg, DIC, pulmonary edema, renal/hepatic dysfunction)
  • Hemoconcentration (↑ hemoglobin, leukocytes, platelets, BUN)

Management

  • Stabilization (ie, airway, breathing, circulation)
  • Rapid cooling (evaporative techniques are best tolerated in the elderly)
    • Antipyretics/dantrolene are NOT indicated
  • Management of end-organ complications

BUN = blood urea nitrogen; DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation.

"]],"ischemic-stroke":[[36316,"Criteria for thrombolytics in stroke","

Criteria for thrombolytics in stroke

Inclusion criteria

  • Ischemic stroke with disabling neurodeficits
  • Symptom onset <3-4.5 hr before treatment initiation

Strict exclusion criteria*

  • ICH on CT scan, history of ICH, suspected SAH
  • Ischemic stroke in the past 3 months

"]],"insomnia-therapy":[[37376,"Nonpharmacological treatment of insomnia","

Nonpharmacological treatment of insomnia

Sleep
hygiene

Encourage good sleeping habits

  • Maintain regular sleep schedule, avoid naps
  • Avoid caffeine after lunch
  • Avoid alcohol, smoking, large meals near bedtime
  • Keep bedroom quiet, dark & cool
  • Exercise regularly but not right before bedtime

Stimulus
control

Break link between bedroom & frustration/fear

  • Use bed only for sleep & sexual activity (no reading, television, eating)
  • Go to bed only when sleepy & leave bedroom if unable to sleep

Relaxation

Reduce tension/stress

  • Progressive muscle relaxation (contract & relax muscles in sequence)
  • Relaxation response (abdominal breathing, focus on peaceful image)

Sleep
restriction

Improve sleep efficiency (ratio of time asleep to time in bed)

  • Restrict time in bed to time of actual sleep (based on sleep diary)
  • Increase time in bed as efficiency improves

Cognitive
therapy

Change maladaptive beliefs

  • Manage catastrophic concern about effect of insomnia
  • Provide realistic expectations about the need for sleep

insomnia

Secondary
insomnia

"], [82456,"Diagnosis of idiopathic Parkinson disease","

Diagnosis of idiopathic Parkinson disease*

Essential criterion

  • Motor parkinsonism = bradykinesia + either rest tremor or rigidity

Exclusion criteria

  • Vertical (supranuclear) gaze palsy
  • Cerebellar signs (eg, limb ataxia, evoked nystagmus)
  • Cortical sensory loss (eg, astereognosis)
  • Progressive aphasia
  • Antidopaminergic medication use (eg, haloperidol)

Supportive features

  • Excellent response to dopaminergic therapy (eg, levodopa)
  • Asymmetric limb findings (eg, tremor, rigidity)
  • Olfactory dysfunction
  • Abnormal dopaminergic function on neuroimaging

Red flags

  • Early postural instability (eg, recurrent falls or need for wheelchair)
  • Early bulbar dysfunction (eg, dysarthria, dysphagia)
  • Absence of nonmotor signs (eg, sleep disturbance, constipation)
  • Severe orthostatic hypotension (eg, ≥30 mm Hg systolic drop)
  • Symmetric symptoms, hyperreflexia

*Established Parkinson disease is parkinsonism + no exclusion criteria + 2 supportive criteria (no red flags).
Probable Parkinson disease is parkinsonism + no exclusion criteria + (supportive criteria ≥ red flags).

Mild

  • >5 steps, recovers unaided

  • Stands safely, falls during test if not caught by examiner

Severe

Clinical features

  • Headache, vomiting
  • Seizure
  • Focal neurologic deficits
  • Altered mental status

Imaging

  • Head CT scan: intraparenchymal, intraventricular, or subarachnoid hyperdense fluid collection

Management

  • Supportive (eg, antiepileptics)
  • Reduction of intracranial pressure (eg, elevate head of bed, surgical decompression)

AVM = arteriovenous malformation; HHT = hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.

"]],"adult-primary-brain-tumors--schwannoma":[[51066,"Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)","

Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)

Epidemiology

  • Median age 50
  • Usually unilateral (bilateral associated with NF2-related schwannomatosis)

Clinical manifestations & pathophysiology

  • Sensorineural hearing loss & imbalance (Schwann cell tumor of vestibulocochlear nerve [CN VIII])
  • ± Facial numbness &/or paralysis (compression of trigeminal [CN V] & facial [CN VII] nerves)

Diagnostic studies

  • Audiogram
  • MRI with contrast of internal auditory canal

  • Radiation therapy

"]],"idiopathic-intracranial-hypertension":[[51069,"Idiopathic intracranial hypertension","

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

Risk factors

  • Women of childbearing age
  • Recent weight gain/obesity
  • Medications (eg, retinoids/vitamin A, tetracyclines, growth hormone)

Pathophysiology

  • Impaired CSF resorption & intracranial venous hypertension

Clinical
features

  • Headache/nausea/vomiting
  • Visual changes (transient obscurations; vision loss; diplopia due to abducens nerve [CN VI] palsy)
  • Pulsatile tinnitus
  • Retrobulbar pain/neck pain/back pain

Diagnosis

  • Papilledema & enlarged blind spots
  • MRI to rule out mass lesions/hydrocephalus
  • MR venography to rule out venous thrombosis
  • Lumbar puncture: elevated opening pressure

Treatment

  • Weight loss, including bariatric surgery
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide, topiramate)

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid.

"]],"neurocutaneous-disorders--tuberous-sclerosis-complex":[[51099,"Tuberous sclerosis complex","

Tuberous sclerosis complex

  • Mutation (inherited or de novo) in TSC1 or TSC2 gene

  • Dermatologic

    • Shagreen patches
  • Neurologic

    • Epilepsy (eg, infantile spasms)
    • Intellectual disability
    • Autism & behavioral disorders (eg, hyperactivity)
  • Cardiovascular: rhabdomyomas
  • Renal: angiomyolipomas

Surveillance

  • Tumor screening
    • Regular skin & eye examinations
    • Serial MRI of the brain & kidney
    • Baseline echocardiography & serial ECG
  • Baseline electroencephalography
  • Neuropsychiatric screening
"]],"retinal-disorders--retinal-artery-occlusion":[[51414,"Amaurosis fugax","

Amaurosis fugax

  • Papilledema

Central retinal vein occlusion

Cataracts

"]],"childhood-primary-brain-tumors--medulloblastoma":[[53843,"Medulloblastoma","

Medulloblastoma

"]],"childhood-primary-brain-tumors--craniopharyngioma":[[54282,"Craniopharyngioma","

Craniopharyngioma

  • Benign, slow growing

ADH = antidiuretic hormone; GH = growth hormone.

"]],"other-demyelinating-and-dysmyelinating-disorders--peripheral-neuropathy":[[57037,"Distal symmetric polyneuropathy","

Distal symmetric polyneuropathy

Triggers

  • Diabetes mellitus (diabetic neuropathy)
  • Long-standing HIV infection
  • Uremia
  • Medications (eg, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole)
  • Chemotherapy (eg, cisplatin, paclitaxel)

  • Damage to distal sensory peripheral nerve axons

  • Symptoms begin in toes/feet, progress proximally over time

  • ↓ Ankle/Babinski reflexes

  • Treat underlying cause
  • Pain management: gabapentinoid, tricyclic antidepressant, duloxetine &/or capsaicin cream
"]],"headaches--cluster":[[57346,"Cluster headache","

Cluster headache

Symptoms

  • Multiple short attacks (15-180 min) of severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain
  • Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea/nasal congestion)
  • Agitation or restlessness
  • Attacks occurring in clusters (6-12 weeks) separated by periods of remission

Acute treatment

  • 100% oxygen at 6-12 L/min for 15 min
  • Sumatriptan (subcutaneous)
  • Zolmitriptan nasal spray

Preventive treatment

  • Verapamil
  • Lithium
  • Topiramate
"]],"neonatal-intraventricular-hemorrhage":[[57471,"Intraventricular hemorrhage","

Intraventricular hemorrhage

Pathophysiology

  • Rupture of fragile germinal matrix vessels

Risk factors

  • Prematurity
  • Very low birth weight 

Clinical findings

  • Often asymptomatic
  • Seizures or apnea
  • Full fontanelle
  • Acute anemia

Diagnosis

  • Cranial ultrasonography*
    • Hyperechoic material (blood) within germinal matrix ± extension to ventricles or parenchyma

*Performed if symptomatic or as routine screening if <32 weeks gestational age.

"]],"glaucoma":[[58554,"Glaucoma in children","

Glaucoma in children

    • Impaired drainage of intraocular fluid

"]],"strabismus":[[58716,"Strabismus","

Strabismus (ocular misalignment)

Clinical findings

  • Constant eye deviation at any age
  • Intermittent eye deviation at age >4 months
  • Eye deviation on cover test
  • Asymmetric corneal light reflexes
  • Asymmetric intensity of red reflexes

"], [58819,"Amblyopia","

Amblyopia

Definition

  • Functional reduction in visual acuity due to visual disturbances in early childhood
  • Unilateral (most common): ≥2-line difference in best-correct vision between eyes (eg, 20/30 & 20/50)
  • Bilateral: best-corrected vision worse than 20/40 at age ≥4

Etiology

  • Strabismus
  • Uncorrected refractive error
  • Vision deprivation (eg, cataracts, ptosis)

Management

  • Treat underlying condition (eg, corrective lenses for refractive error, surgery for cataract)
  • Encourage use of amblyopic eye (when unilateral)
    • Patching eye with better vision
    • Cycloplegic drops to blur normal eye
"]],"cerebral-perfusion":[[59345,"Management of traumatic brain injury","

Management of traumatic brain injury

Goal

Interventions

Maintain CPP
(= MAP − ICP)

  • Maintain MAP: isotonic fluids, vasopressor therapy
  • Reduce ICP: head elevation, sedation, osmotic therapy (eg, hypertonic saline, mannitol), decompressive interventions (eg, CSF removal, craniectomy)

Prevent ICH

  • Antifibrinolytic therapy (ie, tranexamic acid) within first 3 hr
  • Reversal of preexisting anticoagulation

Other
measures

  • Prevent seizures (eg, levetiracetam, phenytoin)
  • Control blood glucose (eg, insulin to target 140-180 mg/dL glucose)
  • Maintain normothermia (eg, antipyretics, surface-cooling devices)

CPP = cerebral perfusion pressure; CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; ICH = intracranial hemorrhage; ICP = intracranial pressure; MAP = mean arterial pressure.

"]],"retinal-disorders--retinitis-pigmentosa":[[59444,"Retinitis pigmentosa","

Retinitis pigmentosa

Etiology

  • Genetic dystrophy
  • Progressive retinal degeneration (photoreceptors, pigmented epithelium)

    • Night blindness
    • Peripheral visual field loss
  • Loss of cones:

Funduscopic changes

  • Retinal vessel attenuation (likely due to altered metabolic demand)
  • Optic disc pallor (optic nerve atrophy and gliosis)
  • Pigment accumulation (characteristic bone-spicule pattern around vessels)
"]],"lens-disorders--lens-dislocation":[[59686,"Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis)","

Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis)

Anterior uveitis

Common causes/
associations

"]],"dyskinesias":[[61344,"Clinical features of tremors","

Clinical features of tremors

Essential

  • Bilateral action tremor of the hands
  • Head tremor without dystonia
  • No other neurologic signs
  • Improves with alcohol

Parkinson disease

  • Resting tremor; ↓ with voluntary movement
  • Pill-rolling
  • Asymmetric; hands & legs

Cerebellar

  • Usually associated with ataxia &/or dysmetria
  • ↑ Steadily as hand approaches target

Orthostatic

  • Legs & trunk
  • Occurs only when standing

Physiologic

  • Low amplitude, not visible under normal conditions
  • ↑ With sympathetic activity (eg, drugs, hyperthyroidism, anxiety, caffeine)
  • Worse with movement
  • Most common cause of action tremor
"], [61519,"Tremor","

Tremor

Clinical features

Essential

  • Action tremor
  • Bilateral hands &/or head
  • Improves with alcohol

Parkinson disease

  • Resting tremor (decreases with movement)
  • Hands & legs
  • "Pill-rolling"
  • Associated parkinsonian features (eg, rigidity, masked faces, short-stepped gait)

Cerebellar

  • Action tremor (increases as hand reaches target)
  • Associated ataxia, dysmetria, or gait disorder

Physiologic

  • Action & rest tremor
  • Low amplitude, high frequency (ie, "fine" tremor)
  • Not visible under normal circumstances
  • Enhanced with sympathetic activation (eg, anxiety, caffeine, hyperthyroidism)

"]],"dementia-continued--frontotemporal-dementia":[[67947,"Comparison of frontotemporal dementia & Alzheimer disease","

Comparison of frontotemporal dementia & Alzheimer disease

Criteria

Frontotemporal dementia

Alzheimer disease

Macroscopic examination

  • Pronounced atrophy of frontal & temporal lobes
  • Mild-to-moderate generalized brain atrophy

Onset

  • Early (50s & 60s)

"]],"opioid-analgesics":[[72244,"Strategies for safe opioid prescribing","

Strategies for safe opioid prescribing

Optimize nonopioid interventions

  • Use acetaminophen/NSAIDs, supportive care (eg, heat/ice) for mild/moderate pain
  • Avoid routine opioid use for chronic pain

Optimize opioid dose and duration

  • Limit therapy to <5 days for acute pain
  • Use lowest dose resulting in adequate pain control
  • Avoid long-acting opioids

Optimize monitoring 

  • Counsel patients on safe use; arrange close follow-up 
  • Educate patients on safe disposal of unused opioids

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Opioid medications in patients with impaired kidney function

Recommended

Avoid

  • Fentanyl

  • Methadone

  • Morphine

  • Codeine

"]],"trigeminal-neuralgia":[[73469,"Trigeminal neuralgia","

Trigeminal neuralgia

Pathophysiology

  • Compression of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) root (eg, vascular loop, multiple sclerosis plaque)

  • Paroxysmal attacks of unilateral, severe, stabbing pain lasting seconds to 2 min

"]],"neurotransmitter-changes-with-disease":[[74002,"Neurotransmitter systems of the CNS","

Neurotransmitter systems of the CNS

Neurotransmitter & receptor pair

Functions in the CNS

Ionotropic: Ligand-gated ion channels
Transmembrane proteins that allow ions to cross the membrane

 Glutamate [E]
→ NMDA receptor: Ca2+ & Na+ influx

Long-term potentiation of learning & memory

GABA [I]
→ GABAA receptor*: Cl− & HCO3− influx

Sedation, anxiolytic & anticonvulsive

Glycine [I]
→ Glycine receptor: Cl− influx

Inhibits spinal interneurons (prevents spasticity)

Metabotropic: G protein–coupled receptors
Act through second messengers (eg, cAMP, PKA)

Dopamine
→ D1-5 receptors

Modulates attention, movement & reward

Serotonin
→ 5-HT receptors**

Modulates mood, nausea & trigeminovascular nociception (migraine)

Norepinephrine
→ α & β adrenoceptors

Promotes vigilance, attention & emotional memory

Histamine
→ H3 receptors

Promotes wakefulness

*GABAB is a G-coupled metabotropic receptor that increases K+ efflux (hyperpolarization).

**Except 5-HT3 receptor, an ionotropic receptor that primarily increases Na+ influx (depolarization).

 

[E] = excitatory (postsynaptic potential); [I] = inhibitory postsynaptic potential; PKA = protein kinase A.

"]],"motor-neuron-signs":[[79763,"Upper vs lower motor neuron signs","

Upper vs lower motor neuron signs

UMN signs*

  • Spasticity (eg, ↑ tone, clasp-knife rigidity)
  • Hyperreflexia; pathologic reflexes (eg, Babinski, Hoffman)
  • Pseudobulbar affect (eg, inappropriate crying or laughing)

LMN signs**

  • Weakness (eg, flaccidity, ↓ tone)
  • Atrophy (amyotrophy)
  • Fasciculations (often with associated cramping)

*From loss of descending inhibition to anterior horn cells.

**From denervation.

LMN = lower motor neuron; UMN = upper motor neuron.

General

  • Aberrant, reward-based, destructive behaviors (eg, pathologic gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping)
  • Primarily seen with dopamine agonists (reduce motor symptoms by D2 receptor stimulation)

Pathophysiology

  • Overstimulation of D3 receptor–mediated reward pathways

Risk factors

  • Dose and duration of treatment
  • Younger age, male sex
  • Comorbid depression and/or anxiety

Management

  • Gradual tapering of dopamine agonist
  • ± Increase levodopa dose to control motor symptoms
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy for persistent symptoms
"]],"retinal-disorders--diabetic-retinopathy":[[101346,"Common ocular complications of diabetes mellitus","

Common ocular complications of diabetes mellitus

Refractive
changes

  • Hyperglycemia, blurred vision
  • Acute myopia & ↓ acuity; no other examination findings

Cataract

  • Blurred vision, ↓ acuity, ↑ glare
  • Lens opacity, ↓ red reflex, ↓ fundus detail

Glaucoma

  • Open-angle: painless peripheral vision loss; ↑ IOP
  • Angle-closure: conjunctival redness, corneal edema, middilated pupil, ↑ IOP

Diabetic
retinopathy &
complications

  • Nonproliferative: cotton-wool spot, retinal hemorrhage, microaneurysm
  • Proliferative: neovascularization arising from the disc or retinal vessels
  • Macular edema: thickening/edema of macular retina
  • Vitreous hemorrhage: vitreous blood obscuring fundus
  • Tractional retinal detachment: detachment with fibrovascular bands & no tears

IOP = intraocular pressure.

"], [129068,"Proliferative diabetic retinopathy","

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy

Clinical presentation

  • Decreased or fluctuating vision; sudden vision loss
  • Floaters (vitreous hemorrhage) or scotomas (blind spots)

Funduscopic findings

  • Neovascularization
  • Vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage
  • Fibrous tissue formation
  • Retinal ischemia

Management

  • Glucose optimization
  • Pars plana vitrectomy for nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment
  • Panretinal photocoagulation or anti-VEGF (ie, ranibizumab) injections to treat neovascularization

VEGF = vascular endothelial growth factor.

"]],"retinal-disorders--age-related-macular-degeneration":[[101551,"Age-related macular degeneration","

Age-related macular degeneration

Risk factors

  • Advancing age (exponentially after age 60)
  • Smoking

Clinical features

  • Gradual central vision loss
  • Impaired dark adaptation
  • May have acute-on-chronic vision loss*

Examination findings

Dry AMD

  • Drusen clustered around the macula
  • Retinal atrophy

Progression to wet AMD

  • Neovascularization
  • Subretinal fluid &/or hemorrhage

Treatment

  • Smoking cessation
  • Antioxidant supplement (vitamins C & E, zinc, copper, lutein)
  • Anti-VEGF intravitreal injections
  • ± Laser photocoagulation of neovascularization

*Due to subretinal fluid accumulation &/or hemorrhage.

AMD = age-related macular degeneration; VEGF = vascular endothelial growth factor.

"]],"anticonvulsants--lamotrigine":[[103382,"Lamotrigine","

Lamotrigine

Mechanism of action

  • Blocks sodium channels & ↓ glutamate

Indications

  • Epilepsy
  • Bipolar disorder

Adverse effects

  • Serious skin rashes, including SJS & TEN
  • DRESS
  • CNS depression (eg, fatigue, ataxia, dizziness)
  • Mood changes (eg, depression, suicidal ideation)

Safety considerations

  • Titrate slowly to reduce risk of rash
  • Drug interactions with glucuronidation (use color-coded starter kits)

CNS = central nervous system; DRESS = drug reaction with eosinophilia & systemic symptoms; SJS = Stevens-Johnson syndrome; TEN = toxic epidermal necrolysis.

"]],"neurodegenerative-disease-therapy--alzheimer-disease":[[104238,"Drugs used for Alzheimer's disease","

Drugs used for Alzheimer's disease

Drug class

Adverse effects

Key points

Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors
(eg, donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine)

  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Diarrhea
  • Titrate slowly (eg, every 6 weeks)
  • Take donepezil at bedtime
  • Bradycardia
  • Donepezil: QT prolongation
  • Use caution with drugs that decrease heart rate (eg, beta-blockers)
  • Insomnia
  • Change donepezil to morning administration

NMDA inhibitor
(eg, memantine)

  • Dizziness, confusion, headache
  • ER capsules can be opened & sprinkled on applesauce
  • Namzaric (donepezil/memantine): only for patients stabilized on donepezil 10 mg daily*

Amyloid beta monoclonal antibodies
(eg, aducanumab, lecanemab)

  • Infusion-related reactions
  • Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA)
  • IV only
  • Role in treatment not yet well defined

*All strengths of Namzaric contain donepezil 10 mg; donepezil requires titration from a starting dose of 5 mg to avoid gastrointestinal adverse effects.

ER = extended release; NMDA = N-methyl-D-aspartate.

"]],"anticonvulsants--valproate":[[104341,"Valproate","

Valproate

Mechanism
 of action

  • Blocks sodium channels & ↑ GABA

Indications

  • Focal or generalized seizures (broad spectrum)
  • Bipolar disorder
  • Migraine prophylaxis

Boxed warnings

  • Hepatic failure
  • Fetal harm (neural tube defects & ↓ cognitive scores)
  • Pancreatitis

Adverse
effects

  • Alopecia
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Weight changes (gain more likely)
  • Nausea & vomiting
  • Hyperammonemia
  • CNS effects (eg, somnolence, dizziness)

Monitoring

  • Therapeutic range: 50–100 mcg/mL (total level)
  • LFTs
  • CBC with differential (especially platelets)

CBC = complete blood count; GABA = gamma-aminobutyric acid; LFTs = liver function tests.

"]],"spinal-cord-lesions--spinal-muscular-atrophy":[[105088,"Spinal muscular atrophy","

Spinal muscular atrophy

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal recessive deletion in SMN1 gene → deficiency of SMN protein
  • Degeneration of motor neurons (anterior horn cells & lower brainstem nuclei) → progressive muscle atrophy

Variants

  • Onset, severity, & presenting symptoms vary
    • Severe (infantile, most common): diffuse, flaccid paralysis
    • Moderate (toddler): delay/loss of motor skills
    • Mild (adolescent): symmetric proximal weakness (legs >arms)

Examination findings

  • Lower motor neuron signs (eg, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, weakness)
  • Tongue fasciculations

Diagnosis

  • SMN1 gene analysis
SMN = survival motor neuron.
"]],"common-causes-of-hearing-loss--presbycusis":[[116296,"Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss)","

Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss)

Etiology

  • Increasing incidence with age >60
  • Cochlear hair cell loss
  • Degeneration of spiral ganglion cells in the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)

Clinical features

  • Insidious, progressive, symmetric SNHL impacting high frequencies first
  • Difficulty hearing with background noise
  • Impaired speech discrimination
  • Tinnitus (nonpulsatile)
  • Can lead to social isolation &/or depression

Work-up

  • Bedside screening hearing tests (eg, finger rub, whisper, tuning fork)
  • Formal audiometry

Treatment

  • Hearing aids (amplification)
  • Education of patient & family

SNHL = sensorineural hearing loss.

"]],"anticonvulsants--gabapentinoids":[[117240,"Gabapentin and pregabalin","

Gabapentin and pregabalin

Common
uses

  • Focal onset seizures (adjunctive)
  • Neuropathic pain (eg, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia)
  • Postherpetic neuralgia
  • Restless legs syndrome
  • Anxiety
  • Alcohol withdrawal

Adverse
effects

  • CNS depression (eg, somnolence, ataxia)
  • Dizziness
  • Peripheral edema
  • Weight gain

Additional
notes

  • Structurally similar to GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter
  • Gabapentin enacarbil (Horizant) is an extended-release prodrug of gabapentin (Neurontin)
  • Lyrica (pregabalin) is more potent than gabapentin
  • Dosage adjustment required for CrCl < 60 mL/min

CNS = central nervous system; GABA = gamma-aminobutyric acid.

"]],"retinal-disorders--retinoblastoma":[[118628,"Retinoblastoma","

Retinoblastoma

Etiology

  • Mutation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene

Clinical presentation

  • Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex)
  • Most present prior to age 5 years

Diagnosis

  • Off-white mass seen on dilated funduscopic examination
  • May present with strabismus, nystagmus, or red, inflamed eye
  • Diagnosis confirmed using ultrasonography, CT scan, or MRI

Management

  • Mass removal via radiation, chemotherapy, or enucleation
  • Long-term follow-up due to recurrence and risk for other cancers (eg, osteosarcoma)
"]],"common-cranial-nerve-lesions":[[119799,"Cranial nerve lesions","

Cranial nerve lesions

I (Olfactory)

  • Anosmia (loss of smell)

II (Optic)

  • Monocular blindness
  • Loss of pupillary reflex (afferent limb)

III (Oculomotor)

  • Diplopia, down & out eye deviation, ptosis
  • Mydriasis, loss of pupillary reflex (efferent limb)

IV (Trochlear)

  • Eye extorsion with head tilt to compensate
  • Vertical diplopia

V (Trigeminal)

  • Facial hemianesthesia, loss of corneal reflex (afferent limb)
  • Weakness of mastication muscles
  • Jaw deviation toward the side of lesion (unopposed action of opposite pterygoid)

VI (Abducens)

  • Horizontal diplopia with impaired eye abduction

VII (Facial)

  • Facial paralysis (nasolabial flattening, impaired eyelid closure)
  • Loss of taste in anterior two-thirds of tongue
  • Hyperacusis (stapedius paralysis),
  • Loss of corneal reflex (efferent limb)

VIII (Vestibulocochlear)

  • Sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo

IX (Glossopharyngeal)

  • Loss of sensation & taste in posterior one-third of tongue
  • Loss of gag reflex (afferent limb)

X (Vagus)

  • Dysphagia, hoarseness, impaired cough reflex
  • Loss of gag reflex (efferent limb)

XI (Accessory)

  • Impaired shoulder shrug (trapezius paralysis)
  • Impaired head turning (sternocleidomastoid paralysis)

XII (Hypoglossal)

  • Tongue weakness with deviation toward the side of lesion

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["psych"] = {"child-abuse":[[31138,"Features of possible child abuse","

Features of possible child abuse

Risk
factors

Caregiver background

  • Young or single parents
  • Lower education levels
  • Substance use disorder
  • Psychiatric conditions (depression, impulse control disorders)
  • History of childhood abuse

Home environment

  • Unstable family situation (eg, divorce, conflict)
  • Financial difficulties, job loss
  • Lack of social support
  • Domestic violence

Children

  • Physical, intellectual, or emotional disabilities
  • Unplanned pregnancy/unwanted child

Clinical
presentation

  • Unexplained or implausible injuries
  • Injuries in different stages of healing
  • Malnutrition
  • Sudden behavioral or scholastic changes

Management

  • Document objective findings from evaluation
  • Report suspected abuse to child protective services
"], [81247,"Medical child abuse","

Medical child abuse

When to
suspect

  • Persistent or recurrent unexplainable illness
    • Nonphysiologic symptom clusters
    • Inconclusive diagnostic testing
    • Ineffective medical therapies
  • Reported signs/symptoms incongruous with clinical findings or seen only in presence of specific caregiver
  • Siblings who have died or have unexplained illness
  • Seeking care from multiple facilities or specialists
  • Reluctance to accept less severe diagnosis

Management

  • Report to child protective services
  • Case-specific medical evaluation for child abuse (eg, urine toxicology screen)

Communication
strategies

  • Focus on best interest/safety of child
  • Avoid assigning blame
  • Inform family of legal mandate to report
  • Use direct, honest & specific language (eg, "I suspect abuse")
"]],"obsessive-compulsive-disorders":[[32007,"Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder)","

Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder)

Features

  • Recurrent hair pulling resulting in hair loss
  • Repeated attempts to decrease/stop hair pulling
  • Not due to a medical/dermatological condition (eg, alopecia areata)
  • Not due to another mental disorder (eg, body dysmorphic disorder)

Examination
findings

  • Irregular patches of hair loss
  • Hair shafts of variable lengths
  • Noninflammatory, nonscarring

Treatment

  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy (habit reversal therapy)
"], [34698,"Body dysmorphic disorder","

Body dysmorphic disorder

Clinical features

  • Preoccupation with ≥1 perceived physical defects
  • Defects not observable or appear slight to others
  • Repetitive behavior or mental acts performed in response to the preoccupation
  • Significant distress or impairment
  • Variable insight (good, poor, absent/delusional beliefs)

Management

  • Antidepressants (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors)
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy
"], [73124,"Obsessive-compulsive disorder","

Obsessive-compulsive disorder

Clinical features

  • Obsessions
    • Recurrent, intrusive, anxiety-provoking thoughts, urges, or images (eg, contamination, symmetry, harm)
  • Compulsions
    • Responds to obsessions with repeated behaviors or mental acts (eg, cleaning, checking, counting)
    • Behaviors not connected realistically with preventing feared events (eg, counting to prevent harm to a loved one)
  • Time-consuming (>1 hr/day) or causing significant distress or impairment

Management

  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy (exposure & response prevention)

Comorbidities

  • Major depressive disorder/increased suicide risk
  • Anxiety disorders
  • Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
  • Tic disorders (eg, Tourette's)

Course & prognosis

  • Adolescent onset with chronic course
  • High rates of comorbid psychiatric disorders
"]],"psychoactive-drug-intoxication-and-withdrawal--opioids":[[32024,"Clinical features of acute opioid intoxication","

Clinical features of acute opioid intoxication

Risk factors

  • Substance use disorder
  • Chronic opioid use
  • Hospitalization (especially postoperative)
  • Hepatic or renal insufficiency

Clinical findings

  • Somnolence, AMS
  • Pinpoint pupils (miosis)
  • Shallow breathing & ↓ respiratory rate
  • Bradycardia, hypothermia, ↓ bowel sounds
  • Respiratory acidosis on ABG analysis

Management

  • Naloxone (may need repeated administration)
  • Airway management & ventilation
  • Exclude other AMS causes (eg, hypoglycemia)

ABG = arterial blood gas; AMS = altered mental status.

"], [33206,"Opioid withdrawal","

Opioid withdrawal

Time course

  • 4 to 48 hr after opioid cessation
  • Immediately after opioid antagonist (life-threatening)

Clinical
presentation

  • Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting, cramping, diarrhea, ↑ bowel sounds
  • Cardiac:↑ pulse, ↑ blood pressure, diaphoresis
  • Psychologic: insomnia, yawning, dysphoric mood
  • Other: myalgia, arthralgia, mydriasis, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection

Diagnosis

  • History & examination alone (clinical diagnosis)

Management

  • Opioid agonist: methadone or buprenorphine
  • Nonopioid: clonidine or adjunctive medications (antiemetics, antidiarrheals, benzodiazepines)
"]],"psychoactive-drug-intoxication-and-withdrawal--alcohol":[[32062,"Alcohol withdrawal syndrome","

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome

Manifestations

Symptoms/signs

Onset since last drink (hr)

Mild withdrawal

Anxiety, insomnia, tremors, diaphoresis, palpitations, gastrointestinal upset, intact orientation

6-24

Seizures

Single or multiple generalized tonic-clonic

12-48

Alcoholic hallucinosis

Visual, auditory, or tactile; intact orientation; stable vital signs

12-48

Delirium tremens

Confusion, agitation, fever, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hallucinations

48-96

"], [106473,"Clinical features of alcohol intoxication vs withdrawal","

Clinical features of alcohol intoxication vs withdrawal

Intoxication

Withdrawal

Sensorium

  • Relaxation
  • Somnolence
  • Coma
  • Restlessness
  • Agitation
  • Delirium

Psychiatric

  • Euphoria
  • Disinhibition
  • Emotional lability
  • Anxiety
  • Paranoia
  • Hallucinations

Neurologic

  • Slurred speech
  • Incoordination
  • Unsteady gait
  • Tremors
  • Hyperreflexia
  • Seizures

Autonomic

  • Tachycardia
  • Hypotension
  • Hypothermia
  • Bradypnea
  • Tachycardia
  • Hypertension
  • Hyperthermia
  • Diaphoresis
"]],"risk-factors-for-suicide-death":[[32383,"Suicide risk assessment","

Suicide risk assessment

Acute modifiable risk factors

  • Suicidal thoughts, plan & intent
  • Presence/severity of psychiatric illness
  • Impulsivity
  • Hopelessness
  • Psychosis/agitation
  • Intoxication (disinhibition)/active substance use
  • Recent psychosocial stressors
  • Medical illness/pain
  • Lack of social support/living alone
  • Access to means (eg, weapons, medications)

Static risk factors

  • Age (young adult & >70)
  • Sex
    • Attempts: female > male
    • Completion: male > female
  • Past suicide attempts
  • Family history of suicide/psychiatric illness
"], [32384,"Suicide assessment: ideation, intent & plan","

Suicide assessment: ideation, intent & plan

Evaluate ideation

  • Wish to die, not wake up (passive)
  • Thoughts of killing self (active)
  • Frequency, duration, intensity, controllability

Evaluate intent 

  • Strength of intent to attempt suicide; ability to control impulsivity
  • Determine how close patient has come to acting on a plan (rehearsal, aborted attempts)

Evaluate plan

  • Specific details: method, time, place, access to means (eg, weapons, pills), preparations
    (eg, gathering pills, changing will)
  • Lethality of method
  • Likelihood of rescue
"], [33523,"Management of suicidality","

Management of suicidality

Management

Imminent risk of suicide (voiced intent, high number of unmanaged risk factors, collateral concerns raised)

  • Ensure safety: hospitalize immediately (involuntary if necessary) & start 1:1 for constant observation
  • Remove personal belongings & objects in room that may present self-harm risk
  • Security may be required to hold against will
 

Nonimminent risk of suicide (no intent, strong social supports available, outpatient follow-up plan is reasonable)

  • Create safety plan (eg, coping skills, social supports, crisis numbers)
  • Ensure close follow-up (eg, psychiatry, therapy, intensive outpatient program)
  • Plan to address modifiable risk factors (eg, depression, psychosis, substance use, pain)
  • Ensure family or friends available to support patient
  • Remove access to potential means (eg, secure firearms & medications)
"], [75356,"Suicide risk assessment: evaluate ideation, method, plan, intent","

Suicide risk assessment: evaluate ideation, method, plan, intent

Suicidal
ideation

  • Wish to die, not wake up (passive)
  • Thoughts of killing self (active)

Method/
accessibility

  • Thoughts of specific method (eg, weapons, pills)
  • Accessibility of method (eg, medication, gun)
  • Lethality of method (eg, gunshot to head, jumping from high floor, potentially lethal overdose of pills)

Preparations/
planning

  • Steps taken toward making a suicide attempt: collecting pills, obtaining a gun, giving valuables away, writing a will or suicide note
  • Specific planning of time, place, details

Intent

  • Strength of intention to act on suicidal thoughts
  • Time frame (next 48 hr, weeks to months)
"]],"electroconvulsive-therapy":[[32385,"Electroconvulsive therapy","

Electroconvulsive therapy

Indications

Conditions treated

  • Unipolar & bipolar depression
  • Catatonia
  • Bipolar mania

Specific indications

  • Treatment resistance
  • Psychotic features present
  • Emergency conditions
    • Refusal to eat or drink
    • Imminent risk for suicide
  • Pharmacotherapy contraindicated due to comorbid medical illness or poor tolerability
  • Pregnancy when pharmacotherapy is undesirable or ineffective
  • History of ECT response

Safety

  • No absolute contraindications
  • Increased risk  
    • Severe cardiovascular disease, recent myocardial infarction
    • Space-occupying brain lesion
    • Recent stroke, unstable aneurysm

ECT = electroconvulsive therapy.

"], [34512,"Electroconvulsive therapy for depression","

Electroconvulsive therapy for depression

 

Indications

  • Treatment resistance
  • Psychotic features
  • Emergency conditions
    • Pregnancy
    • Refusal to eat or drink
    • Imminent risk for suicide
 

Safety

  • No absolute contraindications
  • Increased risk  
    • Severe cardiovascular disease,
      recent myocardial infarction
    • Space-occupying brain lesion
    • Recent stroke, unstable aneurysm
"]],"normal-infant-and-child-development--preschool":[[32756,"Developmental milestones of preschoolers","

Age

(years)

  • Rides tricycle

"]],"personality-disorders--paranoid":[[33276,"Paranoid personality disorder","

Paranoid personality disorder

Clinical features

  • Pervasive pattern of distrust & suspiciousness beginning in early adulthood & occurring in a variety of settings (no clear delusions)
    • Believes being exploited & deceived by others
    • Interprets benign comments & events as threats; reacts angrily
    • Bears grudges
    • Questions loyalty of partner without justification

Differential diagnosis

  • Delusional disorder (delusions only)
  • Schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations, disorganization, negative symptoms)
  • Schizotypal personality disorder (eccentric behavior & thinking, unusual perceptual experiences)
"]],"major-depressive-disorder":[[33354,"Major depressive episode & grief reaction","

Major depressive episode & grief reaction

Major depressive episode

Grief reaction

  • ≥2 weeks; ≥5 of 9 symptoms: low mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, appetite change, low energy, psychomotor changes, guilt/worthlessness, concentration difficulty, suicidal ideation
  • May occur in response to a variety of stressors, including loss of a loved one
  • Marked social & occupational dysfunction
  • Suicidality related to hopelessness & worthlessness
  • Normal reaction to loss (bereavement)
  • Sadness more specific to thoughts of the deceased 
  • "Waves" of grief at reminders
  • Self-esteem usually preserved
  • Functional decline less severe
  • Thoughts of dying involve wish to join the deceased; active suicidality uncommon
  • Intensity decreases over time
"], [33834,"Differential diagnosis of depressed mood","

Differential diagnosis of depressed mood

Major depressive disorder

  • ≥2 weeks
  • ≥5 of 9 symptoms: depressed mood & SIGECAPS
  • Significant functional impairment
  • No lifetime history of mania

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)

  • Chronic depressed mood ≥2 years
  • ≥2 of the following: appetite disturbance, sleep disturbance, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, hopelessness

Adjustment disorder with depressed mood

  • Onset within 3 months of identifiable stressor
  • Marked distress &/or functional impairment
  • Does not meet criteria for another DSM-5-TR disorder

Normal stress response

  • Not excessive or out of proportion to severity of stressor
  • No significant functional impairment

SIGECAPS = Sleep disturbance, loss of Interest, excessive Guilt, low Energy, impaired Concentration, Appetite disturbance, Psychomotor agitation/retardation, and Suicidal ideation. 

"], [42287,"Major depressive disorder","

Major depressive disorder

Diagnosis

  • ≥5 of the following symptoms lasting ≥2 weeks (at least 1 symptom must be either depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure):
    • Depressed mood
    • Loss of interest or pleasure
    • Change in appetite or weight
    • Insomnia or hypersomnia
    • Psychomotor retardation or agitation
    • Low energy
    • Poor concentration or indecisiveness
    • Thoughts of worthlessness or inappropriate guilt
    • Recurrent thoughts of death or suicide
  • No history of mania or hypomania
  • Not due to substances or another medical condition
"]],"psychoactive-drug-intoxication-and-withdrawal-continued":[[33448,"Acute drug intoxication","

"]],"psychiatric-emergencies--serotonin-syndrome":[[33501,"Serotonin toxicity","

Serotonin toxicity

Causes

  • Serotonergic medications, especially in combination (eg, SSRI/SNRI, TCA, tramadol)
  • Drug interactions: serotonergic medication & MAOI or linezolid
  • Intentional overdose of serotonergic medications
  • Serotonergic substances (eg, MDMA, dextromethorphan, amphetamines)

Clinical
features

  • Mental status changes (eg, anxiety, agitation, delirium)
  • Autonomic dysregulation (eg, diaphoresis, hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, vomiting, diarrhea)
  • Neuromuscular hyperactivity (eg, tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia)

Management

  • Discontinuation of all serotonergic medications
  • Supportive care, sedation with benzodiazepines
  • Serotonin antagonist (cyproheptadine) if supportive measures fail
  • Immediate sedation, paralysis & tracheal intubation if temperature >41.1 C (106 F)

"]],"transtheoretical-model-of-change":[[34534,"Stages of change model","

Stages of change model

Stage

Motivational interviewing

Precontemplation

Not ready to change: patient does not acknowledge negative consequences

  • Encourage patient to evaluate consequences of current behavior
  • Explain & personalize the risk
  • Recommending action is premature

Contemplation

Thinking of changing: patient acknowledges consequences but is ambivalent

  • Encourage evaluation of pros & cons of behavior change
  • Promote new, positive behaviors

Preparation

Ready to change: patient decides to change

  • Encourage small initial steps
  • Reinforce positive outcome expectations 

Action

Making change: patient makes specific, overt changes

  • Help identify appropriate change strategies & enlist social support
  • Promote self-efficacy for dealing with obstacles

Maintenance

Changes integrated into patient’s life; focus on relapse prevention

  • Follow-up support; reinforce intrinsic rewards
  • Develop relapse prevention strategies
IdentificationBehavior is automatic: changes incorporated into sense of self
  • Praise changes

"]],"psychiatric-emergencies--lithium-toxicity":[[35356,"Lithium toxicity","

Lithium toxicity

Etiology

  • Overdose
  • Volume depletion
  • Reduced glomerular filtration
  • Drug interactions
    • Thiazide diuretics
    • NSAIDs (not aspirin)
    • ACE inhibitors

Features

Acute

  • GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
  • Neurologic findings occur much later

Chronic

  • Neurologic: ataxia, confusion, agitation, neuromuscular excitability (tremor)

Management

  • Bowel irrigation (asymptomatic acute overdose)
  • Intravenous hydration
  • Hemodialysis
    • Severe toxicity (seizures, encephalopathy)
    • >5 mEq/L
    • >4 mEq/L in patients with impaired kidney function
  • Lithium level every 4-6 hr

GI = gastrointestinal; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

"]],"psychiatric-emergencies--neuroleptic-malignant-syndrome":[[35982,"Neuroleptic malignant syndrome","

contraindications

Clinical features

Mitigation

Nicotine withdrawal syndrome

  • Increased appetite
  • Dysphoria/irritability
  • Insomnia & restlessness
  • Behavioral therapy, nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion

Weight gain

"], [79822,"Smoking cessation interventions by stage of change","

Smoking cessation interventions by stage of change

Not ready to quit

  • Conduct motivational interviewing (4R): relevance, risks, rewards, roadblocks
  • Repeat at every visit
  • Prescribe varenicline* to facilitate reduce-to-quit strategy

Ready to quit

  • Set a firm quit date & discard smoking paraphernalia
  • Provide behavioral counseling & engage support systems
  • Prescribe pharmacotherapy (eg, varenicline, bupropion, NRT)

Struggling to quit

  • Reinforce partial achievements
  • Identify triggers & link them to other (distracting) activities
  • Use biofeedback loops (eg, exhaled CO monitoring, gamification using mobile app)

Recently quit

  • Congratulate & offer continued support
  • Continue pharmacotherapy for 12 weeks
  • Encourage active reflection (anticipated problems, "how has your life changed?")

*2-fold higher rate of durable abstinence.

CO = carbon monoxide; NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.

"]],"eating-disorders--anorexia-nervosa":[[37606,"Anorexia nervosa","

Vascular

Functional

  • Reduced cardiac output & blood pressure
  • Diminished exertional & orthostatic response

"]],"schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders--schizoaffective-disorder":[[37651,"Schizoaffective disorder","

Schizoaffective disorder

"]],"gender-dysphoria":[[37672,"Gender dysphoria","

  • Desires to be another gender
  • Dislikes own anatomy, desires sexual traits of another gender
  • Believes feelings/reactions are of another gender

"]],"personality-disorders":[[38255,"DSM-5 personality disorders","

Odd/eccentric
