"]],"major-depressive-disorder--persistent-depressive-disorder":[[38313,"Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)","

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)

Clinical features

  • Chronic depressed mood ≥2 years (1 year in children/adolescents)
  • No symptom-free period for >2 months
  • Presence of ≥2 of the following:
    • Poor appetite or overeating
    • Insomnia or hypersomnia
    • Low energy or fatigue
    • Low self-esteem
    • Poor concentration or difficulty making decisions
    • Feelings of hopelessness

Specifiers

  • With pure dysthymic syndrome: criteria for major depressive episode never met
  • With intermittent major depressive episodes

"]],"somatic-symptom-and-related-disorders--conversion-disorder":[[38397,"Functional neurologic symptom disorder (conversion disorder)","

Schizophrenia symptoms

Positive

(pathologic excesses)

Good

Poor

  • Predominantly positive symptoms
  • No family history
  • Short duration of active symptoms
  • Onset in childhood or adolescence

"]],"bipolar-disorder":[[38666,"Bipolar & related disorders","

Bipolar & related disorders

Manic episode

  • Symptoms more severe
  • 1 week unless hospitalized
  • Marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or hospitalization necessary
  • May have psychotic features (makes episode manic by definition)

Hypomanic episode

  • Symptoms less severe

  • Symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment or necessitate hospitalization
  • No psychotic features

Bipolar I

  • Manic episode(s)
  • Depressive episodes common but not required for diagnosis

Bipolar II

  • Hypomanic episode(s)
  • ≥1 major depressive episodes

Cyclothymic disorder

  • ≥2 years of fluctuating, mild hypomanic & depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for hypomanic or major depressive episodes

  • Atypical antipsychotics (eg, risperidone, olanzapine)

Acute depression

  • Lamotrigine

"]],"malingering-vs-factitious-disorder-vs-somatic-symptom-disorders":[[38873,"Key features of somatic symptom disorder & related conditions","

Key features of somatic symptom disorder & related conditions

Somatic symptom disorder

≥1 unexplained symptoms; excessive thoughts, anxiety & behaviors in response to symptoms

Minimal to no symptoms; preoccupation with idea of having a serious illness

Neurologic symptom(s) incompatible with anatomy or pathophysiology

"], [78859,"Factitious disorder—key features & differential diagnosis","

Factitious disorder—key features & differential diagnosis

Factitious disorder

  • Intentional falsification of symptoms/inducing injury
  • External rewards absent; goal is to assume the patient role

Malingering

  • Intentional falsification with obvious external rewards (financial benefits, housing, medications)

Personality disorders

  • Enduring patterns of maladaptive interpersonal behavior that may include deliberate self-harm (borderline) & desire to be taken care of (dependent) but do not involve intentional deception

Somatic symptom disorders

  • Excessive illness anxiety/preoccupation with somatic symptoms & treatment seeking; no intention to deceive
"], [106358,"Psychosomatic disorders","

Psychosomatic disorders

Malingering

  • Intentional falsification or exaggeration of illness
  • Goal: secondary gain (eg, narcotics, shelter)

Factitious disorder

  • Intentional fabrication of symptoms or self-imposed injury or illness
  • Goal: assume sick role (no tangible secondary gain)

Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder)

  • Unintentional neurologic symptom(s) incompatible with anatomy or pathophysiology
  • Goal: no specific goal (often associated with comorbid psychiatric illness)
"]],"schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders":[[38889,"Differential diagnosis of DSM-5 psychotic disorders","

Differential diagnosis of DSM-5 psychotic disorders

Brief psychotic disorder

≥1 days & <1 month, sudden onset, full return to function

Schizophreniform disorder

≥1 months & <6 months, same symptoms as schizophrenia, functional decline not required

Schizophrenia

≥6 months (includes ≥1 months of active symptoms, can include prodromal & residual periods), requires functional decline

Schizoaffective disorder

Mood episode with concurrent active-phase symptoms of schizophrenia + ≥2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of prominent mood symptoms

Delusional disorder

≥1 delusions & ≥1 months, no other psychotic symptoms, normal functioning apart from direct impact of delusions

"], [67457,"Brief psychotic disorder","

Brief psychotic disorder

Key features

  • Acute onset, typically associated with severe stressor
  • Psychotic symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior

"]],"dissociative-disorders":[[39448,"Dissociative disorders","

Dissociative disorders

Depersonalization/ derealization disorder

  • Persistent or recurrent experiences of 1 or both:
    • Depersonalization (feelings of detachment from, or being an outside observer of, oneself)
    • Derealization (experiencing surroundings as unreal)
  • Intact reality testing

Dissociative amnesia

  • Inability to recall important personal information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature
  • Not explained by another disorder (eg, substance use, posttraumatic stress)

Dissociative identity disorder

  • Marked discontinuity in identity & loss of personal agency with fragmentation into ≥2 distinct personality states

"]],"ego-defenses":[[40956,"Key defense mechanisms","

Key defense mechanisms

Immature

  • Acting out: expressing unacceptable feelings through actions
  • Denial: behaving as if an aspect of reality does not exist
  • Displacement: transferring feelings to less threatening object/person
  • Intellectualization: focusing on nonemotional aspects to avoid distressing feelings
  • Passive aggression: avoiding conflict by expressing hostility covertly
  • Projection: attributing one's own feelings to others
  • Rationalization: justifying behavior to avoid difficult truths
  • Reaction formation: transforming unacceptable feelings/impulses into the opposite
  • Regression: reverting to earlier developmental stage
  • Splitting: experiencing a person/situation as either all positive or all negative

Mature

  • Altruism: deriving pleasure from helping others, often at a personal cost
  • Humor: using humor to deflect anxiety or uncomfortable feelings
  • Sublimation: channeling impulses into socially acceptable behaviors
  • Suppression: putting unwanted feelings aside to cope with reality
"]],"childhood-and-early-onset-disorders--oppositional-defiant-disorder":[[41614,"Oppositional defiant disorder","

Oppositional defiant disorder

Diagnosis

Pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness for ≥6 months

  • Argues with adults, defies authority figures, refuses to follow rules
  • Deliberately annoys others
  • Blames others for own mistakes or misbehavior
  • Easily annoyed, angry, resentful, or vindictive
  • Not due to another mental disorder

Treatment

  • Parent management training
  • Psychotherapy (anger management, social skills training)
  • No pharmacotherapy for ODD but assess for comorbid ADHD & treat if present

ADHD = attention deficit hyperactivity disorder; ODD = oppositional defiant disorder.

"]],"childhood-and-early-onset-disorders--conduct-disorder":[[42569,"Conduct disorder","

Conduct disorder

Clinical features

  • Pattern of violating major societal norms or rights of others over the previous 12 months
  • Aggression & cruelty toward people & animals
  • Destruction of property, setting fires
  • Serious violation of rules (truancy, running away)
  • Deceitfulness &/or theft (lying, stealing)
"]],"eating-disorders--bulimia-nervosa":[[44158,"Bulimia nervosa","

Bulimia nervosa

Clinical features

  • Recurrent episodes of binge eating & inappropriate compensatory behavior (eg, vomiting, laxatives, excessive exercise)
  • Excessive preoccupation with body weight & shape
  • Body weight within or above normal range
  • Symptoms: abdominal pain, bloating, constipation, lethargy, irregular menses

Physical examination

  • Hypotension, tachycardia
  • Dental enamel erosion, caries
  • Dorsal hand calluses
  • Parotid gland swelling

Laboratory findings

  • Hypokalemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
"]],"tricyclic-antidepressants":[[44480,"Tricyclic antidepressant pharmacology","

Tricyclic antidepressant pharmacology

Inhibitory effects

Consequences

Central & peripheral muscarinic acetylcholine receptors

Tachycardia, delirium, dilated pupils, flushing, decreased sweating, hyperthermia, ileus, urinary retention

Peripheral α1-adrenergic receptors

Peripheral vasodilation (orthostatic hypotension)

Cardiac fast sodium channels

Conduction defects, arrhythmias

Presynaptic (norepinephrine & serotonin) neurotransmitter reuptake

Antidepressant & anxiolytic effects, seizures, tremors

Histamine (H1) receptors

Sedation, increased appetite

"]],"medically-supervised-opioid-withdrawal-and-relapse-prevention":[[46146,"Mechanism of action","

                                                Pharmacotherapy for opioid use disorder

Mechanism of action

Characteristics

  • μ opioid receptor partial agonist
  • Lower risk for respiratory suppression/lethal overdose
  • Lower risk for misuse
  • Daily clinic dosing not required

Methadone

  • μ opioid receptor full agonist

  • Greater risk for misuse
  • Adverse effects: risk for hyperalgesia, hypogonadism, QTc prolongation
  • Daily clinic dosing required
"], [80760,"Treatment of opioid use disorder","

Treatment of opioid use disorder

Mechanism

Advantages & disadvantages

Buprenorphine*

Partial μ opioid agonist

  • Lower risk for misuse & lethal overdose
  • Does not require complete withdrawal prior to initiation
  • Slightly less effective at keeping patients in treatment

Methadone

Full μ opioid agonist

  • More effective at patient retention
  • Does not require complete withdrawal prior to initiation
  • Significantly higher risk for misuse & lethal overdose

Naltrexone

Pure opioid antagonist

  • Does not cause physiologic dependence
  • Requires complete opioid withdrawal prior to initiation
  • Increased risk for overdose with noncompliance and relapse

Nonmedication therapy

Psychosocial interventions

  • Helpful adjunct to medication-assisted treatment
  • Used alone in motivated patients who want to avoid medications
  • Less effective than medication-assisted treatment

*Sublingual buprenorphine may sometimes be combined with naloxone (opioid antagonist with poor sublingual bioavailability) to prevent abuse by crushing or dissolving buprenorphine.

"]],"amnesias--korsakoff-syndrome":[[46417,"Korsakoff syndrome","

Korsakoff syndrome

Causes

  • Extreme thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency resulting from:
    • Chronic alcohol consumption (most common)
    • Eating disorders &/or chronic malnutrition

Characteristic findings

  • Retrograde & anterograde amnesia
  • Preserved long-term memory
  • Confabulation (memory fabrication without the intention to lie)
  • Lack of insight
"]],"selective-serotonin-reuptake-inhibitors":[[57608,"SSRI-associated sexual dysfunction","

SSRI-associated sexual dysfunction

Features

  • Decreased libido
  • Anorgasmia
  • Delayed ejaculation
  • Common cause of nonadherence

Assessment & management

  • Rule out sexual dysfunction due to depression, medical conditions, primary sexual disorder, stress/relationship issues, substance abuse
  • Switch to non-SSRI antidepressant: bupropion or mirtazapine
  • Adjunctive therapy with sildenafil or bupropion
  • Dose reduction for patients on high-dose SSRI (monitor for loss of efficacy)

SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

"], [106841,"Select adverse effects of SSRIs","

Select adverse effects of SSRIs

SSRIs

Adverse effects

 

Paroxetine

  • Weight gain
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Teratogenicity
  • Withdrawal syndrome
  • Orthostasis
  • Sedation

Fluvoxamine

  • Nausea
  • Sedation

Sertraline

  • Diarrhea
  • Activation/anxiety/nervousness
  • Insomnia

Fluoxetine

  • Activation/anxiety/nervousness
  • Insomnia

Citalopram

  • QTc prolongation

Escitalopram

  • QTc prolongation

SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

"]],"personality-disorders--borderline":[[58680,"Borderline personality disorder","

Borderline personality disorder

Diagnostic criteria

  • Pervasive pattern of unstable relationships, self-image & affects & marked impulsivity, with ≥5 of the following features:
    • Frantic efforts to avoid abandonment
    • Unstable & intense interpersonal relationships
    • Markedly & persistently unstable self-image
    • Impulsivity in ≥2 areas that are potentially self-damaging
    • Recurrent suicidal behaviors or threats of self-mutilation (eg, cutting)
    • Affective instability (marked mood reactivity)
    • Chronic feelings of emptiness
    • Inappropriate & intense anger
    • Transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation

Treatment

  • Primary treatment: psychotherapy (several types effective; best evidence for dialectical behavior therapy)
  • Adjunctive pharmacotherapy to target mood instability & transient psychosis (second-generation antipsychotics, mood stabilizers)
  • Antidepressants if comorbid mood or anxiety disorder
"]],"childhood-and-early-onset-disorders--tourette-syndrome":[[60403,"Tourette syndrome","

Tourette syndrome

Clinical
features

  • Both multiple motor & ≥1 vocal tics (not necessarily concurrent, >1 year) 
    • Motor: facial grimacing, blinking, head/neck jerking, shoulder shrugging, tongue protrusion
    • Vocal: grunting, sniffing/snorting, throat clearing, barking, yelling, coprolalia (obscenities)
  • Onset age <18

Comorbidity

  • Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder

Treatment

  • Education/watchful waiting if mild & nondisabling
  • Behavioral therapy (habit reversal training)
  • Antidopaminergic agents
    • Tetrabenazine (VMAT2 inhibitor)
    • Antipsychotics (receptor blockers)
  • α2 Adrenergic receptor agonists

Prognosis

  • Severity peaks at age 10-12
  • Majority resolve or improve in adulthood; tics persist in one-third

VMAT2 = vesicular monoamine transporter type 2.

"]],"psychoactive-drug-intoxication-and-withdrawal-continued--cannabis-cannabinoids":[[61017,"Adverse effects of cannabis use","

Adverse effects of cannabis use

General

  • ↑ Increased injury & death from motor vehicle collision
  • ↑ Use of other drugs
  • ↓ Educational attainment*

Ophthalmologic

  • Conjunctival vasodilation 

Dental

  • Dry mouth
  • Leukoplakia, gingivitis & candidiasis*

Pulmonary

  • Wheezing & cough

Cardiovascular

  • ↑ Sympathetic activity (eg, tachycardia)

Gastrointestinal

  • Hyperemesis syndrome*

Reproductive

  • ↓ Spermatogenesis*

Neuropsychiatric

  • ↓ Short-term memory, coordination & judgment
  • Anxiety, paranoia & psychosis (high dose)
  • ↓ Hippocampal volume*
  • ↑ Risk of psychiatric disease* (eg, depression, bipolar disease)

*Associated only with chronic or heavy use.

"], [61210,"Cannabis withdrawal","

Cannabis withdrawal

Clinical features

  • Cessation of heavy, prolonged cannabis use (daily, months)
  • ≥3 signs/symptoms (must include at least 1 physical symptom)

Psychologic

  • Irritability, anger
  • Depressed mood
  • Anxiety, restlessness
  • Decreased appetite/weight loss
  • Sleep disturbance

Physical

  • Abdominal pain
  • Headache
  • Shakiness/tremors
  • Fevers, chills
  • Sweating
"], [116588,"Cannabis (marijuana) intoxication","

Cannabis (marijuana) intoxication

Manifestations

  • Increased appetite
  • Euphoria
  • Dysphoria/panic
  • Slow reflexes, impaired time perception
  • Dry mouth (xerostomia)
  • Conjunctival irritation
"]],"factitious-disorders--factitious-disorder-imposed-on-self":[[63693,"Factitious disorder (imposed on self)","

Factitious disorder (imposed on self)

Behavioral
characteristics

  • Intentional falsification of illness:
    • Feigning illness
    • Self-induced illness
    • Exacerbation of preexisting illness
  • Motivation by internal factors rather than external gain (eg, financial compensation)

Clinical
presentation

  • Overt/dramatic symptoms
  • Frequent visits for medical care
  • Patient possibly refusing consent to release records or tampering with test samples
  • More common in health care workers

Diagnostic
confirmation

  • Direct observation or discovery of medical supplies (eg, medications, syringes)
  • Confirmatory testing (eg, sulfonylurea screen, stool laxative screen)
  • Medical record review
"]],"major-depressive-disorder--mdd-with-seasonal-pattern":[[63891,"Seasonal affective disorder","

Seasonal affective disorder

Clinical features

  • Recurrent episodes & remission of major depression, mania, or hypomania during certain times of year
  • Seasonal pattern: fall-winter onset, spring-summer onset
  • Symptoms similar to MDD (eg, depressed mood, anhedonia, loss of energy)
  • Atypical symptoms: increased appetite (especially to carbohydrates), weight gain, hypersomnia
  • Symptoms often improve with sunshine

Treatment

  • Antidepressants (eg, SSRIs, buproprion)
  • Light box therapy
  • Psychotherapy
  • Treatment resistance: ECT

ECT = electroconvulsive therapy; MDD = major depressive disorder; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

"]],"elimination-disorders":[[64508,"Medical conditions causing enuresis","

Medical conditions causing enuresis

Etiology

Symptoms

Findings

Constipation*

  • Infrequent & hard stools
  • Encopresis
  • ± Palpable stool mass

Bladder dysfunction*

  • Daytime incontinence
  • Weak stream, urgency, straining
  • ± Recurrent urinary tract infections

Urinary tract infection

  • Dysuria, urgency, frequency
  • Abdominal pain
  • Positive urine culture

Chronic kidney disease

  • Daytime incontinence
  • Weight loss, fatigue
  • Hypertension
  • Proteinuria, hematuria

Diabetes mellitus

  • Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia
  • Weight loss, fatigue
  • Glucosuria

Diabetes insipidus

  • Polyuria, polydipsia
  • Low urine specific gravity

Obstructive sleep apnea

  • Snoring
  • Hyperactivity, inattention
  • Adenotonsillar hypertrophy

*Often a clinical diagnosis.

"], [65004,"Nocturnal enuresis in children","

Nocturnal enuresis in children

Primary

Secondary

Definition

  • Nighttime incontinence at age ≥5 without prior prolonged period of continence
  • Nighttime incontinence at age ≥5 after prolonged period of continence

Causes

  • Brain maturation delay
  • Genetics (eg, family history)
  • Underlying medical condition (eg, UTI, type 1 diabetes mellitus)
  • Psychologic stressors

Initial evaluation

  • Urinalysis*
  • Urinalysis

Management

  • Reassurance
  • Behavioral modifications (eg, evening fluid restriction)
  • Bedwetting alarm
  • Treatment of underlying condition

*Urinalysis is performed because a developing secondary condition (eg, type 1 diabetes mellitus) may overlap with primary nocturnal enuresis.

UTI = urinary tract infection.

"]],"medically-supervised-opioid-withdrawal-and-relapse-prevention--naltrexone":[[65937,"Naltrexone","

Naltrexone

Mechanism of action

  • Opioid μ receptor antagonist
  • Blocks sedating, analgesic, euphoric effects of opioids

Use & benefits

  • Adjunct therapy for moderate to severe alcohol use disorder
    • Decreases alcohol cravings & frequency of heavy drinking days
    • Can be initiated when a patient is still consuming alcohol
  • Adjunct therapy for opioid use disorder*

Safety & contraindications

  • Should not be prescribed with an opioid (antagonist effect)
  • Can precipitate immediate opioid withdrawal if given to a patient with long-term (>3 weeks) opioid use
  • Avoid in a patient with liver failure or hepatitis

*In the setting of low patient compliance with an oral agent (eg, methadone).

"]],"psychoactive-drug-intoxication-and-withdrawal-continued--nicotine":[[68793,"Nicotine poisoning","

Nicotine poisoning

Epidemiology

  • Children age <6 are particularly susceptible
  • Toxicity dependent on amount & type of exposure*:
    • Ingested (eg, cigarette ends, nicotine gum, concentrated liquid nicotine)
    • Cutaneous (eg, green tobacco sickness from tobacco leaves)
    • Inhaled (eg, e-cigarettes)

Clinical features

  • Biphasic response due to action of nicotine at acetylcholine receptors:
    • Stimulatory phase (eg, hypertension, tachycardia, seizures, myoclonus)
    • Inhibitory phase (eg, hypotension, bradycardia, coma)
  • Muscarinic symptoms (eg, vomiting, diarrhea, bronchorrhea, salivation, wheezing)

Treatment

  • Primarily supportive
  • Decontamination if transdermal exposure
  • Benzodiazepines for seizures
  • Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia & muscarinic symptoms

*Highly concentrated nicotine liquid used in e-cigarettes can be toxic in small amounts.

"]],"trauma-and-stress-related-disorders--post-traumatic-stress-disorder":[[69722,"Posttraumatic stress disorder","

Posttraumatic stress disorder

Risk factors

  • Military combat
  • Sexual trauma
  • Conflict & displacement
  • Physical injury
  • Medical illness (eg, MI, stroke, ICU stay)
  • Childhood abuse

Clinical features

  • Traumatic event exposure
  • Reexperiencing symptoms (eg, nightmares, flashbacks, intrusive memories)
  • Avoidance symptoms (eg, reminders of the trauma, amnesia to details of event)
  • Negative cognitions & mood (eg, emotional detachment, decreased interest in activities, negative worldview)
  • Hyperarousal symptoms (eg, sleep disturbance, hypervigilance, easy startle, irritability)
  • Duration ≥1 month

Treatment

  • Trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy
  • Antidepressants (eg, SNRIs, SSRIs)

Course

  • Onset typically within months of trauma; 25% delayed onset (≥6 months)
  • Commonly chronic (one-third remain symptomatic after 10 years)

ICU = intensive care unit; MI = myocardial infarction; SNRIs = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors; SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

"]],"psychotherapy--motivational-interviewing":[[69765,"Motivational interviewing: components","

Motivational interviewing: components

Engaging

  • Start a nonjudgmental, open-ended conversation
  • Collaborate to set the agenda
  • Elicit patient strengths

Focusing

  • Ask the patient to identify 1 or 2 behavior targets

Evoking

  • Elicit change talk to get the patient's:
    • Commitment
    • Reasons to change

Planning

  • Guide the patient toward:
    • Identifying specific next steps
    • Anticipating obstacles
    • Deciding how to measure success
"]],"trauma-and-stress-related-disorders--adjustment-disorder":[[70440,"Adjustment disorder","

Adjustment disorder

Clinical features

  • Mood & behavioral symptom onset within 3 months of identifiable stressor
  • Marked distress &/or functional impairment
  • Does not meet criteria for another DSM-5 disorder

Differential diagnosis

  • Normal stress response
    • Not excessive, no significant impairment
  • Acute stress disorder
    • Traumatic event, intrusive reexperiencing
  • Major depressive disorder
    • ≥2 weeks, 5/9 symptoms: depressed mood + SIGECAPS

Management

  • Psychotherapy is treatment of choice
  • Adjunctive pharmacotherapy
    • Short-term, reserved for rapid relief of impairing symptoms (eg, sleep aid, anxiolytic)

SIGECAPS = Sleep disturbance, loss of Interest, excessive Guilt, low Energy, impaired Concentration, Appetite disturbance, Psychomotor agitation/retardation, & Suicidal ideation.

"]],"malingering":[[73053,"Malingering","

Malingering

Key feature

  • Falsification or exaggeration of symptoms to obtain external reward (eg, financial gain, avoidance of work or criminal prosecution)

Associated findings suggestive of malingering

  • Discrepancy between subjective distress & objective findings
  • Symptoms present only while observed
  • Inconsistencies in history/reluctance to provide information
  • Nonadherence/refusal of invasive procedures
  • Antisocial personality disorder
  • Analgesic, sedative medication misuse/abuse
"]],"childhood-and-early-onset-disorders--intellectual-disability":[[73974,"Common causes of intellectual disability","

Common causes of intellectual disability

Syndrome

Dysmorphic features

Comorbid conditions

Down syndrome

  • Upslanting palpebral fissures
  • Flat nasal bridge
  • Epicanthal folds
  • Single palmar crease
  • Heart disease (eg, AV canal defect)
  • Short stature, obesity
  • Hearing loss

Fragile X syndrome

  • Long face with prominent chin & forehead
  • Large, protruding ears
  • Macroorchidism
  • Macrocephaly
  • Self-injurious behavior (eg, hand biting)
  • Anxiety, autistic behaviors
  • Tall stature

Fetal alcohol syndrome

  • Smooth philtrum
  • Thin vermillion border
  • Small palpebral fissures
  • Seizures
  • Growth restriction

AV = atrioventricular.

"], [80953,"Secondary causes of behavioral change in patients with intellectual disability","

Secondary causes of behavioral change in patients with intellectual disability

Gastrointestinal disorders

  • Constipation, gastroesophageal reflux, bowel obstruction

Occult infection

  • Cellulitis, cystitis, otitis media, pneumonia

Unrecognized pain

  • Dental caries, menstrual pain, unreported trauma/fracture

Sensory impairment

  • Cerumen impaction, visual problems

Psychiatric disorders

  • Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder

Sleep disorders

  • Obstructive sleep apnea, insomnia
"]],"childhood-and-early-onset-disorders--attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder":[[74965,"Pharmacotherapy for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder","

Pharmacotherapy for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

Category

Medication

Adverse effects

Stimulant

Methylphenidate

Weight loss, decreased appetite, insomnia, abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, tics (rare), addiction potential

Amphetamine salts

Nonstimulant

Clonidine

Sedation, dry mouth, constipation, irritability, anxiety, hypotension, abdominal pain, sleep disturbances (eg, nightmares)

Guanfacine

Atomoxetine

Dry mouth, decreased appetite, insomnia, hyperhidrosis, erectile dysfunction

"], [99540,"Conditions mimicking attention deficit hyperactivity disorder*","

Conditions mimicking attention deficit hyperactivity disorder*

Diagnosis

Historical clues

Initial evaluation

Learning disability

  • Symptoms predominantly in academic setting
  • Neuropsychological testing

Hearing impairment

  • Delayed speech
  • Audiology evaluation

Mental health conditions

(eg, anxiety, depression, ODD)

  • Excessive worrying (anxiety), pervasive sadness (depression), defiance (ODD)
  • Interview & standardized screening questionnaires

Obstructive sleep apnea

  • Snoring, daytime sleepiness
  • Obesity
  • Sleep study

Absence seizure

  • Discrete episodes unresponsive to stimuli
  • Automatisms
  • EEG

*Symptoms of hyperactivity (eg, inability to sit still, frequent interruptions) &/or inattention (eg, distractibility, difficulty following directions). 

EEG = electroencephalogram; ODD = oppositional defiant disorder.

"]],"psychoactive-drug-intoxication-and-withdrawal--amphetamines":[[75626,"Methamphetamine intoxication","

Methamphetamine intoxication

Clinical features

  • Euphoric or dysphoric mood (eg, anxiety, irritability)
  • Agitated behaviors (eg, restlessness, tremor)
  • Bruxism, poor dentition
  • Psychotic symptoms
    • Delusions (eg, paranoia, grandiosity)
    • Hallucinations
    • Formication (eg, "bugs crawling under the skin")
  • Anorexia
  • Decreased need for sleep
  • Sympathomimetic effects (eg, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, diaphoresis)
"]],"panic-disorder":[[75980,"Panic disorder","

Panic disorder

Clinical
features

  • Recurrent & unexpected panic attacks with ≥4 of the following:
    • Chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, choking
    • Trembling, sweating, nausea, chills
    • Dizziness, paresthesia
    • Derealization, depersonalization
    • Fear of losing control or dying
  • Worry about additional attacks, avoidance behavior

Treatment

  • Antidepressants (SSRI/SNRI)
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy

SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

"]],"eating-disorders":[[81684,"Type 1 diabetes mellitus & disordered eating","

Type 1 diabetes mellitus & disordered eating

Etiology & risk factors

  • Sense of lack of control related to food intake & weight
  • Comorbid anxiety & depression
  • Body image dissatisfaction
  • Adolescent girls, overweight/obese

Presentation

  • Insulin restriction (diabulimia)
    • Poorly controlled hyperglycemia (rising hemoglobin A1c)
    • Recurrent DKA
  • Food restriction or purging
    • Episodic hypoglycemia

Screening

  • Diabetes-specific screening questionnaire starting at age 10

DKA = diabetic ketoacidosis.

"], [92082,"SCOFF questionnaire","

SCOFF questionnaire

  1. Do you make yourself Sick because you feel uncomfortably full?
  2. Do you worry that you have lost Control over how much you eat?
  3. Have you recently lost more than One stone (14 lb) in a 3-month period?
  4. Do you believe yourself to be Fat when others say you are too thin?
  5. Would you say that Food dominates your life?
"]],"psychotherapy--behavioral-therapy":[[85571,"Parent management training","

Parent management training

Focus

Parent interventions

Antecedents

(communication
leading to
wanted/unwanted
behaviors)

  • Use (promote wanted behavior):
    • clear instructions
    • calm tones & supportive gestures
    • alternative choices
  • Avoid (promote unwanted behavior):
    • nagging
    • threats
    • harsh comments
    • physical intimidation

Behaviors

(practicing effective
parent-child
interactions)

  • Shaping:
    • small behavioral goals adding to bigger changes
  • Role-play wanted behaviors:
    • artificial situations first
    • build to realistic scenarios

Consequences

(for wanted/
unwanted
behaviors)

  • Reinforce wanted behaviors:
    • praise (verbal, nonverbal)
    • token/point system rewards
  • Manage unwanted behaviors:
    • extinction (eg, ignore, walk away)
    • mild punishment (eg, privilege loss)
"]],"psychiatric-emergencies--acute-dystonia":[[92154,"Medication-induced dystonia","

Medication-induced dystonia

Precipitating medications
(dopamine antagonists)

  • Antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol)
  • Antiemetics (eg, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)

Clinical features

  • Onset minutes to 24 hours after starting medication
  • Sudden, sustained contraction of muscles, most often impacting the neck, mouth, tongue, & extraocular muscles
  • Painful, distressing, often with tachycardia &/or hypertension
  • Preserved mental status
  • ± Other extrapyramidal effects (eg, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia)

Treatment

  • Cessation (or ↓ dose) of offending medication (if possible)
  • Anticholinergics (eg, diphenhydramine, benztropine)
"]],"grief":[[100406,"Depression vs grief","

Depression vs grief

Major depressive disorder

Grief

Prolonged grief disorder

Emotions

  • Generalized & persistent sadness or low mood
  • Anhedonia
  • Feeling worthless
  • Intermittent sadness or low mood
  • Happiness & humor possible
  • Intense yearning/longing
  • Loneliness/numbness

Thought content

  • Pervasive pessimism
  • Self-loathing
  • Suicidal thoughts focused on feelings of hopelessness & worthlessness
  • Self-esteem intact
  • Active suicidality uncommon
  • Preoccupation with thoughts of deceased
  • Difficulty accepting or disbelief
  • Feeling lost (identity disrupted)
  • Suicidal thoughts focused on reuniting with the deceased

Behavior

  • Functional decline
  • Changes in appetite, sleep & energy
  • Less functional decline
  • Functional decline
  • ± Changes in appetite, sleep & energy

Duration

  • ≥2 weeks
  • Persistent
  • Weeks to months
  • Intermittent
  • ≥12 months
  • Persistent
"]],"factitious-disorders--factitious-disorder-imposed-on-another":[[107525,"Factitious disorder (imposed on another)","

Factitious disorder (imposed on another)

Definition

  • Intentional falsification of symptoms or induction of illness in another person (eg, child, older person)

Characteristics of caregiver (offender)

  • Motivated by desire to assume caregiver role (no external gain)
  • Female > male (95% are female, often primary caretaker)

Clinical presentation

  • Frequent visits
  • History is incongruent with clinical findings
  • Unexplained illness persists despite comprehensive evaluation
  • Caregiver seeks multiple opinions (eg, doctor shopping)
  • Symptoms improve when caregiver is absent

Intervention

  • Seek information from other observers (eg, teacher, other family members)
  • Review previous medical records from all available sources
  • Create a multidisciplinary team of specialists for case analysis
  • Involve child/adult protective services
"]]};

// Tables under First Aid headings (owner's tables, made by tools/table_build.py — edit tools/table_map.py and re-run). (window.FA_TABLES = window.FA_TABLES || {})["gen"] = {"lysosomal-storage-diseases--gaucher-disease":[[31630,"Gaucher disease","

Gaucher disease

Etiology

  • Autosomal recessive, ↑ prevalence in Ashkenazi Jews
  • Glucocerebrosidase deficiency → glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages

Clinical
features

  • Can present at any age
  • Visceral organ involvement: splenomegaly (severe), hepatomegaly
  • Bone/bone marrow infiltration
    • Anemia, thrombocytopenia
    • Bone pain
  • Failure to thrive, delayed puberty

Management

  • Enzyme replacement
"]],"osteogenesis-imperfecta":[[31858,"Type II osteogenesis imperfecta","

Type II osteogenesis imperfecta

Pathophysiology

  • Type I collagen defect
  • Most types are autosomal dominant
  • Type II OI can be sporadic (de novo mutation)

Ultrasonography
findings

  • Multiple fractures
  • Short femur
  • Hypoplastic thoracic cavity
  • Fetal growth restriction
  • Intrauterine demise

Prognosis

  • Lethal

OI = osteogenesis imperfecta.

"], [40247,"Osteogenesis imperfecta","

Osteogenesis imperfecta

Pathogenesis

  • >90% autosomal dominant
  • Type I collagen gene (COL1A1) defect

Clinical features

  • Mild to moderate
    • Frequent fractures
    • Blue sclera
    • Conductive hearing loss
    • Short to normal stature
    • Dentinogenesis imperfecta
    • Joint hypermobility
  • Lethal (type II)
    • In utero and/or neonatal fractures
    • Pulmonary failure
"]],"consent-for-minors":[[31862,"Exceptions to informed consent by parent/guardian in minors","

Exceptions to informed consent by parent/guardian in minors

Emergency care

  • Condition in which treatment delay
    can cause serious impairment or death 

Emancipated minor
(adolescents)

  • Parent
  • Married
  • Military service
  • Financially independent
  • High school graduate
  • Homeless

Specific medical care
(adolescents)

  • Sexually transmitted infection
  • Substance use disorder (most states)
  • Pregnancy care (most states)
  • Contraception
"]],"chemoprophylaxis-and-post-exposure-prophylaxis":[[31970,"Occupational HIV postexposure prophylaxis","

Occupational HIV postexposure prophylaxis

High-risk contact

(prophylaxis recommended)

Exposure of:

  • Mucous membrane, nonintact skin, or percutaneous exposure

Exposure to:

  • Blood, semen, vaginal secretions, or any body fluid with visible blood (uncertain risk: cerebrospinal fluid, pleural/pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, peritoneal fluid, amniotic fluid)

Low-risk contact

(prophylaxis not recommended)

Exposure to:

  • Urine, feces, nasal secretions, saliva, sweat, tears (with no visible blood)

Timing

  • Initiate urgently, preferably in the first few hours
  • Continue for 4 weeks

Regimen

Treatment with ≥3-drug regimen recommended:

  • Two nucleotide/nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (eg, tenofovir, emtricitabine)

PLUS:

  • Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (eg, raltegravir), protease inhibitor, or nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor
"], [32666,"Postexposure prophylaxis for sexual assault","

Postexposure prophylaxis for sexual assault

Infection

Medication

Chlamydia

 Doxycycline

Gonorrhea

 Ceftriaxone

Trichomonas vaginalis

Metronidazole

HIV

Multidrug regimen (eg, tenofovir-emtricitabine with raltegravir)

Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B vaccine ± hepatitis B immunoglobulin

"], [51744,"Pertussis postexposure prophylaxis","

Pertussis postexposure prophylaxis

Indications (regardless of vaccination history)

  • Close contact (eg, household members, direct contact with secretions) with symptomatic patient
  • High-risk patients, even with limited exposure (eg, pregnant, infant, immunodeficient)

Treatment

  • Age <1 month: azithromycin
  • Age ≥1 month: azithromycin, clarithromycin, or erythromycin
"], [92571,"Rabies prophylaxis guidelines","

Rabies prophylaxis guidelines

Status

Recommendation

Preexposure prophylaxis

  • Rabies vaccine (4 doses)

Postexposure prophylaxis, previously unvaccinated

  • Rabies vaccine (4 doses, abridged schedule)

AND

  • Rabies immunoglobulin

Postexposure prophylaxis, previously vaccinated

  • Rabies vaccine (2 doses)
"]],"sympathomimetics--cocaine":[[32018,"Cardiovascular effects of cocaine intoxication","

Cardiovascular effects of cocaine intoxication

Physiologic effects

  • Hypertension & tachycardia
  • Coronary vasoconstriction
  • ↑ Platelet activity & thrombus formation

Clinical manifestations

  • Myocardial ischemia or infarction
  • Aortic dissection
  • Neurologic ischemia or stroke

Treatment

  • Benzodiazepines & nitroglycerin
  • β blockers should be avoided
  • CCBs for persistent chest pain
  • Phentolamine for persistent hypertension
  • ± PCI for myocardial infarction

CCBs = calcium channel blockers; PCI = percutaneous coronary intervention.

"]],"paraneoplastic-syndromes--hypercalcemia":[[32505,"Hypercalcemia of malignancy","

Hypercalcemia of malignancy

Cause

Tumor type

Mechanism

Diagnostic

PTHrP*

  • Squamous cell
  • Kidney & bladder
  • Breast & ovarian
  • PTH mimic
  • ↓ PTH
  • ↑ PTHrP

Bone metastases

  • Breast
  • Multiple myeloma
  • ↑ Osteolysis
  • ↓ PTH & PTHrP
  • ↓ Vitamin D

1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D

  • Lymphoma
  • ↑ Calcium absorption
  • ↓ PTH
  • ↑ Vitamin D

*PTHrP causes ~80% of malignancy-associated hypercalcemia.

PTH = parathyroid hormone; PTHrP = PTH-related protein.

"]],"disorders-of-imprinting":[[32781,"Imprinting disorders","
Imprinting disorders

Prader-Willi syndrome

Angelman syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Absent expression of paternally inherited alleles on chromosome 15
  • Corresponding maternal alleles are physiologically imprinted/silenced
  • Absent expression of maternally inherited alleles on chromosome 15
  • Corresponding paternal alleles are physiologically imprinted/silenced

Common causes

  • Paternal microdeletion
  • Maternal uniparental disomy
  • Maternal microdeletion
  • Paternal uniparental disomy
  • Maternal gene mutation

Clinical features

  • Neonatal hypotonia
  • Hyperphagia/obesity
  • Hypogonadism
  • Developmental delay & intellectual disability (mild)
  • Ataxia, seizures
  • Inappropriate laughter/smiling
  • Developmental delay & intellectual disability (severe)
"], [80543,"Prader-Willi syndrome","

Prader-Willi syndrome

Clinical features

  • Hypotonia
  • Weak suck/feeding problems in infancy
  • Hyperphagia/obesity
  • Short stature
  • Hypogonadism
  • Intellectual disability
  • Dysmorphic facies
    • Narrow forehead
    • Almond-shaped eyes
    • Downturned mouth

Diagnosis

  • Loss of expression on paternal chromosome 15 (q11-q13)

Complications

  • Sleep apnea (70%)
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus (25%)
  • Gastric distension/rupture
  • Death by choking (8%)
"]],"quantifying-risk":[[34642,"Common measures of therapeutic efficacy","

Common measures of therapeutic efficacy

Term

Definition

Calculation

Absolute risk reduction (ARR)

Percentage indicating the actual difference in event rate between control & treatment groups

ARR = control rate – treatment rate

Relative risk reduction (RRR)

Percentage indicating relative reduction in the treatment event rate compared to the control group

RRR = ARR / control rate

Relative risk (RR)

Ratio of the probability of an event occurring in the treatment group compared to the control group

RR = treatment rate / control rate

Number needed to treat (NNT)

Number of individuals who need to be treated to prevent a negative outcome in 1 patient

NNT = 1 / ARR

"]],"decision-making-capacity":[[34653,"Assessment of decision-making capacity","

 Assessment of decision-making capacity

Criterion

Patient task

Communicates a choice

Patient able to clearly indicate preferred treatment option

Understands information provided

Patient understands condition & treatment options

Appreciates consequences

Patient acknowledges having condition & likely consequences of treatment options, including no treatment

Rationale given for decision

Patient is able to weigh risks & benefits & offer reasons for decision

"]],"ehlers-danlos-syndrome":[[34661,"Clinical features of Ehlers-Danlos & Marfan syndromes","

Clinical features of Ehlers-Danlos & Marfan syndromes

Classic Ehlers-Danlos

Marfan

Skin

  • Transparent & hyperextensible
  • Easy bruising, poor healing
  • Velvety with atrophy & scarring
  • No features other than striae

Musculoskeletal

  • Joint hypermobility
  • Pectus excavatum
  • Scoliosis
  • High, arched palate
  • Joint hypermobility
  • Pectus excavatum or carinatum
  • Scoliosis
  • Tall with long extremities

Cardiac

  • Mitral valve prolapse
  • Progressive aortic root dilation
  • Mitral valve prolapse

Other

  • Abdominal & inguinal hernias
  • Uterine prolapse
  • Lens & retinal detachment
  • Spontaneous pneumothorax

Genetics

  • COL5A1 & COL5A2 mutation
  • Autosomal dominant
  • FBN1 mutation
  • Autosomal dominant
"]],"motivational-interviewing":[[34759,"Motivational interviewing","

Motivational interviewing

Indications

  • Substance use disorders
  • Other behaviors in patients who are not ready to change

Principles

  • Acknowledge resistance to change
  • Address discrepancies between behavior & long-term goals
  • Enhance motivation to change
  • Nonjudgmental

Technique (OARS)

  • Ask Open-ended questions (encourage further discussion)
  • Give Affirmations
  • Reflect & Summarize main points
"], [69318,"Motivational interviewing","

Motivational interviewing

Indications

  • Substance use disorders
  • Other behaviors in patients who are not ready to change

Principles

  • Acknowledge resistance to change
  • Address discrepancies between behavior & long-term goals
  • Enhance motivation to change (support self-efficacy)
  • Remain nonjudgmental

Technique
(OARS)

  • Ask Open-ended questions (encourage further discussion)
  • Give Affirmations
  • Reflect & Summarize main points
"]],"glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase-deficiency":[[34899,"Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency","

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

Epidemiology

  • Hemolytic anemia due to oxidative stress (infection, sulfa drugs, fava beans)
  • X-linked: Asian, African, or Middle Eastern descent

Manifestations

  • Pallor & fatigue
  • Dark urine, jaundice & icterus
  • Abdominal/back pain

Laboratory
findings

  • Hemolysis: ↓ hemoglobin, ↓ haptoglobin,
    ↑ bilirubin & LDH, ↑ reticulocytes
  • Peripheral smear: bite cells & Heinz bodies
  • Negative Coombs test
  • ↓ G6PD activity level (may be normal during attack)

Management

  • Remove or treat responsible agent/condition
  • Provide supportive care

G6PD = glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase.

"]],"specific-toxicity-treatments--acetaminophen":[[35769,"Acute acetaminophen toxicity","

Acute acetaminophen toxicity

Pathophysiology

  • Depletion of intrahepatic glutathione → accumulation of NAPQI (toxic metabolite of acetaminophen)

Clinical features
(time from ingestion)

  • ≤24 hr
    • Asymptomatic or nonspecific symptoms (eg, nausea, vomiting, fatigue)
  • 24-72 hr
    •  ↑ AST, ALT
  • 72-96 hr
    • AST/ALT levels peak (sometimes >10,000 U/L)
    • Severe cases:  ↑ PT/PTT, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, ↑ bilirubin, acute kidney injury
  • 4-14 days
    • Recovery

Diagnosis

  • Serum acetaminophen level (4-24 hr)
  • Liver function tests, BUN/creatinine, electrolytes

Treatment

  • Activated charcoal (if <4 hr)
  • N-acetylcysteine

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; BUN = blood urea nitrogen; NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine.

"]],"causes-of-medical-errors":[[36888,"Alert fatigue","

Alert fatigue

Definition

  • Health care workers become desensitized to all clinical alarms & alerts, including those of clinical significance 

Causes

  • Exposure to high frequency of alarms
  • Exposure to numerous false alarms (alarms of clinical insignificance)

Examples

  • Alerts (eg, drug-drug interactions) in electronic medical records
  • Automated devices (eg, infusion pumps, telemetry devices)
  • Patient sensors (eg, fall-prevention sensors) 

Prevention strategies

  • Minimize environmental distractions
  • Reduce alarm frequency & false alarm likelihood
  • Examples: decrease sensitivity of fall-prevention sensor to prevent minor patient movement from triggering alarm; minimize low-risk alerts in clinical decision support systems
"], [60666,"Common cognitive errors in medicine","

Common cognitive errors in medicine

Type of bias

Definition

Example

Anchoring

  • Fixating on initial impressions to make a diagnosis
  • Related to confirmation bias & premature closure
  • Burning throat pain diagnosed as acid reflux despite weight loss
  • Correct diagnosis is lung malignancy

Availability

  • Allowing recently seen or memorable (high-stakes) cases to sway diagnosis
  • Dyspnea diagnosed as influenza during peak influenza season
  • Correct diagnosis is pulmonary embolism

Confirmation

  • Emphasizing evidence that supports presumed diagnosis & overlooking information that supports other diagnoses
  • Related to anchoring bias
  • Burning throat pain after eating spicy food diagnosed as acid reflux despite weight loss
  • Correct diagnosis is malignancy

Framing

  • Allowing diagnostic approach to be influenced by context & presentation of information
  • Abdominal pain diagnosed as opioid withdrawal in patient described as drug seeking
  • Correct diagnosis is bowel obstruction
"], [61797,"Features of effective teams","

Features of effective teams* in health care

Safety culture

  • Resource commitment to safety

Collaboration

  • Shared understanding & prioritization of goals
  • Distinct roles that avoid a steep hierarchy

Psychologic safety

  • Asking questions & voicing concerns encouraged
  • Avoiding blame or retaliation

Responsiveness

  • Feedback respected & promptly acted on

Situational awareness

  • Persistent mindfulness & safety vigilance
  • Cross-checking of each other's actions

Transparency

  • Prompt disclosure of errors & safety information

*Poor teamwork is a leading root cause of sentinel events; improved communication reduces medical errors & improves patient/clinical outcomes.

"], [72884,"Patient safety procedures in the surgical setting","

Patient safety procedures in the surgical setting

Preoperative
verification

  • Patient identity, operative site, type of operation, & side (verified/documented by ≥2 providers)
  • Performed in preoperative holding area
  • Should involve patient (or surrogate) and 2 patient identifiers

Site marking

  • Mark (eg, "YES" + initials) on each operative site (do not mark nonoperative sites)
  • Clearly mark using permanent marker

Surgical
time-out

  • Occurs immediately prior to skin incision
  • Repeat verification of patient identity, operative site & side
  • Entire surgical team participates & all concerns addressed
"], [126874,"Contributing factors for medical errors","

Contributing factors for medical errors

Category

Factors

Examples

Patient

  • Clinical condition
  • Language
  • Cultural or religious beliefs
  • Social support
  • Patient & care provider do not speak the same language.
  • Opposition to blood products prevents transfusion.

Staff

  • Fatigue
  • Language
  • Stress
  • Mental impairment
  • Physician begins task at end of 24-hr call.
  • Nurse is taking opioids for pain when assisting with procedure.

Equipment

  • Unavailability
  • Disrepair
  • Ultrasonographic machine is not available on the floor for central line placement.

Work environment

  • Staffing workloads
  • Error reporting policy & practice
  • Physical design of patient care area

"]],"necrosis":[[46219,"Patterns of tissue necrosis","

Patterns of tissue necrosis

Type

Etiology

Morphology

Liquefactive necrosis

  • Severe bacterial infections (eg, gangrene)
  • CNS infarcts
  • Necrotic tissue is digested by hydrolytic enzymes into a viscous fluid:
    • Infected abscess fluid is creamy yellow due to dead leukocytes (pus)
    • Brain infarcts resolve into CSF-filled spaces

Fibrinoid necrosis

  • Hypertension
  • Vasculitis
  • Damaged vessels leak fibrin/immune complexes
  • Eosinophilic layer of proteinaceous material in vessel walls

Fat necrosis

  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Trauma (subcutaneous adipose tissue)
  • Free fatty acids released by active enzymes (eg, lipases) or mechanical damage
  • Fatty acids combine with calcium, forming chalky-white deposits (saponification)

Caseous necrosis

  • Mycobacterial infections
  • Fungal infections (eg, Histoplasma, Cryptococcus, Coccidioides)
  • Friable, cheeselike material composed of cell fragments & amorphous proteinaceous debris
  • Surrounded by epithelioid macrophages & giant cells (granuloma)

Coagulative necrosis

  • Irreversible ischemic injury outside CNS
  • Tissue architecture is preserved due to denaturation of lytic enzymes:
    • Cells are anucleate with eosinophilic cytoplasm
    • Leukocytes eventually infiltrate & digest necrotic tissue

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid.

"], [62155,"Human factors engineering strategies","

Human factors engineering strategies

Reliability

Strategy

Description & examples

Highest

Forcing functions

  • Hard stops in design or process to eliminate risk for incorrect use
  • Example: each anesthesia gas fits only one compatible socket & is not interchangeable

Computerized automation

  • Automated processes to remove human effort & variations that cause error
  • Example: automated vital signs monitoring

Environment & physical layout

  • Workspace design to facilitate correct action & minimize error
  • Example: look-alike drugs stocked in different locations

High

Standardization & simplification

  • Uniform processes to minimize variation, complexity & learning curve
  • Example: every hospital unit follows the same process for heparin administration

Human-machine redundancy

  • Repetitive step to confirm correct action in an error-prone process
  • Example: barcode scanning of medications in addition to visual inspection

Medium

Reminders, alerts & double-checks

  • Processes prompting providers to check actions to reduce errors
  • Examples: drug-drug interaction alerts; time-out before procedures

HFE seeks to reduce error risk by designing systems based on expected human behaviors.  Less reliable HFE strategies include training, policy changes & education.

HFE = human factors engineering.

"], [86414,"Classification of medical errors","

Classification of medical errors

Preventable adverse event

  • Event that results from human or systems error
  • Example: wrong diagnosis, wrong drug selection

Negligent adverse event

  • Preventable event caused by clear deviation from standard of care
  • Example: drug administered to patient with known allergy 

Nonpreventable adverse event

  • Unforeseen event not preventable by following established standards of care
  • Example: rare adverse effect of appropriately administered drug

Sentinel event

  • Serious preventable error causing irreversible patient harm or death
  • Example: wrong-site surgery, wrong-patient error

Near-miss event

  • Preventable event that is intercepted before harm reaches patient
  • Example: nurse catches a miscalculated dose of medication before it is administered to the patient

"], [119952,"Common patterns of dyslipidemias & their causes","

Common patterns of dyslipidemias & their causes

High LDL (eg, >100-130 mg/dL)

  • ↑ LDL formation (eg, excess VLDL or Apo-B hepatic synthesis)
  • ↓ LDL clearance (eg, ↓ LDL-R expression, ↑ PCSK9, ↓ LDL-R binding caused by defective Apo B)

High TGs (eg, >150 mg/dL)

  • ↑ Hepatic VLDL synthesis
  • ↓ Chylomicron or VLDL clearance (eg, defective Apo E)
  • ↓ HDL activity (eg, ↑ CETP activity)
  • ↓ LPL activity (eg, defective Apo C-II → ↓ TG lipolysis)
  • Worsened by metabolic inflammation (eg, insulin resistance)

Low HDL (eg, <40-50 mg/dL)

  • Most commonly a sequela of ↑ LDL & TG
  • Isolated ↓ HDL can occur if ↓ synthesis (eg, defective Apo A-1)

Apo A-1 = apolipoprotein A-1; Apo B = apolipoprotein B; Apo C-II = apolipoprotein C-II; Apo E = apolipoprotein E; CETP = cholesteryl ester transfer protein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9; TG = triglyceride.

"]],"phenylketonuria":[[80868,"Phenylketonuria","

Phenylketonuria

Pathophysiology

  • Autosomal recessive mutation in gene for phenylalanine hydroxylase
  • Impaired metabolism of phenylalanine to tyrosine → ↑ phenylalanine causes neurologic injury

Clinical features

  • Neurologic: microcephaly, developmental delay, seizures, severe intellectual disability
  • Nonneurologic: musty body odor, hypopigmentation (eg, skin, hair, eyes), eczema

Diagnosis

  • ↑ Phenylalanine levels:
    • Universal newborn screening
    • Serum amino acid analysis

Treatment

  • Phenylalanine-restricted diet (ie, avoidance of protein-rich foods)
  • Dietary/supplemental tyrosine

Prognosis

  • Preventable disease manifestations with early treatment
  • Delayed diagnosis/treatment → irreversible neurologic injury

"]],"drug-effect-modifications":[[82144,"Mechanisms of drug tolerance","

Mechanisms of drug tolerance

Tolerance

Mechanism

Example

Acquired pharmacokinetic

  • ADME: ↓ Absorption, ↑ Distribution, or
    ↑ Metabolism & Excretion (eg, enzyme induction)
  • ↓ Plasma drug concentration relative to naïve state
  • Rifampin (CYP3A4 inducer) accelerates metabolism of warfarin
  • Carbamazepine induces its own metabolism after repeated dosing

Acquired pharmacodynamic

  • ↓ Cellular response to drug (eg, receptor downregulation)
  • Unchanged plasma drug concentration relative to naïve state
  • Chronic opioid use: ↓ expression & responsivity of μ receptor system
  • Frequent albuterol rescue inhaler:
    ↓ expression of airway β2 receptors

Innate

  • Genetic (eg, polymorphisms) & epigenetic (eg, DNA methylation) differences
  • Leads to pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic tolerance
  • Tolerance apparent from first dose
  • Slow metabolizer CYP2C19 allele:
    ↓ clopidogrel activation
    (↓ antiplatelet effect)
  • Slow metabolizer CYP2D6 allele:
    ↓ codeine conversion to morphine
    (↓ analgesic effect)

Behavioral (functional)

  • Ability to compensate for drug-induced impairment through learning & practice
  • Maintaining appearance & mannerisms to appear nonintoxicated at work

Withdrawal syndrome

  • Rebound hypertension, sweating, anxiety & tremors
    • Occurs with abrupt discontinuation
    • Avoid by tapering dose gradually

Cardiac effects

  • ↓ HR & BP

"]],"lipoprotein-functions":[[119949,"Lipoproteins","

Lipoproteins

Structure & synthesis

Function & clearance

VLDL

  • Formed in liver
  • Contains ↑ TGs, ↓ cholesterol
  • Transports TGs
  • Becomes IDL as TG content reduces
  • Requires Apo C-II (LPL co-factor) & ApoE

LDL

  • Formed when IDL is depleted of TGs; also formed in liver
  • Contains ↑ cholesterol, ↓ TG
  • Transports cholesterol
  • Mainly cleared by liver; can be taken up by other tissues
  • Requires LDL-R & apo-B100

HDL

  • Formed in intestine & liver
  • Begins as nascent HDL (↓ TG & ↓ cholesterol); mature HDL has more cholesterol
  • Scavenges excess cholesterol & returns to liver
  • Supports function & clearance of other lipoproteins
  • Requires Apo A-I

Chylomicron

  • Formed in intestines from dietary lipids; ↑↑ TGs & ↓ cholesterol
  • Transports TGs from diet
  • Becomes chylomicron remnants when TG content depleted
  • Requires Apo B-48, ApoE & Apo C-II (LPL cofactor)

Apo B-48 = apolipoprotein B-48; Apo B-100 = apolipoprotein B-100; Apo C-II = apolipoprotein C-II; ApoE = apolipoprotein E; IDL = intermediate-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; TG = triglyceride.

"]],"key-enzymes-in-lipid-transport":[[119951,"Key enzymes involved in cholesterol transport & synthesis","

Key enzymes involved in cholesterol transport & synthesis

HMG-CoA reductase

  • Rate-limiting step in endogenous cholesterol production
  • ↑ Cholesterol synthesis

PCSK9

  • Binds to & promotes degradation of LDL-R
  • ↓ LDL-R & ↑ cholesterol levels

LPL

  • Lipolyzes TGs within lipoproteins into FFAs for cellular uptake → catabolizes VLDL & chylomicrons into remnants
  • ↓ Level of FFAs & TG in the blood

CETP

  • Transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to LDL/VLDL
  • ↑ TG content of HDL → ↓ quality & ↓ levels of HDL

LCAT

  • Esterifies free cholesterol for transport by HDL
  • ↑ Reverse transport of cholesterol to liver

CETP = cholesteryl ester transfer protein; FFA = free fatty acid; LCAT = lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9; TG = triglyceride.

"]],"protein-energy-malnutrition":[[120082,"Protein-energy malnutrition","

Protein-energy malnutrition

Kwashiorkor
(with edema)

Marasmus
(without edema)

Pathophysiology

Malnutrition due to protein deficiency

  • ↓ Oncotic pressure (edema, ascites)
  • ↓ Carrier lipoproteins (fatty liver)
  • ↓ Immunoglobulins (infections)

Malnutrition due to total calorie deficiency (protein, carbohydrates, fats)

  • ↓ Protein & fat stores (wasting)

Presentation

  • Ascites, edema
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Flaky dermatitis (eg, ↓ keratin)
  • No ascites or edema
  • Emaciation (loose, hanging skin)
  • Disproportionate head size

Management

  • Refeeding (eg, RUTF)
  • Complications:
    • Bacterial infection (eg, empiric antibiotics)
    • Dehydration (eg, ORS)
    • Hypothermia (eg, warm blankets)

Prognosis

Worse prognosis due to higher risk for infection, cardiac failure & refeeding syndrome (eg, ↓ PO4–, ↓ K+, ↓ Mg2+)

Better (but still guarded) prognosis

ORS = oral rehydration solution; RUTF = ready-to-use therapeutic food (eg, provides complete nutrition).

Fabry disease

Pathophysiology

  • X-linked recessive
  • α-galactosidase A deficiency results in accumulation of globotriaosylceramide

Clinical features

  • Neuropathic pain
  • Angiokeratomas
  • Telangiectasias
  • Glomerular disease (eg, proteinuria)
  • Cerebrovascular disease (eg, TIA, stroke)
  • Cardiac disease (eg, left ventricular hypertrophy)

"]],"normal-aging--special-senses":[[129375,"Normal age-related ocular changes","

Normal age-related ocular changes

Structure

Key changes

Clinical feature

Cornea

  • Flattening of curvature
  • Decreased endothelial cell density
  • Reduced corneal sensitivity
  • Slight reduction in refractive power
  • Clarity maintained
  • Mild risk of dry eye

Lens

  • Lens fibers & proteins accumulate → thicker, less flexible
  • Yellowing or brunescence from pigment deposition & oxidative damage
  • Increased light scatter
  • Presbyopia (loss of near focus)
  • Increase in refractive power
  • Reduced blue light perception
  • Glare, especially at night

Vitreous humor

  • Liquefaction (synchysis)
  • Posterior vitreous detachment common
  • Floaters, flashes of light
  • Predisposition to retinal tears or detachment

Retina

  • Decline in rod photoreceptors (faster than in cones)
  • Lipofuscin accumulation in RPE
  • Slower dark adaptation
  • Reduced night & peripheral vision
  • Slower adjustment to dim light

RPE = retinal pigment epithelium.
